questions.ideal: Run in a pipeline using the official Playwright Docker image, shard the suite across machines, define projects for Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, publish HTML or Allure and JUnit reports, upload traces and videos, and use tags to run smoke on every commit and the full suite nightly.

questions.q: How do you set up a new Playwright project and what does the config file control?
questions.ideal: Running npm init playwright installs the test runner, browsers and an example. The playwright.config file controls testDir, timeout and retries, workers, the reporter such as HTML report, and a use block with baseURL, headless and trace settings. Projects define which browsers or devices to run, like Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

questions.q: Explain browser, browser context and page in Playwright.
questions.ideal: A browser is a launched Chromium, Firefox or WebKit instance. A browser context is like an isolated incognito profile with its own cookies and local storage, and it is lightweight and fast to create. A page is a single tab inside a context. Playwright gives every test a fresh context, so tests stay isolated.

questions.q: What are web first assertions in Playwright and how are they different from normal assertions?
questions.ideal: Web first assertions like expect locator toBeVisible, toHaveText or page toHaveURL automatically retry until the condition passes or the expect timeout expires. A normal assertion checks a value once, so it can fail if the page is still updating. You must await them, and they make tests more stable and less flaky.

questions.q: What is Playwright codegen and when would you use it?
questions.ideal: Codegen, run with npx playwright codegen, opens a browser and records your actions as test code with recommended locators. It is great for quickly finding a reliable locator through the inspector or creating a starting point. The generated code should be refactored into page objects and proper assertions before going into the suite.

questions.q: How do you run Playwright tests headed, for one browser, or only matching tests from the command line?
questions.ideal: Use npx playwright test to run everything headless. Add headed to see the browser, project equals chromium to run one browser, and grep with a pattern to filter by test title or tag. You can pass a specific file name or line. The ui mode gives a watch and time travel view, and debug opens the inspector.

questions.q: Which browsers and languages does Playwright support?
questions.ideal: Playwright supports Chromium, which covers Chrome and Edge, Firefox, and WebKit, the engine behind Safari, on Windows, Linux and macOS. Bindings exist for JavaScript and TypeScript with the built in test runner, plus Python, Java and dotnet C sharp. The Node test runner has the richest features like fixtures, projects and sharding.

questions.q: How do you capture screenshots and videos in Playwright tests?
questions.ideal: You can call page screenshot with fullPage for a full page capture, or locator screenshot for one element. In the config use block, set screenshot to only on failure and video to retain on failure, so artifacts are kept just for failing tests. They are attached to the HTML report for debugging.

questions.q: What are test only, skip, fixme and describe used for in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Test describe groups related tests. Test only runs just that test while debugging, and should never be committed. Test skip skips a test, optionally on a condition such as a browser. Fixme marks a known broken test so it is skipped. Test slow triples the timeout, and tags or annotations help filter tests in reports.

questions.q: How do you debug a failing Playwright test using the trace viewer?
questions.ideal: Enable trace on first retry or retain on failure in the config. The trace zip opens with npx playwright show trace or from the HTML report. It shows a timeline of actions with before and after DOM snapshots, the network tab, console logs and source, so you can see exactly what the page looked like when a step failed in CI.

questions.q: How do you work with iframes in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Playwright uses page frameLocator with a selector for the iframe, then chains normal locators inside it, so there is no switching like Selenium. Nested frames are handled by chaining frameLocator again. A locator contentFrame can also convert an iframe element to a frame locator. Auto waiting still applies inside frames.

questions.q: How do you handle a link that opens a new tab or popup in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Start waiting before the click: create a promise with context waitForEvent page, or page waitForEvent popup, then click the link and await the promise to get the new page. Then wait for its load state and run assertions on it. Both pages stay usable, so there is no switching, and you can close the popup after.

questions.q: How do you handle JavaScript alerts, confirms and prompts in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Playwright auto dismisses dialogs by default. To handle them, register a listener with page on dialog before the action, read the dialog message and type, then call accept, optionally with prompt text, or dismiss. Register the listener first, otherwise the alert, confirm or prompt is dismissed before you can check it.

questions.q: How do you test file upload and file download in Playwright?
questions.ideal: For upload, call locator setInputFiles with a file path or buffer, or handle the filechooser event when there is no input element. For download, start waitForEvent download before the click, then use saveAs or path to store it and check suggested filename and contents to verify the file.

questions.q: How do retries and timeouts work in Playwright, and what are the risks of retries?
questions.ideal: Retries rerun a failed test, and Playwright marks tests that pass on retry as flaky in the report. The test timeout limits the whole test, expect timeout limits assertions, and action or navigation timeout limits each step. The risk is that retries hide real problems, so flaky tests must be tracked and fixed at the root cause.

questions.q: What are soft assertions and expect poll in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Expect soft records a failure but lets the test continue, so you collect all failures on a page in one run. Expect poll repeatedly calls a custom async function, such as an API check, until the value matches. Expect toPass retries a block of code until it passes. Both avoid hard coded sleeps.

questions.q: How do you write data driven or parameterized tests in Playwright?
questions.ideal: You loop over a data array, often loaded from a JSON or CSV file, and declare a test for each row with a unique title so reports stay clear. For parameters that change the whole run, like user role or locale, use fixture options and set them per project in the config.

questions.q: How do you use Playwright for API testing and combine it with UI tests?
questions.ideal: The request fixture gives an APIRequestContext to send get and post calls and assert status and JSON response. It shares cookies with the browser context, so you can log in through the API or use storage state. A common pattern is creating test data through the API for setup, then verifying in the UI, which is faster and more stable.

questions.q: How does visual regression testing work in Playwright and how do you avoid false failures?
questions.ideal: Expect toHaveScreenshot compares a page or element against a stored baseline snapshot. To avoid false failures, mask dynamic content like dates, disable animations, set a threshold or maxDiffPixels, and generate baselines in the same environment, usually a Docker image, because fonts differ by OS. Run update snapshots only after reviewing intended changes.

questions.q: How do you create custom fixtures in Playwright, and what is the difference between test and worker scope?
questions.ideal: Use test extend to define a fixture with setup code, call use to hand the value to the test, then run teardown after. Test scoped fixtures run per test, like a logged in page or page objects injected into tests. Worker scoped fixtures run once per worker, for expensive things like a database connection or account. Fixtures can depend on other fixtures.

questions.q: How do you handle dynamic lists, shadow DOM and duplicate elements with Playwright locators?
questions.ideal: Playwright locators are strict, so duplicates throw an error. I narrow them with chaining, filter with hasText or has, or getByRole with a name. Nth, first and last are a last resort. Shadow DOM is pierced automatically by CSS locators. For unstable markup, ask developers to add data-testid and use getByTestId.

questions.q: How would you test a chat feature where two users interact at the same time?
questions.ideal: I create two browser contexts in the same test with browser newContext, each logged in as a different user, often via separate storage state files. Each context has its own page, so user A sends a message and I assert it appears on user B page in real time, then reply and assert both sides. Close both contexts at the end.

questions.q: What are global setup, teardown and project dependencies in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Global setup runs once before all tests, for example to seed a database or log in and save storage state. The newer approach is a setup project and project dependencies, where test projects depend on the setup project, so it appears in the report with trace support. A teardown project cleans up afterwards.

questions.q: What is Playwright component testing and when would you use it?
questions.ideal: Component testing mounts a single React, Vue or Svelte component in a real browser using the mount fixture, in isolation from the full app. You pass props, trigger events and assert callbacks and rendering. It gives faster feedback than end to end tests and suits complex widgets, while E2E tests still cover full user journeys.

questions.q: How do you emulate mobile devices, geolocation and permissions in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Playwright devices give descriptors like iPhone with viewport, user agent and hasTouch, used in a project or new context. Context options also set geolocation, grant permissions, locale and timezone. This tests responsive and location based behaviour quickly, though it is emulation, so real device checks are still needed for critical mobile flows.

questions.q: Your company wants to migrate a large Selenium suite to Playwright. How would you plan it?
questions.ideal: Start with a pilot or proof of concept on a few critical flows and compare stability and execution time metrics. Do not convert line by line, rewrite using Playwright patterns like fixtures, auto waiting and web first assertions. Migrate by priority, keep both suites in a parallel run until coverage matches, and plan training for the team.

questions.q: How do you keep test data isolated when Playwright runs tests in many parallel workers?
questions.ideal: Shared state between parallel workers causes conflicts. Each test creates unique data through API setup, using random or timestamped names. For pre created accounts, use testInfo workerIndex or parallelIndex to give each worker its own user. Fixtures handle cleanup in teardown, and tests never depend on another test order.

questions.q: How do you run Playwright reliably inside Docker and a CI pipeline?
questions.ideal: Use the official Playwright Docker image whose version matches the package version, or run npx playwright install with deps on CI. Pin versions for consistent browsers and screenshots. In GitHub Actions or Jenkins, set workers to fit available CPU, enable retries and traces, and upload the HTML report and traces as artifacts.

questions.q: How would you automate accessibility checks with Playwright?
questions.ideal: I use the axe-core AxeBuilder package to scan pages for WCAG violations, filtering by tags and excluding known issues, and fail the test on new violations. ARIA snapshot assertions verify the accessibility tree, and keyboard tests check focus order. Automation catches maybe a third of issues, so manual screen reader testing is still needed.

questions.q: How do you test time dependent features like session expiry or countdowns in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Playwright clock API lets you install fake timers or set a fixed time before the page loads. Then fast forward or run for a duration to trigger a session timeout, expiry or countdown without real waiting. This makes tests deterministic and fast, instead of sleeping for minutes or depending on the machine time.

questions.q: How would you design reporting and observability for a large Playwright suite?
questions.ideal: I use multiple reporters: HTML with traces for debugging, JUnit for CI integration, and Allure or a custom reporter to push results to a dashboard with history and trends. Tracking flakiness and duration per test shows what to fix. A merge step combines shard reports, and failures send a Slack notification with links.

questions.q: What do you look for when reviewing a Playwright pull request from a junior engineer?
questions.ideal: I check for hard waits like waitForTimeout, brittle XPath instead of getByRole or test id locators, and missing web first assertions. Tests must be independent with no order dependency or shared state. I look for duplication that belongs in a page object or fixture, clear naming, lint rules passing and secrets not hard coded.

questions.q: How do you test real time features that use WebSockets in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Listen with page on websocket to capture the socket, then use framesent and framereceived events to assert the messages. To isolate the UI, routeWebSocket can mock the server and push events on demand. For real time live updates, use web first assertions that wait for the UI to reflect the message instead of fixed sleeps.

questions.q: How do you install the browsers that Playwright needs, and why are they separate from the npm package?
questions.ideal: After adding the npm package you run npx playwright install to download browser binaries for Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. They are separate because each Playwright version is pinned to matched patched browser builds. On Linux and CI you add --with-deps to install system dependencies, or use the official Docker image so the pipeline has everything.

questions.q: What is the difference between the playwright library and the @playwright/test runner?
questions.ideal: The playwright library is just the automation API to launch browsers and drive pages, useful for scripts or other test frameworks. The @playwright/test test runner adds fixtures like page, web first expect assertions, parallel workers, retries, projects, a config file and reporters. For end to end testing you normally use the runner.

questions.q: What is the difference between fill and pressSequentially in Playwright?
questions.ideal: fill clears the field and sets the value at once, firing an input event, which is fast and preferred. pressSequentially, the replacement for type, sends key events one keystroke at a time, optionally with a delay. You use it when the page has special handling per key, like autocomplete suggestions or input masks.

questions.q: How do you work with checkboxes, radio buttons and select dropdowns in Playwright?
questions.ideal: For checkboxes and radio buttons use check, uncheck or setChecked, which verify the state actually changed, and assert with toBeChecked. For native select dropdowns use selectOption with a value, label or index, including multiple options, and assert with toHaveValue. Custom dropdowns built from divs need clicks on the options instead.

questions.q: How do you perform keyboard and mouse actions like hover, key presses and right click in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Use locator hover for mouse over menus, locator press for a key press like Enter or shortcuts with modifiers such as Control+A, and click with button right for a context menu. dblclick does a double click. For low level control page.keyboard and page.mouse move to coordinates, press down and up, and type text.

questions.q: What is Playwright UI mode and how does it help during development?
questions.ideal: UI mode, started with npx playwright test --ui, gives a visual runner where you filter and run a single test, use watch mode to rerun on save, and step through a timeline with time travel DOM snapshots. It shows network, console and errors for debugging, and has a locator picker to build robust locators quickly.

questions.q: How do you debug a Playwright test step by step with the inspector?
questions.ideal: Running with --debug or PWDEBUG=1 opens the Playwright inspector and a headed browser window. Adding page.pause stops at that line. You can step over each action, see the highlighted element, and try locators. The VS Code extension lets you set a breakpoint in the IDE and debug tests directly with live locator highlighting.

questions.q: What happens if you forget await before a Playwright action or assertion?
questions.ideal: Playwright actions return a promise, so without await the test continues before the action finishes, causing a race condition. A web first assertion without await never really checks anything and may pass falsely, and errors become unhandled after the test ends. This leads to flaky, random failures. The eslint rule no-floating-promises catches it.

questions.q: How do you read text from elements in Playwright, and what is the difference between textContent, innerText and allTextContents?
questions.ideal: textContent returns all text including hidden elements, innerText returns only rendered visible text respecting CSS, and allTextContents returns an array for every matching element. For input fields use inputValue. For checks it is better to use toHaveText or toContainText assertions because they auto retry rather than reading text once.

questions.q: What does test isolation mean in Playwright, and how is it achieved?
questions.ideal: Each Playwright test gets a fresh browser context, like a new incognito profile, so cookies, local storage and session are not shared. Tests are independent and can run in parallel and in any order. This avoids shared state leaking between tests and cascading failures. Common setup like login is reused through storage state rather than test dependency.

questions.q: Why does Playwright recommend locators over ElementHandle?
questions.ideal: A locator is lazy, it is resolved again every time you act on it, so it survives DOM changes and re-renders and includes auto wait and actionability checks plus strictness. An ElementHandle from page.$ points to one specific node that can become stale or detached after re-render. Handles are discouraged and kept only for rare low level cases.

questions.q: What is a strict mode violation in Playwright, and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal: Locators are strict, so an action on a locator that resolved to more than one element throws a strict mode violation. The fix is a more specific locator that is unique, like getByRole with an accessible name, chaining inside a parent, or filter with hasText or has. Using first or nth works but is fragile, so use it only when order really matters.

questions.q: When would you use serial mode in Playwright, and what are the downsides?
questions.ideal: test.describe.configure with mode serial runs tests in order in one worker, so dependent steps can share a page set up in beforeAll. If one fails, the remaining tests are skipped and the whole group retries together. It loses parallel speed and isolation, so it is mostly an anti pattern; independent tests are preferred.

questions.q: How do you tag Playwright tests and run only a subset such as smoke tests?
questions.ideal: You add tags in the test details, like tag @smoke or @regression, or in the title. Then run npx playwright test --grep @smoke to include, or --grep-invert to exclude. Projects in the config can also set grep so the CI pipeline runs a smoke suite on every commit and full regression nightly. Annotations add extra metadata to reports.

questions.q: What is page.evaluate used for, and what are its limitations?
questions.ideal: page.evaluate runs JavaScript inside the browser context, for example reading window values, local storage or manipulating the DOM, and returns a serializable return value. Arguments must be passed explicitly and be serializable, because the function cannot see Node closure variables in scope. It bypasses user actions, so do not use it to fake clicks in real tests.

questions.q: How do you wait for a specific API response after an action in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Start the promise before the click, for example const resp = page.waitForResponse with a url or predicate, then click, then await the promise. Starting after the click can miss a fast response, a race. You can assert the status code or parse the json response body. Often a web first assertion on the UI result is enough instead.

questions.q: How do you perform drag and drop in Playwright?
questions.ideal: The simplest way is locator dragTo a target locator, or page.dragAndDrop with source and target selectors. If a library uses custom events, do it manually with hover on the source, mouse down, move with steps over the target, then mouse up. HTML5 native drag usually works with dragTo. Then assert the new position or order.

questions.q: How do you attach extra files or logs to a Playwright test report?
questions.ideal: Use testInfo.attach inside a test or fixture to add an attachment like a screenshot, json data, text logs or a file path, and it appears in the HTML report for that test. Wrapping actions in test.step groups them as named steps. Fixtures often attach browser console logs or API responses only when a test fails.

questions.q: How do you chain and filter locators to target an element inside a specific row or card?
questions.ideal: You scope a locator by chaining from a parent, for example the row or card that matters, then find the child inside. filter with hasText narrows rows by text, and has or hasNot narrows by a child locator. For example get role row, filter hasText Alice, then getByRole button Edit. This avoids brittle index based XPath.

questions.q: How do you run the same Playwright tests against different environments?
questions.ideal: I read the environment from process.env, often loaded from a .env file with dotenv, and set baseURL in playwright.config so tests use relative paths. Different projects or an ENV variable select dev, staging or prod like settings. Credentials come from CI secrets, never committed. Tests then run unchanged against each environment.

questions.q: How can you record and replay network traffic with HAR files in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Playwright can record traffic to a HAR file using recordHar on the context or routeFromHAR with update true. Later routeFromHAR replays matching requests from the file, making tests deterministic and backend independent. You scope it with a url pattern so only APIs are mocked. HAR files go stale, so plan to update them when the API changes.

questions.q: What is ARIA snapshot testing in Playwright, and when is it better than screenshots?
questions.ideal: toMatchAriaSnapshot compares the accessibility tree of a region, roles, names and states, against a YAML template. It checks semantic structure without being affected by pixels, fonts or rendering like screenshots are, so it is more stable across browsers. It also nudges accessible markup. Templates support regex and partial matching and are refreshed with --update-snapshots.

questions.q: What is addInitScript used for in Playwright?
questions.ideal: addInitScript runs code in every page before page scripts load, on each navigation, at page or context level. It is used to mock or override browser APIs, freeze Math.random or Date for determinism, seed local storage or feature flags config, or disable analytics. Because it runs first, the app sees the stubbed values from the start.

questions.q: How do you create custom expect matchers in Playwright?
questions.ideal: Use expect.extend to add a custom matcher that returns pass and a message function, often wrapping polling logic so it retries like built in assertions. Add TypeScript type declarations for autocomplete. Domain matchers like toHaveCartCount make tests readable and reusable. They still work with soft assertions and appear clearly in the report.

questions.q: How do you test a Chrome extension with Playwright?
questions.ideal: Extensions need Chromium with a persistent context, created with launchPersistentContext and args like --disable-extensions-except and --load-extension pointing to the build folder. You get the background service worker from the context to read the extension id, then open the popup page by its URL and test it like a normal page.

questions.q: How do you test offline behaviour and slow networks in Playwright?
questions.ideal: context.setOffline true simulates no connection, so you can check offline messages, PWA service worker cache fallback and retry after reconnect. For slow networks, route requests and add delays, or use a CDP session in Chromium for network throttling. route abort simulates failed calls. Assert the error message and recovery when the network returns.

questions.q: How would you test a chart or game drawn on an HTML canvas with Playwright?
questions.ideal: Canvas has no DOM elements, so locators cannot see inside. I use visual comparison with toHaveScreenshot, click at coordinates and check tooltip on hover, and evaluate to read app state that developers expose for testing. I also ask for accessibility fallbacks like a hidden data table or data attributes, and verify the API data behind the chart.

questions.q: How do you automate a login flow that requires MFA or an OTP code with Playwright?
questions.ideal: Best is a test account with MFA disabled or a bypass in test environments. If MFA must be tested, generate a TOTP code from the shared authenticator secret using a library, or read the OTP from an email API or SMS API inbox. Then save storage state so other tests reuse the session instead of repeating MFA.

questions.q: Can you collect performance metrics with Playwright, and how?
questions.ideal: Playwright is not a load tool, but you can collect page performance with evaluate on the Performance API like navigation timing, measure web vitals such as LCP and CLS through PerformanceObserver, use CDP and Chrome tracing, or run Lighthouse via a plugin. Assert against a budget or threshold to catch regression, comparing trends rather than single runs.

questions.q: How do you detect flaky tests before they are merged in Playwright?
questions.ideal: In the pull request pipeline run new or changed tests with --repeat-each, say 10 or 20 times, with several workers to add load and retries set to 0. --fail-on-flaky-tests fails the run if any test only passed on retry. --only-changed can select changed tests. This catches flakiness before it reaches the main suite.

questions.q: How would you structure Playwright tests in a large monorepo with several web apps?
questions.ideal: I keep a shared library package with common fixtures, page components, auth helpers and utilities, and separate Playwright config or projects per app. Teams own their tests through CODEOWNERS. CI runs only tests of affected apps using the monorepo graph. A single Playwright dependency version across workspaces avoids browser mismatch.

questions.q: Your full Playwright suite takes an hour. How would you run only relevant tests per pull request?
questions.ideal: I use test impact analysis: --only-changed runs test files affected by the git diff, and coverage mapping links source modules to tests. Every PR also runs a tagged smoke set of critical journeys. The nightly full suite and pre release full run catch what selection misses. I measure missed bugs to tune the trade off between speed and risk.

questions.q: How would you test an application built from micro frontends owned by different teams?
questions.ideal: Each team tests its micro frontend in isolation with component tests and mocked APIs. Shared events and props between them are treated as a contract and tested. A smaller suite tests the composition in the shell app, covering critical journeys end to end. Since they deploy independently, I run compatibility smoke tests against current production versions of the others.

questions.q: How can Playwright tests be used for synthetic monitoring in production?
questions.ideal: Synthetic monitoring runs a few Playwright scripts against production on a schedule, every few minutes, covering critical journeys like login, search and checkout with dedicated test accounts that cause no side effects or real orders. Failures trigger alerts to on call with traces and screenshots. Tools like Checkly run Playwright this way; flakiness must be very low.

questions.q: How would you justify choosing Playwright over Cypress, or the reverse, for a team?
questions.ideal: Playwright runs out of process, supports multiple tabs and popups, all three engines including WebKit for Safari, multiple languages, and free parallel and sharding. Cypress runs in browser with strong developer experience and a mature ecosystem, but limits multi tab and cross origin. I decide by app needs, browser coverage, team skills and existing architecture, ideally with a pilot.

questions.q: Your Playwright CI jobs crash randomly with out of memory errors. How do you investigate?
questions.ideal: I check worker count against container limits for CPU and memory, since each worker runs a browser. I reduce workers, record video and trace only on failure, and look for leaks where browser contexts or pages are not closed in custom fixtures. In Docker, small /dev/shm causes Chromium crashes, so use --ipc=host or larger shm.

questions.q: How would you test a checkout that uses a third party payment iframe like Stripe?
questions.ideal: Use the provider sandbox or test mode with test cards, and reach fields inside the cross origin iframe with frameLocator. Cover success, decline and 3D Secure challenge flows. Verify the backend order status after the webhook arrives. For most UI tests mock the payment step, keeping a few real sandbox end to end tests.

questions.q: How do you upgrade Playwright versions safely across a large suite?
questions.ideal: I read release notes for breaking changes, then upgrade on a separate branch with the matching Docker image and browsers. I run the full suite several times and compare against a baseline, expecting visual screenshots to change with new browser versions. Upgrading regularly in small steps, every release or two, is far safer than a big jump.

questions.q: How would you automate tests for an application that uses SSO with SAML or OAuth through an identity provider?
questions.ideal: I avoid driving the identity provider UI in every test. A setup project logs in once per role through the real SSO flow and saves storage state, or gets a token via API login or a test bypass in non production. Dedicated test users exist in the IdP like Okta. A few tests still cover the real SAML or OIDC redirect flow.

questions.q: How are AI agents and the Playwright MCP server changing test automation, and what are the risks?
questions.ideal: The Playwright MCP server lets LLM agents drive a browser using the accessibility snapshot instead of screenshots. Playwright test agents like planner, generator and healer can explore an app, write tests and fix broken locators. Risks include hallucination, wrong assertions that hide bugs and costs, so generated tests need human review and must follow team conventions.

questions.q: What is Selenium WebDriver, and what are the different locators?
questions.ideal: Selenium WebDriver automates browsers through browser drivers like chromedriver. Locators are id, name, class name, tag name, link text, partial link text, CSS selector and XPath.

questions.q: What are implicit, explicit and fluent waits in Selenium, and which should you use?
questions.ideal: Implicit wait applies globally to element lookups, explicit wait with WebDriverWait waits for a specific condition, and fluent wait adds polling and ignored exceptions. Prefer explicit waits, avoid Thread.sleep and avoid mixing implicit with explicit.

questions.q: Explain the Page Object Model and how you structure a Selenium framework with TestNG or pytest.
questions.ideal: The Page Object Model keeps locators and actions in page classes. A framework adds a base class and driver factory, data driven tests through TestNG DataProvider or pytest parametrize, config files, utilities and reports such as Extent or Allure.

questions.q: What are StaleElementReference and NoSuchElement exceptions, and how do you handle them?
questions.ideal: A stale element means the DOM changed after you found it, so locate it again. NoSuchElement means a wrong locator or the element is not loaded yet, so check the locator and use explicit waits. ElementNotInteractable usually means hidden, covered or inside an iframe.

questions.q: How do you handle frames, windows, alerts, drag and drop and file uploads in Selenium?
questions.ideal: Switch into frames with switchTo().frame, move between windows with window handles, handle alerts with accept or dismiss, use Actions for hover and drag and drop, upload by sending the file path with sendKeys, and use JavascriptExecutor as a last resort.

questions.q: What is Selenium Grid, and how do you run tests in parallel and across browsers?
questions.ideal: Selenium Grid sends tests to nodes through a hub using RemoteWebDriver and browser options. For parallel runs make the driver thread safe with ThreadLocal and configure TestNG or pytest-xdist. Grid can run in Docker or on cloud providers like BrowserStack.

questions.q: Your Selenium tests are flaky and slow in CI. How do you improve reliability and speed?
questions.ideal: Replace sleeps with explicit waits, use stable locators, make tests independent with API or database setup instead of UI steps, run headless and in parallel, capture screenshots and logs on failure, stabilise the environment and track flaky tests rather than only retrying.

questions.q: How would you design a scalable automation architecture covering UI, API and CI/CD with reporting?
questions.ideal: Use layers: UI page objects, an API service layer, utilities and test data management. Follow the test pyramid, run smoke on each commit and regression nightly in CI/CD using Docker and Grid, publish Allure dashboards, enforce code review and schedule suite maintenance.

questions.q: What are the components of the Selenium suite?
questions.ideal: The Selenium suite has Selenium IDE, a browser extension for record and playback, Selenium WebDriver, which drives browsers through browser drivers like ChromeDriver and GeckoDriver using the W3C protocol from languages such as Java and Python, and Selenium Grid, which runs tests remotely and in parallel across machines and browsers.

questions.q: What is the difference between findElement and findElements?
questions.ideal: FindElement returns a single web element, the first match, and throws NoSuchElementException if nothing is found. FindElements returns a list of all matches and returns an empty list instead of throwing, so it is useful to check whether an element exists by checking size zero or to loop through multiple elements.

questions.q: What is the difference between driver close and driver quit?
questions.ideal: Driver close closes only the current window or tab, and the session continues if other windows remain. Driver quit closes all windows, ends the WebDriver session and stops the driver process. Always call quit in teardown, otherwise leftover browser and driver processes leak memory on CI machines.

questions.q: What is the difference between absolute and relative XPath, and what are XPath axes?
questions.ideal: Absolute XPath starts from the root with a single slash and is brittle, breaking on any layout change. Relative XPath starts with double slash and uses attributes and functions like contains, text and starts-with. Axes like parent, ancestor, following-sibling and preceding navigate relative to a known element, useful for dynamic tables and labels.

questions.q: How do CSS selectors compare with XPath in Selenium?
questions.ideal: CSS selectors use simple syntax for id, class and attribute matching, are readable and often slightly faster. XPath is more powerful, it can match by visible text and traverse backward to a parent or ancestor, which CSS cannot. I prefer id or CSS for most locators and use XPath when text or upward traversal is needed.

questions.q: How do you handle dropdowns in Selenium?
questions.ideal: For a native select tag, wrap the element in the Select class and use selectByVisibleText, selectByValue or selectByIndex, and getOptions to verify all options. Custom dropdowns built with div or li elements are not select tags, so you click to open them and then click the option element, using waits.

questions.q: What is the difference between driver get and navigate to, and what navigation methods exist?
questions.ideal: Driver get opens a URL and waits for the page load. Navigate to does the same but is part of the navigation interface that also offers back, forward and refresh, which work with browser history. In practice both load the page the same way, and navigation methods are used to test back button and reload behaviour.

questions.q: How do you read text and attributes and check element state in Selenium?
questions.ideal: GetText returns visible text, and getAttribute or getDomAttribute reads values such as value, href or class. IsDisplayed checks visibility, isEnabled checks if a button or field is enabled, and isSelected checks checkboxes and radio buttons. GetCssValue reads styles like colour, useful for validation messages.

questions.q: What is the Actions class used for in Selenium?
questions.ideal: The Actions class performs advanced user gestures: moveToElement for mouse hover menus, contextClick for right click, doubleClick, dragAndDrop and clickAndHold, and keyboard actions like keyDown with control or shift. You chain the steps and call perform, which builds and runs the sequence.

questions.q: When and how do you use JavascriptExecutor in Selenium?
questions.ideal: JavascriptExecutor runs JavaScript through executeScript, used to scroll with scrollIntoView, click an element hidden behind an overlay, set a value, or read page state. It should be a last resort because it bypasses real user behaviour, so a JS click may pass even when a real user could not click the element.

questions.q: How do you capture a screenshot automatically when a test fails?
questions.ideal: Cast the driver to TakesScreenshot and call getScreenshotAs with output type file or bytes. To do it automatically, implement a TestNG ITestListener and capture in onTestFailure, naming the file with the test name and timestamp. Then attach it to the Extent or Allure report for quick debugging.

questions.q: Explain TestNG annotations and useful attributes like priority, groups and dependsOnMethods.
questions.ideal: TestNG annotations run in order: BeforeSuite, BeforeTest, BeforeClass, BeforeMethod, then Test, then AfterMethod and AfterClass for teardown. Priority controls order, groups tag tests like smoke or regression, and dependsOnMethods skips a test if its prerequisite fails. The testng.xml suite file selects groups, classes and parallel settings.

questions.q: How do you do data driven testing with TestNG DataProvider and Excel?
questions.ideal: A DataProvider method returns a two dimensional object array, and the test runs once for each row. Data is often read from Excel with Apache POI, or from JSON or CSV files. Setting parallel true runs iterations in parallel. This separates test data from logic and covers multiple sets of inputs with one test method.

questions.q: How do you handle dynamic web tables in Selenium?
questions.ideal: I locate the table, get all rows with tr and cells with td, and loop through them to find a value. For a specific row, dynamic XPath like a row containing text then a following sibling cell works well. For pagination, loop clicking next page until the value is found or the last page is reached.

questions.q: How do you run Selenium headless and configure browser options?
questions.ideal: Use ChromeOptions or FirefoxOptions and addArguments, for example headless equals new, window size, incognito and disable notifications. Preferences set the download path, and capabilities set things like page load strategy or accept insecure certs. Set a fixed window size in headless mode because the default is small and can hide elements.

questions.q: How are browser drivers managed in modern Selenium, and what is Selenium Manager?
questions.ideal: Earlier you downloaded ChromeDriver and set the path with system setProperty, and version mismatch with the browser broke tests. WebDriverManager automated this. Since Selenium 4.6, the built in Selenium Manager automatically detects the browser, then downloads and caches a compatible driver executable, so no setup is needed.

questions.q: What are the major changes and new features in Selenium 4?
questions.ideal: Selenium 4 moved fully to the W3C protocol, replacing JSON Wire. It added relative locators like above, below and near, newWindow to open a new tab or window, element level screenshots, Chrome DevTools and the newer BiDi protocol, a redesigned Grid with Docker support, and Selenium Manager for drivers.

questions.q: How can you use Chrome DevTools Protocol or BiDi with Selenium?
questions.ideal: Through the DevTools interface or the newer WebDriver BiDi, Selenium can intercept and mock network requests, capture console logs and JavaScript errors, emulate geolocation and network conditions, read performance metrics, and register basic authentication. CDP is Chromium only, so BiDi is the cross browser standard going forward.

questions.q: How do you interact with elements inside shadow DOM in Selenium?
questions.ideal: In Selenium 4, call getShadowRoot on the host element to get a SearchContext, then findElement inside it using a CSS selector, because XPath is not supported in shadow roots. For nested shadow DOM, repeat the step for each level. Older versions used executeScript returning shadowRoot via JavaScript.

questions.q: How do you handle SSL certificate errors, basic auth popups, captcha and OTP in automation?
questions.ideal: Set acceptInsecureCerts true for SSL certificate errors. Basic auth popups are handled with credentials in the URL or the BiDi or DevTools authentication handler. Captcha should not be automated, ask developers to disable it in the test environment or use a test key. For OTP, use a fixed test value or fetch it via an API, database or test email inbox.

questions.q: Why do you need ThreadLocal WebDriver for parallel execution?
questions.ideal: With parallel execution, a static shared driver is not thread safe, so tests interfere with each other's browser. ThreadLocal gives each thread its own driver instance, accessed through get and set in a driver factory. Call quit and then remove in teardown to avoid memory leak when threads are reused.

questions.q: What is Page Factory, and how does it differ from a plain Page Object Model?
questions.ideal: Page Factory uses the FindBy annotation and initElements to create proxy elements with lazy initialization, located only when used. A plain page object model stores By locators and finds elements on demand. Many teams now avoid Page Factory because cached proxies can cause stale element issues and it does not support Selenium 4 features cleanly.

questions.q: How do you rerun failed tests automatically in TestNG, and what are the risks?
questions.ideal: Implement IRetryAnalyzer with a max retry count and attach it to tests, or apply it globally with IAnnotationTransformer as a listener. TestNG also creates testng-failed xml to rerun failures. The risk is masking real flaky behaviour or product bugs, so retried tests must be reported and tracked, not ignored.

questions.q: How do you integrate Cucumber BDD with Selenium?
questions.ideal: Feature files written in Gherkin describe scenarios with Given, When and Then. Step definitions in Java glue each step to Selenium page object calls. A runner class with CucumberOptions sets features, glue and tags. Hooks with Before and After start and quit the driver, and scenario outline with examples handles data driven cases.

questions.q: How would you run Selenium Grid on Docker or Kubernetes for scalable execution?
questions.ideal: Run the Grid with Docker Compose using the official hub and browser node images, and connect through RemoteWebDriver. Dynamic Grid starts a fresh container per session. On Kubernetes, use the Helm chart with KEDA autoscaling to scale nodes with the queue. Video recording containers capture sessions, and nodes are destroyed after runs to keep them clean.

questions.q: When would you use a cloud grid like BrowserStack or Sauce Labs instead of your own grid?
questions.ideal: A cloud grid like BrowserStack, Sauce Labs or LambdaTest gives many browsers and real devices with no infrastructure maintenance. Trade offs are cost and licensed concurrency limits, network latency, and security, since internal apps need a secure tunnel. Teams often run most tests on an in house Docker grid and use cloud for wide device coverage.

questions.q: Locators keep breaking after every UI release. How do you fix this long term?
questions.ideal: I work with developers to add stable test attributes like data-testid to components, ideally as a coding standard checked in review. Locators stay centralized in page objects so one change fixes all tests. Avoid index and absolute XPath. Self healing tools like Healenium can help, but stable test ids are the real fix.

questions.q: How do you set up reporting and logging in a Selenium framework?
questions.ideal: Use a TestNG listener to feed results into Extent Reports or Allure, attaching screenshots and step logs on failure. Log4j or SLF4J writes logs with levels to console and file per test. In Jenkins or CI, publish the Allure report and archive logs so anyone can see history and failure reasons.

questions.q: How do you design a Selenium framework to run against multiple environments and browsers?
questions.ideal: Keep environment details like URLs in config properties or YAML per environment, such as QA, staging and UAT. Choose the environment and browser through command line system properties, for example Maven with dash D, which CI pipeline parameters pass in. A driver factory creates the right browser. Credentials come from secrets or a vault, never from code.

questions.q: When should you not use Selenium UI tests, and how does the test pyramid guide this?
questions.ideal: The test pyramid says most tests should be fast unit tests, then API or service layer tests, and only a few UI end to end tests for critical journeys. UI tests are slow, expensive and flaky, so validation logic and calculations belong lower. Too many UI tests is the ice cream cone anti pattern.

questions.q: How do you handle test data setup and preconditions in a Selenium suite without making tests slow?
questions.ideal: I create preconditions through API calls or direct database inserts instead of UI steps, which is much faster and more reliable. Login can be bypassed by injecting session cookies. Each test creates its own independent data and cleans it up in teardown, so tests run in any order and in parallel.

questions.q: Your manager asks whether to choose Selenium, Playwright or Cypress for a new project. How do you decide?
questions.ideal: I evaluate against requirements: team language skills like Java, browser support including Safari or WebKit, mobile needs through Appium, speed and stability, multi tab and iframe support, ecosystem and cloud support. Selenium is mature and multi language, Playwright is fast with auto waiting, Cypress is JavaScript only. I run a short proof of concept on real flows before deciding.

questions.q: Explain the architecture of Selenium WebDriver from your test code to the browser.
questions.ideal: Your test uses a client library or language binding like Java or Python. Commands are sent as JSON over HTTP using the W3C WebDriver protocol to a browser driver such as ChromeDriver or GeckoDriver. The driver creates a session with a session id and executes the commands natively in the browser, then returns the response.

questions.q: How do you set up a Selenium Java project with Maven?
questions.ideal: I create a Maven project and add dependencies in pom.xml for selenium-java and a test framework like TestNG or JUnit, plus logging and reporting libraries. The Surefire plugin runs tests and can point to testng.xml. Then mvn test runs everything from the command line or CI. Selenium Manager handles drivers automatically in recent versions.

questions.q: What is the difference between hard assert and soft assert in TestNG?
questions.ideal: A hard assert stops execution of the test immediately when it fails. A soft assert, using SoftAssert, continues and collects failures, so multiple checks on one page can all be reported. You must call assertAll at the end, otherwise failures are silently ignored. Use hard asserts for critical preconditions.

questions.q: Why is Thread.sleep considered bad practice in Selenium tests?
questions.ideal: Thread.sleep is a hard wait for a fixed time. If the page is faster it wastes time and makes the suite slow; if slower, the wait is not enough and tests become flaky. Explicit waits with WebDriverWait wait only until a condition like visibility or clickability is met, up to a timeout, so they are faster and more reliable.

questions.q: How do you handle checkboxes and radio buttons in Selenium?
questions.ideal: I locate the checkbox or radio button and click it, but first check isSelected so I do not untick something already selected. isEnabled and isDisplayed verify state. For a group sharing the same name attribute I use findElements to get the list and pick by value or label, then assert with isSelected.

questions.q: How do you send special keys like Enter, Tab or Ctrl+A in Selenium?
questions.ideal: The Keys class provides special keys, so element.sendKeys(Keys.ENTER) or Keys.TAB. For combinations like Ctrl+A use Keys.chord or the Actions class with keyDown Control, sendKeys a, keyUp. This is used to select all and clear text, submit forms or move focus. On Mac you use Command instead of Control.

questions.q: How do you control browser window size and position in Selenium?
questions.ideal: driver.manage().window().maximize() maximizes the window, fullscreen goes full screen, and setSize with a Dimension sets an exact resolution, while setPosition moves it. In headless mode use a window-size argument because maximize may not work. Fixed sizes help responsive breakpoints testing and make screenshots consistent.

questions.q: How do you read, add and delete cookies in Selenium?
questions.ideal: driver.manage() gives cookie methods: getCookies and getCookieNamed to read, addCookie to add, deleteCookieNamed and deleteAllCookies to remove. You must be on the same domain before adding a cookie. Cookies are used to verify session behaviour, clear state between tests, or inject a login session to skip the UI login.

questions.q: How do you scroll a page or scroll to an element in Selenium?
questions.ideal: Selenium scrolls automatically before clicks, but sometimes you need it explicitly. Use JavascriptExecutor with scrollIntoView for an element or window.scrollBy for pixels or the bottom of the page. Selenium 4 Actions also has scrollToElement and wheel input. For infinite scroll you scroll in a loop until new items stop loading.

questions.q: How do you run Selenium TestNG tests from the command line or CI?
questions.ideal: I define suites in testng.xml with test tags listing classes and groups to include or exclude. Maven Surefire points at the suite file, so mvn test runs it, and -D passes a system property like browser or environment. The CI pipeline, for example Jenkins or GitHub Actions, runs the same command and publishes reports.

questions.q: What causes ElementClickInterceptedException, and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal: It occurs when another element like an overlay, loading spinner, modal or sticky header covers the target. Fix it by waiting for invisibility of the overlay, waiting for element to be clickable, scrolling with scrollIntoView so the sticky header is not on top, or closing the popup. A JavaScript click works but bypasses real user behaviour, so it is a last resort.

questions.q: What is page load strategy in Selenium, and when would you change it?
questions.ideal: Page load strategy controls when get returns. Normal waits for the load event, eager waits only for DOMContentLoaded, and none returns immediately. I use eager when slow resources like ads or third party scripts delay load but the page is usable, combined with explicit waits for the elements I need.

questions.q: What are TestNG listeners, and how do you use them in a Selenium framework?
questions.ideal: TestNG listeners like ITestListener hook into events such as onTestStart, onTestSuccess and onTestFailure. In onTestFailure we capture a screenshot, browser logs and attach them to reporting like Extent. An annotation transformer can apply a retry analyzer globally. Listeners are registered in testng.xml or with the @Listeners annotation.

questions.q: How do you automate an auto suggest or autocomplete search box in Selenium?
questions.ideal: I type partial text with sendKeys, then use an explicit wait for the suggestion list visibility. findElements gets all options, I loop and match the desired text, then click it. Alternatively use keyboard arrow down and Enter. Then I assert the field value. Locators should target the list container, not dynamic ids.

questions.q: How do you find broken links on a page using Selenium?
questions.ideal: Collect all anchor tags with findElements, read the href attribute, skip empty or javascript links, then send a request using an HTTP client or HttpURLConnection. A status code of 400 or above, like 404 or 500, marks a broken link. Selenium cannot read status codes itself, so this check runs outside the browser.

questions.q: How do you automate a calendar date picker in Selenium?
questions.ideal: If the input accepts typing, sendKeys with the date is simplest. Otherwise click to open the calendar, loop clicking next month until the month and year header matches the target, then click the day cell with a dynamic locator. As a fallback JavaScript can set the value, but then UI events must also fire.

questions.q: How do you verify a file download in Selenium?
questions.ideal: I set the download directory through Chrome options prefs or Firefox preferences, disable the prompt, then click download. I poll until the file exists and the temporary extension disappears, check file name and size, then parse content like CSV or PDF to verify it. On a remote grid I use the Grid managed downloads feature.

questions.q: How do you use pytest fixtures to manage the WebDriver in a Python Selenium framework?
questions.ideal: I define a driver fixture in conftest.py that creates the browser, yields it to the test and calls quit after yield as teardown. Scope can be function for isolation or session for speed. pytest_addoption adds a command line browser option, and parametrize or fixture params run tests on several browsers. A hook captures screenshots on failure.

questions.q: What causes ElementNotInteractableException in Selenium, and how do you resolve it?
questions.ideal: ElementNotInteractableException means the element exists in the DOM but cannot be used, usually because it is hidden with display none, disabled or zero size. Often the locator matches a duplicate hidden element, like a desktop version in a mobile layout, so refine it. Otherwise wait for visibility, open a collapsed menu first, or ensure the field is enabled.

questions.q: How do you test a page with lazy loaded images or infinite scroll in Selenium?
questions.ideal: I scroll with JavaScript or scrollIntoView on the last item, then wait until the number of elements increases. Loop until no more items load or a limit is reached. For lazy images I check the src is set and naturalWidth is greater than zero to confirm they actually loaded. Waits must be condition based, not sleeps.

questions.q: How do you write a custom expected condition in Selenium?
questions.ideal: WebDriverWait until accepts any function that takes the driver and returns a truthy or non null value, so a lambda works, for example waiting until a table has more than five rows or text changes. Configure polling and ignoring exceptions like StaleElementReference. Put them in a reusable utility class so tests stay readable.

questions.q: How do you log every WebDriver action in Selenium 4?
questions.ideal: In Selenium 4 the old EventFiringWebDriver is deprecated. You implement WebDriverListener with methods like beforeClick, afterFindElement or onError, then wrap the driver with EventFiringDecorator. This gives central logging of every action, highlighting elements for debug, timing, and screenshots on error without changing page objects.

questions.q: How do you design a driver factory to support multiple browsers and local or remote execution?
questions.ideal: A driver factory uses the factory pattern to create the driver based on config such as a property or environment variable for browser and execution mode. For local it creates ChromeDriver or FirefoxDriver with options; for grid it creates RemoteWebDriver with capabilities. The driver is stored in ThreadLocal to be thread safe for parallel runs.

questions.q: A test passes in headed mode but fails in headless mode. How do you debug it?
questions.ideal: First take a screenshot and page source in headless mode to see what is different. Common causes are default small window size, so set window size; a different user agent triggering bot detection; rendering, fonts or animations timing. Using Chrome new headless, headless=new, behaves closer to headed and fixes many differences.

questions.q: How do you synchronize Selenium with AJAX heavy single page applications?
questions.ideal: readyState complete only covers the initial load, not AJAX calls. I wait for an explicit condition tied to the result, like expected text or a spinner invisibility. jQuery.active equals zero works for jQuery apps. Some teams expose a pending requests counter or use CDP to wait for network idle, but UI conditions are most reliable.

questions.q: What is a fluent page object, and what are its benefits and drawbacks?
questions.ideal: In a fluent page object each method returns this or the next page object, enabling method chaining like login.enterUser.enterPassword.submit, which reads like a DSL and models navigation flow. Drawbacks are tight coupling to one flow, awkward negative paths, and temptation to hide assertions in pages instead of keeping them in tests.

questions.q: What is the LoadableComponent pattern in Selenium?
questions.ideal: LoadableComponent is a Selenium support class for page objects. You implement load to navigate to the page and isLoaded to assert it is ready, throwing an error if not. Calling get checks isLoaded, calls load if needed and checks again. SlowLoadableComponent adds a timeout, giving consistent page readiness checks.

questions.q: How can you add visual validation to a Selenium framework?
questions.ideal: Selenium can take element or full page screenshots, and libraries like AShot stitch full page images. You compare against a baseline with a pixel diff and tolerance, ignore regions for dynamic content like dates or ads. Commercial tools like Applitools or Percy use AI visual matching to reduce false failures and manage baselines.

questions.q: How do you capture browser console errors during Selenium tests?
questions.ideal: In Chrome you enable logging preferences for the browser log type and read logs after each test, flagging SEVERE JavaScript errors. Selenium 4 BiDi or CDP can listen for console events live. I attach logs to the report and can fail the test when unexpected errors appear, which catches hidden frontend bugs.

questions.q: How do you skip the UI login in most Selenium tests to save time?
questions.ideal: I authenticate through the API to get a token or session cookie, open any page on the same domain first, then use addCookie or set local storage with JavaScript and refresh. Tests start already logged in, saving time and flakiness. A dedicated test still covers the real UI login form.

questions.q: How would you plan an upgrade of a large framework from Selenium 3 to Selenium 4?
questions.ideal: I upgrade dependencies on a branch, then fix deprecated APIs: findElementBy methods, DesiredCapabilities replaced by browser options for strict W3C, new wait Duration signatures. Grid moves to Grid 4 with new components. Selenium Manager can replace WebDriverManager. I pilot on part of the suite, compare pass rates, then roll out incrementally.

questions.q: Would you adopt self healing locators or AI tools in a Selenium framework? Explain the trade offs.
questions.ideal: Self healing tools use AI or fallback attributes to find an element when the primary locator breaks, cutting maintenance from locator breakage. The risk is a false pass when it heals to the wrong element and hides real failures. I would use it only if every healed locator is reported for review and audit, while fixing root causes like test ids.

questions.q: Several teams want to reuse your Selenium framework. How do you turn it into a shared library?
questions.ideal: I extract core pieces like driver factory, waits, reporting and config into a core framework library published as an artifact to a Maven repository with semantic versioning. Teams keep their own page objects and tests. I provide documentation, examples and extension points, avoid breaking changes with backward compatibility, and treat it as an internal product with owners.

questions.q: How do you manage credentials and secrets in a Selenium automation framework?
questions.ideal: Secrets never go in code or the Git repository. Locally they come from environment variables or an ignored file; in CI from masked pipeline secrets or a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault or Azure Key Vault. I use dedicated test accounts with least privilege, rotation of passwords, and make sure logs and reports mask values.

questions.q: How would you add automated accessibility checks to a Selenium suite?
questions.ideal: I integrate axe-core with Selenium to scan key pages and states after load, reporting WCAG violations by impact. Critical violations fail the build as a CI gate, others create tickets. Automation catches about a third of issues, so manual testing with screen reader and keyboard navigation is still needed.

questions.q: How would you test a responsive website across breakpoints and mobile browsers using Selenium?
questions.ideal: I set window size for each breakpoint and check layout, hidden menus and overlap with visual checks. Chrome mobile emulation adds device metrics and user agent. Emulation is not a real device, so a smaller set runs on real devices through a cloud like BrowserStack or Appium with a mobile browser, especially for Safari on iOS.

questions.q: How do you measure and communicate the ROI of a Selenium automation program?
questions.ideal: ROI compares time saved in manual effort hours and faster feedback against the build and maintenance cost. I track defects found by automation, escaped defects, cycle time and release frequency, plus flakiness and pass rate to show stability. I present trends to management and retire tests with low value and high maintenance.

questions.q: Third party widgets like chat bots, ads and cookie banners keep breaking your Selenium tests. How do you handle them?
questions.ideal: I make tests independent of third party widgets: preset the consent cookie or local storage so the cookie banner never appears, disable chat and ads with a feature flag or config in test environments, or block their URLs via proxy or CDP. A separate test verifies the banner itself. This removes a big source of flaky failures.

questions.q: Many tests fail on Selenium Grid with session not created or node timeouts. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.ideal: I check grid logs and the GraphQL or UI status for node capacity, queued requests and session timeout. Session not created often means browser version and driver version mismatch or wrong capabilities. Node crashes point to memory and CPU limits or missing shm in Docker. I tune max sessions, queue timeout and scale nodes.

questions.q: You inherit a legacy Selenium framework with duplicated code, sleeps and flaky tests. How do you refactor it?
questions.ideal: I assess first with metrics on flaky and slow tests. I quarantine or delete low value tests, replace sleeps with explicit waits, extract duplicate code into page objects and utilities, and introduce a driver factory and config. Refactoring is incremental, prioritized by pain, with the boy scout rule, while keeping the suite green.

questions.q: What are the HTTP methods and common status codes, and what is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
questions.ideal: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces a whole resource, PATCH changes part of it and DELETE removes it. Common codes are 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 500. PUT, GET and DELETE are idempotent.

questions.q: What do you check when testing a REST API?
questions.ideal: Check the status code, response body and schema, headers, response time, authentication and authorization, negative cases with invalid input and clear error messages, and that data is stored correctly end to end.

questions.q: Explain API authentication methods: basic auth, API key, bearer token, OAuth 2.0 and JWT.
questions.ideal: Basic auth sends encoded credentials, an API key identifies the client, a bearer token goes in the Authorization header. OAuth 2.0 issues scoped access and refresh tokens, and a JWT is a signed token with claims and an expiry the server can validate without a lookup.

questions.q: How do you automate API tests in Postman, including environments, variables, tests and Newman?
questions.ideal: Organise requests in collections, use environments and variables, write assertions in the Tests tab with pm.test, chain requests by saving values in variables, run data driven with the runner, and run in CI using Newman.

questions.q: How do you write API automation in REST Assured or a Python requests framework?
questions.ideal: In REST Assured you use given, when, then with request and response specifications, validate with JsonPath and JSON schema and map bodies with POJOs. In Python use requests with pytest, fixtures for tokens and base URLs, schema validation and Allure reporting.

questions.q: What is contract testing, and how does it differ from end to end API testing? Mention mocking.
questions.ideal: Contract testing, for example with Pact, verifies that a provider meets what consumers expect without running the whole system, so microservices deploy independently and breaking changes are caught early. Mocks like WireMock isolate services, while end to end tests are slower and cover whole flows.

questions.q: What security tests would you run on an API? Mention the OWASP API risks.
questions.ideal: Test OWASP API risks: broken object level authorization (IDOR), weak authentication and token handling, injection through unvalidated input, missing rate limiting, excessive data exposure, bad CORS and no HTTPS, using tools like Burp or OWASP ZAP.

questions.q: Design an API automation framework for microservices covering data, environments, CI/CD and reporting.
questions.ideal: Build layered code with API client wrappers and reusable specs, externalise environment config, create and clean test data with factories, keep tests independent so they run in parallel, mock dependencies and add contract tests, run in CI/CD and publish Allure or JUnit reports with request and response logs.

questions.q: What is an API, and what is the difference between REST and SOAP?
questions.ideal: An API, or application programming interface, lets two systems communicate. REST is an architectural style using HTTP methods on resources, usually with lightweight JSON, and is stateless. SOAP is a strict protocol that uses XML messages inside an envelope, described by a WSDL contract, with built in standards for security, and is common in banking and legacy systems.

questions.q: What are the parts of an HTTP request and response?
questions.ideal: A request has an endpoint URL, an HTTP method like GET or POST, headers such as content type and authorization, path parameters that identify a resource, query parameters for filtering, and a body or payload. A response has a status code, headers, and a response body, usually JSON.

questions.q: What does idempotent mean in REST, and which HTTP methods are idempotent?
questions.ideal: Idempotent means calling the same request multiple times has the same effect on the server as calling it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, and GET is also safe, being read only. POST is not idempotent, because each call can create a new resource. This matters when testing retries.

questions.q: What does it mean that REST is stateless?
questions.ideal: Stateless means each request carries all information the server needs, such as the auth token, and the server keeps no client session between requests. This improves scalability, because any server behind a load balancer can handle any request. As a tester, I check that every request works independently with the right token.

questions.q: What is Swagger or OpenAPI, and how does it help API testing?
questions.ideal: Swagger, now the OpenAPI specification, documents endpoints, parameters, request and response schema and status codes in a standard format. Testers read it to design tests, use try it out to call APIs, and treat the spec as a contract to validate against. Tools can also generate clients, mocks and tests from it.

questions.q: What are common HTTP headers you check in API testing?
questions.ideal: Common headers are Content-Type, which tells the body format, Accept for the expected response format, and Authorization for tokens. Cache-Control controls caching, User-Agent identifies the client, and CORS headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin plus security headers such as Strict-Transport-Security are checked in responses.

questions.q: What is cURL and how do testers use it?
questions.ideal: cURL is a command line tool to send HTTP requests. You set the method with dash X, headers with dash H and the body with dash d. Testers use it to quickly reproduce a call, share an exact request in a bug report, and import or export it from Postman or browser DevTools.

questions.q: What is the difference between path parameters and query parameters? Give examples.
questions.ideal: A path parameter is part of the URL and identifies a specific resource, like users slash 101. Query parameters come after a question mark and are usually optional, used to filter, sort, search or paginate, like users with status active and page two. Both should be tested with valid, invalid and missing values.

questions.q: What is JSON schema validation and why do you use it in API tests?
questions.ideal: JSON schema validation checks the response structure: required fields, data types, formats, enums and whether additional properties are allowed. It catches contract breaks that value assertions miss. In REST Assured we use matchesJsonSchemaInClasspath, in Postman or JavaScript the AJV library, and in Python the jsonschema library.

questions.q: How do you chain API requests and pass data between them?
questions.ideal: API chaining means extracting a value from one response, such as an access token or created order id, using JSONPath, storing it in a variable, and passing it to the next dependent request. In Postman I use pm environment set, and in REST Assured I extract into a Java variable or shared context.

questions.q: How do you test API pagination, filtering and sorting?
questions.ideal: For pagination I check page size or limit and offset, cursor or next link, and total count against the database. I test first page, last page, an empty page beyond the end, and invalid page values like negative or huge numbers. For sorting and filtering, I verify order ascending and descending, combined filters and no duplicate or missing records across pages.

questions.q: What negative test cases would you write for a create user API?
questions.ideal: Negative tests include missing mandatory fields, invalid data types and formats like a bad email, boundary values like max length, duplicate users returning 409 conflict, extra unknown fields, and requests with no token or an expired token returning 401. I check 400 bad request responses have a clear error message and no stack trace.

questions.q: How do you test rate limiting on an API?
questions.ideal: I send requests above the allowed limit within the time window and expect 429 too many requests with a Retry-After header. I check rate limit headers like remaining and reset values, that access recovers after the window resets, and that limits apply correctly per user, per API key or per IP.

questions.q: How do you test caching behaviour with headers like ETag and Cache-Control?
questions.ideal: I check Cache-Control and max-age values, then send a conditional request with If-None-Match using the ETag, expecting 304 not modified when unchanged. After updating the resource, the ETag must change and the stale cache must be invalidated, so clients receive updated data. Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since works the same way.

questions.q: How do you test a file upload API?
questions.ideal: Upload APIs use multipart form data. I test allowed file types and extensions, files at and over the max size expecting 413 payload too large, empty zero byte files, corrupted files and wrong content type. For security I try malicious files, double extensions and path traversal names. In REST Assured I use the multiPart method.

questions.q: How is testing a GraphQL API different from testing REST?
questions.ideal: GraphQL uses a single endpoint with queries to read and mutations to write, defined by a schema. Errors often return status 200 with an errors array, so tests must check that instead of only the status code. I test field selection, nested queries, query depth limits to stop abuse, and whether introspection is disabled in production.

questions.q: How do you validate API responses against the database in automation?
questions.ideal: After a POST, I query the database through JDBC or a Python driver with SQL and compare stored values with the request and response, confirming persistence, defaults and timestamps. I keep the connection in a utility with credentials from config, use a read only user where possible, and clean up or use transactions with rollback.

questions.q: How do you use service virtualization or mock servers like WireMock in API testing?
questions.ideal: Service virtualization replaces an unavailable or costly dependency, like a third party payment service, with a mock server such as WireMock. Stubs return defined responses, and I can simulate error scenarios, timeouts and slow responses that are hard to trigger for real. Mocks must stay aligned with the real service contract, usually via contract tests.

questions.q: How do you test asynchronous APIs and webhooks?
questions.ideal: An async API often returns 202 accepted with a job id, so I use polling on the status endpoint with a max wait timeout, using Awaitility or retry with backoff, never fixed sleeps. For a webhook, I run a test webhook receiver or listener, trigger the event, then verify the callback payload, signature and retry behaviour.

questions.q: How do you test microservices that communicate through Kafka or message queues?
questions.ideal: I test that the producer publishes the right message to the topic with a valid schema, often checked against a schema registry with Avro or JSON. Then I verify the consumer processes it correctly in the database or downstream API. Edge cases include ordering, duplicate messages needing idempotent handling, poison messages going to a dead letter queue, and retries.

questions.q: How do you test API versioning and backward compatibility?
questions.ideal: I run regression on both versions, such as v1 and v2, to confirm old clients still work. A breaking change like removing or renaming a field or changing a type must only appear in a new version. Contract tests or schema comparison in CI detect this. I also check deprecation and sunset headers and documentation.

questions.q: How do you check API performance as part of API testing?
questions.ideal: I add response time assertions against an SLA threshold in functional tests as an early warning. For real load, I use JMeter, k6 or Gatling with concurrent users and measure throughput, p95 and p99 percentile latency and error rate. I compare with a baseline to spot trends after each release.

questions.q: How do you test idempotency keys and race conditions in a payment API?
questions.ideal: I send the same payment twice with the same idempotency key and expect one charge and the same original response. Then I fire concurrent parallel requests to expose a race condition, like two withdrawals overdrawing a balance. The database must stay consistent through locking, and retries after timeouts must never cause a double charge.

questions.q: How would you test a gRPC service?
questions.ideal: gRPC uses protobuf contracts defined in proto files over HTTP2. I call methods with grpcurl, Postman or generated client stubs in code. I check gRPC status codes like NOT_FOUND and INVALID_ARGUMENT, deadline and timeout handling, unary and streaming calls, and backward compatibility of proto changes.

questions.q: How would you design a test strategy for a public API used by external partners?
questions.ideal: My strategy starts from the OpenAPI contract and verifies the implementation matches it, with backward compatibility checks blocking breaking changes. I test documentation examples, security including auth scopes and rate limits, versioning and deprecation policies, and a stable sandbox for partners. In production, monitoring with synthetic checks tracks the SLA and uptime.

questions.q: API tests keep failing because many teams share the same test environment. How do you fix this?
questions.ideal: Shared environments cause data collisions and unstable dependencies. I make tests create unique, isolated test data and clean it up. Unstable downstream services are replaced by mocks or virtualization for most tests. The long term fix is ephemeral environments created on demand with Docker or Kubernetes per pull request.

questions.q: How would you shift API testing left in a spec first development process?
questions.ideal: In spec first development, the OpenAPI contract is reviewed before code. I lint it with Spectral for standards, publish a mock server like Prism so front end and tests start early, and generate tests with tools like Schemathesis. The CI pipeline validates every pull request against the spec, catching issues before deployment.
