questions.q: How do you test data consistency across microservices that use the saga pattern?
questions.ideal: In a saga, each service does a local transaction and failures trigger compensating actions. I test the happy path and use failure injection at each step, then verify compensation rolls back earlier steps. Because of eventual consistency, I poll for the final state across services instead of asserting immediately, checking no orphaned records remain.

questions.q: An API test fails intermittently in CI. How do you use logs and tracing to find the root cause?
questions.ideal: I log every request and response in the framework with a correlation id header. When an intermittent failure happens, I search server logs and distributed tracing in Jaeger or OpenTelemetry by that trace id to see which downstream dependency failed or slowed. This separates test bugs from environment or product issues and finds the root cause.

questions.q: How would you test the resilience of an API to failures in its dependencies?
questions.ideal: I inject faults with tools like Toxiproxy or chaos experiments: slow dependency latency, timeouts, errors and dropped connections. I verify the API applies timeouts, retries with backoff, opens the circuit breaker after repeated failures, and returns a fallback or graceful degradation instead of hanging or cascading the failure.

questions.q: How do you test integrations with third party APIs you do not control?
questions.ideal: I use the vendor sandbox for realistic checks but mock the third party in most automated tests, so I can simulate errors, timeouts and rate limits. Contract or schema tests detect vendor changes early. I verify our error handling and retries, respect quota and cost, and add production monitoring with synthetic health checks.

questions.q: How do you systematically test role based authorization across hundreds of API endpoints?
questions.ideal: I build a role matrix listing every endpoint and which roles have permissions, then generate data driven tests that call each endpoint with each role and expect success or 403 forbidden. I add object level checks for BOLA or IDOR, accessing another users data by changing ids, and multi tenant isolation tests. Running it in CI keeps authorization coverage complete as endpoints grow.

questions.q: What is the difference between status codes 401 and 403?
questions.ideal: 401 Unauthorized means authentication failed: the token is missing, invalid or an expired token. 403 Forbidden means the caller is authenticated but lacks authorization, for example their role does not have permission. In testing I check each case returns the right code, and that 403 does not leak whether the resource exists.

questions.q: What are JSON and XML, and how do they differ for APIs?
questions.ideal: JSON uses key value pairs, objects and arrays, is lightweight, readable and the default for REST. XML uses nested elements with tags and attributes, is more verbose, and is used by SOAP and older systems. JSON is validated with JSON schema, XML with XSD. Testers must check content type and parse each correctly.

questions.q: What is CRUD, and how do the operations map to HTTP methods and status codes?
questions.ideal: CRUD means create, read, update and delete. Create maps to POST, usually returning 201 Created with a location header. Read is GET returning 200. Update is PUT for full replacement or PATCH for partial, returning 200 or 204. Delete is DELETE returning 204 or 200, and a later GET should return 404.

questions.q: What request body formats can an API accept, like raw JSON, form data and x-www-form-urlencoded?
questions.ideal: Raw JSON uses content-type application/json and is standard for REST. x-www-form-urlencoded sends key value pairs encoded like a query string, typical for HTML forms and OAuth token calls. Multipart form data allows files and binary data with fields. The Content-Type header must match the body or the server returns 400 or 415.

questions.q: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS, and what should an API tester check?
questions.ideal: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, so traffic is encrypted and the server proves identity with a certificate. I check the API rejects or redirects plain HTTP, the certificate is valid and not expired, old TLS versions are disabled, HSTS is set, and sensitive data like tokens and passwords never travel unencrypted.

questions.q: What are good practices for REST resource naming and URI design?
questions.ideal: REST URIs should use nouns for resources, usually plural names like /users, with hierarchy for nested sub resources like /users/10/orders. HTTP methods express actions, so avoid verbs like /getUser. Use lowercase with hyphens and include a version such as /v1. Testers check consistency since inconsistent naming signals deeper design issues.

questions.q: What should a good API error response contain, and how do you test it?
questions.ideal: A good error response uses the correct status code, a stable error code, a human readable message, and field level validation details. It follows a consistent format, such as RFC problem details, across endpoints. I check that no stack trace or internal details like SQL or server paths leak, and that 200 is never returned with an error body.

questions.q: What are 3xx redirect status codes, and how do you test them in an API?
questions.ideal: 3xx codes redirect the client. 301 and 308 are permanent, 302 and 307 temporary; 307 and 308 keep the method and body. The Location header gives the new URL. Clients often follow redirects automatically, so in tests I disable following to assert the status and location, and check redirects do not drop auth headers unsafely.

questions.q: What is URL encoding, and why does it matter in API testing?
questions.ideal: URL encoding, or percent encoding, replaces special characters in URLs, for example a space becomes %20 and an ampersand becomes %26. Without it, query parameters break or get misread. I test values with spaces, ampersand, unicode in UTF-8 and slashes, and check the server handles double encoding safely and does not decode twice.

questions.q: What are 408 and 504 status codes, and how do you test API timeouts?
questions.ideal: 408 Request Timeout means the server waited too long for the client request. 504 Gateway Timeout means a gateway, proxy or load balancer did not get a response from the upstream service in time. I test timeouts by adding delay to a slow dependency with a mock, and check client timeout settings like connect and read timeout.

questions.q: What is CORS, and how do you test it for an API?
questions.ideal: CORS lets browsers call an API from another origin. The browser sends an OPTIONS preflight with the Origin header, and the API answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, allowed methods and headers. I test allowed origins get the headers, unknown ones do not, and that a wildcard is never combined with allow credentials. CORS is browser enforced, not server security.

questions.q: How do you use pre-request scripts in Postman?
questions.ideal: Pre-request scripts run JavaScript before a request is sent. I use them for dynamic data like random emails or timestamp values, setting variables with pm.environment.set, fetching an auth token if expired, or computing an HMAC signature. Scripts at collection level or folder run for every request, avoiding duplication.

questions.q: How do you assert on nested JSON and arrays in API tests?
questions.ideal: I use JSONPath or GPath in REST Assured to reach nested fields like data.user.address.city. For arrays I check size or length, use filter expressions to find the item with a given id, and assert with Hamcrest matchers like hasItem or everyItem. In Postman, JavaScript find and every do the same, avoiding fragile index positions.

questions.q: How do you test token expiry and refresh token flows?
questions.ideal: I call an API with an expired token and expect 401. Then I use the refresh token to obtain a new short lived access token and retry. I check refresh token rotation, that an old refresh token cannot be reused, that logout invalidates or revokes tokens, and that tampered or expired refresh tokens are rejected. Short lifetimes in test configs help.

questions.q: How do you test a DELETE endpoint thoroughly?
questions.ideal: After DELETE I expect 204 or 200, then GET after delete should return 404. A second delete should be idempotent, returning 404 or 204 consistently. I check soft delete if the record is only flagged or archived, cascade effects on related records, permissions on who can delete, and deleting a resource that has dependent data.

questions.q: How do you use POJOs for serialization and deserialization in REST Assured?
questions.ideal: I create POJO model classes for request and response bodies. REST Assured uses Jackson or Gson to serialize a POJO into JSON for the body and deserialize the response with as(User.class). Builder pattern or Lombok reduce boilerplate. Configuring ignore unknown properties keeps tests robust when new fields appear, while explicit assertions check important fields.

questions.q: How do you run data driven API tests with Postman and Newman?
questions.ideal: In Postman you reference data variables like {{username}} and supply a CSV or JSON file, running one iteration per row in the collection runner. Newman runs the collection from the command line with -d data file and -e environment, and reporters like htmlextra or junit produce reports for the CI pipeline such as Jenkins.

questions.q: How do you test an API's handling of unicode and special characters?
questions.ideal: I send names with emoji, non latin scripts like Chinese or Arabic, accents and special characters like quotes and backslashes. I check the round trip: data is stored correctly in UTF-8 and read back unchanged, JSON escaping is correct, and field limit validation counts characters versus byte length consistently. Content type must declare charset.

questions.q: How do you log requests and responses in API automation for debugging?
questions.ideal: REST Assured offers log().all() and log().ifValidationFails() so request and response details appear only on failure. Filters like the Allure filter attach them to reports. In Python, requests hooks or logging do the same. I always mask secrets like tokens and passwords in logs, and include correlation ids to trace server side.

questions.q: How do you test a bulk or batch API endpoint that processes many records at once?
questions.ideal: I test a batch with all valid items, all invalid, and a mix for partial success, checking per item status results or a 207 multi status. I test the maximum size and beyond, duplicates inside the batch, whether the call is atomic with rollback or applies partially, and performance with a large payload against timeouts.

questions.q: What is fuzz or property based testing for APIs, and how would you apply it?
questions.ideal: Fuzz testing sends many generated inputs and mutations, like huge strings, wrong types and boundary numbers, to find crashes. Property based testing generates inputs and checks properties always hold. Tools like Schemathesis or RESTler read the OpenAPI spec and fail on any 500 server errors or schema mismatches. It finds edge cases humans miss.

questions.q: How do you test optimistic concurrency control with ETag and If-Match headers?
questions.ideal: I GET a resource and note its ETag or version. Then I send two updates with the same If-Match value: the first succeeds and changes the ETag, the second must fail with 412 Precondition Failed, or 409 Conflict, instead of a lost update overwrite. I also test missing If-Match when required and wrong ETag values.

questions.q: How do you test date and time fields in an API?
questions.ideal: I check dates follow ISO 8601 with a clear time zone offset or UTC Z suffix, and that inputs in other offsets are converted correctly. I test invalid dates like February 30, leap year, DST changes, start and end boundary of ranges, precision of milliseconds, and epoch formats if used. Filters by date must be inclusive or exclusive as documented.

questions.q: How do you test a SOAP web service?
questions.ideal: I import the WSDL into SoapUI or ReadyAPI, which generates requests. Each request is an XML SOAP envelope with header and body sent by POST. I assert with XPath and XML schema validation, test SOAP fault responses for invalid input, and check WS-Security like signed or encrypted messages. Code based tests use REST Assured or zeep in Python.

questions.q: How would you test a streaming API using server sent events or chunked responses?
questions.ideal: For server sent events I check the text/event-stream content type, parse events and verify order and completeness. I test disconnect and reconnect with Last-Event-ID resuming from the right point, heartbeat or keep alive messages, timeout behaviour, and slow consumers. For chunked responses the client must read incrementally and validate the final assembled result.

questions.q: How do you test that webhook signatures are generated and verified correctly?
questions.ideal: The sender computes an HMAC SHA256 signature of the payload with a shared secret and puts it in a signature header. I test a valid signature is accepted, a tampered payload or wrong secret is rejected, and a timestamp window blocks replay attack with old messages. I also check comparison is constant time and the raw body is used.

questions.q: How do you manage test data creation and cleanup in API automation?
questions.ideal: Each test creates its own test data via API in setup with unique values like a UUID, so tests stay independent and safe in parallel. Teardown deletes what was created, tracking ids in a list. Because teardown can fail, a scheduled purge job removes orphan leftover records by naming prefix or age. Shared static data is read only.

questions.q: How do you test an API that returns large files or very large responses?
questions.ideal: I verify headers like Content-Type, Content-Length and Content-Disposition, stream the body instead of loading it into memory, and compare a checksum like MD5 or SHA against the expected file. I test range requests returning 206 partial content for resume, and measure timeout and performance limits with the biggest realistic files.

questions.q: What is golden file or snapshot comparison in API testing, and what are its pitfalls?
questions.ideal: Golden file testing stores an expected response as a baseline and compares new responses with a diff. It quickly catches unexpected changes in large payloads. Pitfalls are dynamic fields like timestamps and ids, which must be masked or excluded, and lazy updates where people approve new snapshots without review, hiding regressions.

questions.q: How do you test an API that returns localized content based on the Accept-Language header?
questions.ideal: I send different Accept-Language values and check messages and content come back in the right locale with a Content-Language response header. I test unsupported languages use the fallback default language, quality values and priority between multiple languages, and locale specific formats for currency, numbers and dates, plus that cache keys vary by language.

questions.q: How would you use API tests for synthetic monitoring in production?
questions.ideal: I select a small set of critical endpoints and key flows, run them on a schedule from several regions against production, with dedicated test accounts and no harmful side effects. Results feed dashboards and SLOs, and failures trigger alerts with request details. It catches outages, certificate expiry and third party failures before customers report them.

questions.q: You are rewriting a legacy API service. How would you prove the new one behaves the same?
questions.ideal: I mirror production traffic to the new service as shadow traffic, or replay recorded traffic, and compare responses for parity with an automated diff, filtering noise like timestamps. Each mismatch is analysed as a bug or accepted difference. Then a canary gradual rollout sends a small percentage of real users, watching errors and latency before full cutover.

questions.q: Your organisation uses Postman, REST Assured and pytest in different teams. How do you decide on a standard?
questions.ideal: I compare needs: Postman collections are easy for exploratory work and less technical members, while code based tools like REST Assured or pytest scale better with version control, code review, reuse and CI integration. I weigh team skills and the main language, run a pilot, and may standardize on code for regression while keeping Postman for exploration.

questions.q: How would you test an API that wraps a large language model and returns non deterministic answers?
questions.ideal: I test the contract strictly: schema, format, latency, errors, rate limits and token limits. Content is judged by an evaluation set: a golden dataset scored with rubrics, similarity or an LLM judge, using thresholds over many runs because responses are non deterministic. I add safety tests for prompt injection, data leakage and guardrails, and track metrics over versions.

questions.q: How do you test that an API can be deployed with zero downtime?
questions.ideal: I run continuous traffic during deploy and check no errors or dropped in flight requests. Rolling or blue green deploys mean old and new versions run together, so changes must be backward compatible, including the database migration done in expand and contract steps. I test readiness health checks, connection draining, and rollback mid deploy.

questions.q: How would you test an API deployed across multiple regions?
questions.ideal: I test geo routing sends users to the nearest region with acceptable latency, then simulate a region outage to verify failover and disaster recovery. I check replication lag and eventual consistency between regions, data residency rules like GDPR keeping data in region, and configuration drift so region specific settings stay correct.

questions.q: Test data creation is the biggest bottleneck for your API suite. How would you solve it at scale?
questions.ideal: I would build a test data service offering self service, on demand creation through an API, for example create a customer with an active loan. It uses synthetic data from generators like Faker and calls real APIs or seeding scripts. Each test gets unique isolated data, records have expiry or TTL for cleanup, and a stable baseline seed covers reference data.

questions.q: How do you enforce quality and consistency across hundreds of APIs designed by different teams?
questions.ideal: I define API standards and guidelines, require every service to publish an OpenAPI spec, and run linting with Spectral in CI as a gate for naming, errors, pagination and security. An OpenAPI diff check blocks breaking changes without a version bump. Design review for new APIs and shared test templates keep teams consistent.

questions.q: What would you test in an API gateway or service mesh configuration?
questions.ideal: I test routing rules and path rewrites, authentication like JWT validation at the API gateway, rate limiting and quotas, CORS and header transformation. In a service mesh such as Istio I test mTLS between services, retries, timeouts and circuit breaker policies by injecting faults. Config is code, so it is reviewed and tested in CI.

questions.q: Your company ships client SDKs for its API in several languages. How do you test them?
questions.ideal: SDKs are often generated from the OpenAPI spec with code generation, so I test the generator output plus handwritten parts. A shared contract test suite runs in every language against a mock and a real sandbox, across supported runtime versions. Documentation examples and samples are executed in CI, and semver plus backward compatibility checks protect users.

questions.q: What is Appium and how does it work for Android and iOS?
questions.ideal: Appium is an open source cross platform mobile automation tool using the WebDriver protocol with a server and client libraries. It drives Android through UiAutomator2 or Espresso and iOS through XCUITest, for native, hybrid and mobile web apps, configured through capabilities.

questions.q: Which locator strategies do you use in Appium, and how do you inspect elements?
questions.ideal: Prefer accessibility id and resource id, use UiAutomator selectors on Android and iOS predicate or class chain on iOS, and use XPath only as a last resort because it is slow and brittle. Inspect elements with Appium Inspector.

questions.q: How do you handle swipe, scroll, long press and pinch in Appium 2?
questions.ideal: Use W3C Actions with pointer inputs for swipe, long press and pinch, or mobile: executeScript commands such as scrollGesture and swipeGesture, calculating coordinates as percentages of the screen size so tests work on different devices.

questions.q: How do you handle permissions, alerts, app install and reset, and deep links in mobile tests?
questions.ideal: Set capabilities like autoGrantPermissions and autoAcceptAlerts, control app state with noReset or fullReset, install and launch by app path or package, open screens through deep links, and use adb or simctl to prepare the device.

questions.q: How do you design an Appium framework with page objects, parallel runs and reporting?
questions.ideal: Use page objects per screen with a driver factory choosing the platform, make drivers thread safe, assign unique ports and devices for parallel runs, drive tests from TestNG, pytest or Cucumber, keep capabilities in config and report with Allure or Extent.

questions.q: How do you test across many devices with emulators, real devices and cloud farms?
questions.ideal: Use emulators and simulators for fast feedback, real devices for performance, sensors and manufacturer quirks, and cloud farms like BrowserStack or Sauce Labs for broad coverage. Build a device matrix from user analytics covering OS versions and screen sizes, and run in parallel.

questions.q: Your mobile tests are flaky. What causes it and how do you stabilise them?
questions.ideal: Use explicit waits for animations and slow screens, stable locators, a clean app state and data for every test, healthy devices and network, sensible timeouts and sessions, and diagnose with screenshots, video and logcat rather than blind retries.

questions.q: How do you decide what to automate in mobile testing and balance it with manual testing and CI?
questions.ideal: Follow the test pyramid: keep most checks at unit and API level and automate only stable critical flows and regression on the UI. Keep exploratory, usability and gesture heavy testing manual, judge ROI against maintenance cost, run smoke on every build and the full suite nightly on a device farm.

questions.q: What are desired capabilities in Appium, and which ones are mandatory to start a session?
questions.ideal: Capabilities are key value pairs sent when creating a session. platformName and automationName such as UiAutomator2 or XCUITest are mandatory, plus deviceName or udid to pick the device. You give an app path to an apk or ipa, or for an installed app the appPackage and appActivity on Android or the bundleId on iOS.

questions.q: What is the difference between native, hybrid and mobile web apps, and how does Appium test each?
questions.ideal: A native app uses platform SDKs, a hybrid app wraps web pages inside a WebView, and a mobile web app runs in Chrome or Safari. Appium drives native screens directly, but for hybrid apps you switch context from NATIVE_APP to the WEBVIEW context, which needs a matching chromedriver and webview debugging enabled in the build.

questions.q: How do you set up an Appium environment on your machine from scratch?
questions.ideal: Install Node and npm, then Appium 2 globally. Install a JDK and set JAVA_HOME, install the Android SDK and set ANDROID_HOME and the PATH environment variables. Run driver install for uiautomator2 or xcuitest on a Mac with Xcode, verify with appium doctor, and install Appium Inspector to view element trees.

questions.q: Which adb commands do you use regularly as a mobile tester?
questions.ideal: adb devices lists connected devices and emulators, adb install and uninstall manage apks, and logcat captures device logs for crashes. adb shell gives a device shell where pm clear resets app data and dumpsys shows the current activity and package. screencap and screenrecord capture a screenshot or video as bug evidence.

questions.q: What is the difference between an emulator, a simulator and a real device for testing?
questions.ideal: An Android emulator or AVD emulates the hardware, while an iOS simulator from Xcode only simulates the OS on the Mac. Both are cheap and fast for early checks, but a real device is needed for hardware like camera and sensors, real network conditions, performance and OEM specific behaviour. Teams mix local emulators with cloud real devices to control cost.

questions.q: Which types of testing are specific to mobile apps compared to web apps?
questions.ideal: Mobile apps need interruption testing for incoming calls and notifications, installation and upgrade testing, orientation changes between portrait and landscape, and network testing on slow, offline or airplane mode. Battery and power usage matter, and device fragmentation across screen sizes, manufacturers and OS versions makes coverage harder than on web.

questions.q: How do you handle text entry and the soft keyboard in Appium tests?
questions.ideal: Use sendKeys to type and clear to empty a field first. The soft keyboard often covers elements, so check isKeyboardShown and call hideKeyboard. For Enter, back or search use pressKey with an Android keycode. For non English text a unicode keyboard or adb keyboard helps type reliably.

questions.q: How do you find the appPackage and appActivity of an Android app?
questions.ideal: Launch the app and run adb shell dumpsys window, then read mCurrentFocus, which shows the app package and current focus activity. Alternatively run aapt dump badging on the apk or open it in APK Analyzer to read the AndroidManifest launcher activity. These values go into capabilities to start an installed app.

questions.q: How do you implement waits in Appium, and why should you avoid Thread.sleep?
questions.ideal: Use an explicit WebDriverWait with expected conditions like visibility or clickable, and a fluent wait to control polling and ignored exceptions. Keep implicit wait at zero to avoid mixing. Thread.sleep is a hard wait that slows every run and still fails when an animation or loading spinner takes longer than expected.

questions.q: How do you verify a toast message on Android with Appium?
questions.ideal: With the UiAutomator2 driver a toast can be found by xpath on android.widget.Toast and its text read. Timing is critical because the toast disappears in a short duration, so wait immediately after the action. The Espresso driver can also verify toasts, and as a last resort a screenshot with OCR works.

questions.q: How do you start and stop the Appium server from your test code instead of manually?
questions.ideal: Use AppiumServiceBuilder to build an AppiumDriverLocalService with a chosen or any free port, node path and appium main js, and redirect output to a log file. Start the service in a before suite hook and stop it in an after suite hook so the server lifecycle is controlled by the framework and parallel runs get separate ports.

questions.q: How do you capture screenshots, device logs and videos when a mobile test fails?
questions.ideal: Implement a listener such as ITestListener or an after hook that, on failure, takes a screenshot, pulls logcat on Android or syslog on iOS through log types, and stops the screen recording started with startRecordingScreen. All of it is attached to the Allure or Extent report so failures can be analysed without rerunning.

questions.q: How do you test app behaviour when it goes to the background and comes back?
questions.ideal: Call runAppInBackground for some seconds, or press home and use activateApp to bring it to the foreground. terminateApp and queryAppState verify app state transitions. Then assert the screen is resumed with data preserved, entered text kept, and that a session timeout forces relogin when the app was in the background too long.

questions.q: How do you test an app under different network conditions with Appium?
questions.ideal: On Android you can toggle wifi, mobile data and airplane mode through setNetworkConnection or toggle commands. Then verify offline messages, retries and caching when there is no internet. Emulators support netspeed throttling and cloud farms offer network profiles to simulate 2G or 3G speeds, which also shows how timeouts behave.

questions.q: How do you write one page object that works on both Android and iOS?
questions.ideal: Annotate each element with AndroidFindBy and iOSXCUITFindBy, then call PageFactory initElements with an AppiumFieldDecorator, which picks the locator for the running platform. Preferring accessibility id on both sides keeps one cross platform page object, and platform specific flows go into small subclasses or strategy methods.

questions.q: How do you automate device level actions like rotation, GPS location and locking the screen?
questions.ideal: Use rotate or set orientation to switch to landscape and verify layout. setLocation sets latitude and longitude for GPS features, and some teams use a mock location app on real devices. lock and unlock test resume after the lock screen, shake works on simulators, and clipboard commands check copy and paste.

questions.q: What do you need to run Appium tests on a real iOS device?
questions.ideal: XCUITest uses WebDriverAgent, which must be installed on the device, so you need code signing with an Apple developer team id passed as xcodeOrgId and a valid provisioning profile. Provide the device udid, a compatible Xcode, and often a unique WDA bundle id through updatedWDABundleId. Prebuilding WDA speeds up session creation.

questions.q: How do you automate fingerprint or Face ID authentication in mobile tests?
questions.ideal: On an Android emulator you enroll a fingerprint in settings and then send the fingerprint command, like adb emu finger touch, to match. On an iOS simulator Appium supports toggle enrollment and sending a matching or non match Face ID or Touch ID. On a real device biometrics cannot be faked, which is a known limitation, so apps expose a test build bypass.

questions.q: How can you collect mobile app performance metrics during Appium tests?
questions.ideal: On Android, getPerformanceData returns cpu, memory, battery and network traffic for the package, backed by dumpsys meminfo and batteryinfo. Measure cold start and startup time with activity launch timings. Store results per build against a baseline and fail on threshold breaches, watching the trend rather than single runs.

questions.q: When and how would you use image based element finding in Appium?
questions.ideal: Image locators help when there is no accessibility tree, for example canvas, games or custom views. In Appium 2 you install the images plugin, which uses OpenCV to find a template image on screen with a similarity threshold. It is slower and brittle across resolutions, so it is a last resort, while visual testing tools compare full screens to a baseline.

questions.q: How do you automate React Native or Flutter apps with Appium?
questions.ideal: For React Native, developers add testID and accessibility labels that map to accessibility id or content description. Flutter renders its own widgets, so you need semantics labels or the Appium Flutter driver or flutter integration driver. Espresso driver can help on Android. Developer collaboration on stable ids is the key to reliable locators.

questions.q: Compare Appium with Espresso and XCUITest. When would you choose each?
questions.ideal: Espresso and XCUITest are native gray box frameworks inside the app project, so they are faster and have built in synchronization through idling resources. Appium is black box and cross platform with one codebase in many languages, but slower. Developers often use Espresso and XCUITest for component flows while QA uses Appium for end to end journeys.

questions.q: How do you automate testing of push notifications on Android and iOS?
questions.ideal: Trigger the push from a backend API or test endpoint that calls Firebase FCM or APNs. On Android, openNotifications pulls down the notification shade where you verify title and text. On iOS you switch to the springboard bundle com.apple.springboard. Then tap the notification and assert correct navigation into the app.

questions.q: Your hybrid app tests fail to switch to the WebView context. How do you troubleshoot it?
questions.ideal: First check that get contexts lists a WEBVIEW at all, which requires the build to call setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled so it is debuggable. Then check chromedriver version mismatch with the device webview version. Enable chromedriver autodownload with the server flag or point chromedriverExecutableDir to a folder of matching drivers.

questions.q: Your mobile suite takes three hours. How would you bring PR feedback under thirty minutes?
questions.ideal: Run a small smoke suite on the critical path for every PR and push the full regression to nightly. Use parallel runs and sharding across many emulators, including headless emulator images in Docker. Replace UI setup with API setup and seed data, quarantine flaky tests, and track execution time per test to remove slow ones.

questions.q: Design a CI pipeline that builds a mobile app and runs Appium tests on a device farm.
questions.ideal: The pipeline triggers on pull request and nightly, builds with gradle or xcodebuild through fastlane, and handles signing with a keystore and certificates stored as secrets. It uploads the app to a device farm like BrowserStack or AWS Device Farm, runs Appium suites in parallel, then publishes artifacts such as reports, logs and videos and fails the build on test failures.

questions.q: How do you decide which devices and OS versions to cover for an app in the Indian market?
questions.ideal: Start from production analytics and market share to list top OS versions, manufacturers like Samsung, Xiaomi and Vivo, and screen sizes. India has many low end devices with low memory, so include budget devices. Group them into tiers by risk and priority, run tier one on every build and others nightly, and review the coverage matrix each quarter.

questions.q: How do you test app upgrades so existing users do not lose data or get crashes?
questions.ideal: Install the old version from the store build, create user data and log in, then install app with the new build over it. Verify data migration of the local database, preserved login state and settings, and run a smoke regression. Test skipping versions and the force update flow for minimum version, since many crashes come only from the upgrade path.

questions.q: How would you automate a login with OTP and a UPI payment flow on mobile?
questions.ideal: Avoid reading real SMS. Ask developers for a test hook such as a static or mock OTP in non production, or fetch the OTP through a backend API. Use the payment gateway sandbox for payment, and stub the UPI intent since a third party app cannot be automated reliably. Ensure these hooks are disabled in production for security.

questions.q: The app crashes only on a few Android devices in production. How do you investigate?
questions.ideal: Start from crash reporting in Crashlytics to get the stack trace, device models, OEM and OS version. Look for patterns such as out of memory on low RAM devices, ANR on slow ones, or API level differences. Reproduce on the same device in a cloud farm while capturing logcat, then add that device to the regression matrix.

questions.q: How would you add mobile accessibility testing to your automation strategy?
questions.ideal: Automate basic checks that every control has a content description or accessibility labels, run Accessibility Scanner on Android and the Xcode inspector on iOS, and check touch target size and color contrast. Manual testing with TalkBack and VoiceOver screen readers is still required for focus order and announcements, so plan both and treat issues as defects.

questions.q: How would you migrate a large Appium 1 framework to Appium 2?
questions.ideal: Install drivers separately with driver install and pin their versions. Update capabilities to W3C format with the appium vendor prefix, remove the old wd hub base path, and upgrade the java client. Deprecated TouchAction calls must be rewritten with W3C actions or mobile gestures. Migrate in phases, compare results, and add plugins only where needed.

questions.q: What are the UiAutomator2 and XCUITest drivers, and why does Appium need a separate driver per platform?
questions.ideal: Appium is only a server, the real automation happens in a driver. The UiAutomator2 driver wraps Google's UI Automator framework for Android, and the XCUITest driver wraps Apple's XCTest UI framework for iOS through WebDriverAgent. Each platform exposes a different native framework, so Appium uses a platform specific driver behind one common WebDriver API.

questions.q: How does an Appium test script talk to the device, and what is the role of the W3C WebDriver protocol?
questions.ideal: The test uses an Appium client library, such as the Java or Python client, which sends HTTP requests with JSON bodies to the Appium server. The format follows the W3C WebDriver protocol. The server creates a session with a session id and forwards each command to the platform driver, like UiAutomator2 or XCUITest, which executes it on the device and returns the result.

questions.q: How do you create and start an Android emulator for Appium testing?
questions.ideal: In Android Studio I open AVD Manager, pick a device profile such as a Pixel, download a system image for the API level I need, and create the virtual device. I start it from the UI or with emulator -avd name. Then adb devices should list it, for example emulator-5554, which I pass as the udid capability.

questions.q: What is the difference between APK, AAB and IPA files, and which can you install for testing?
questions.ideal: An APK is the installable Android package. An AAB is an Android App Bundle uploaded to Play Store, which generates split APKs, so for testing we usually build an APK or use bundletool. An IPA is a signed iOS app for real devices and needs a provisioning profile, while simulators need a .app build. The file path goes in the app capability for install.

questions.q: What is the difference between driver.quit, terminateApp and closing the app in Appium?
questions.ideal: driver.quit ends the whole Appium session and releases the device, so it belongs in teardown. terminateApp kills only the app process by bundle id or package, while the session stays alive, and activateApp brings it back. backgroundApp sends it to the background temporarily. Older closeApp and launchApp were removed in Appium 2, so I use terminate and activate instead.

questions.q: Which Android developer options and device settings do you change before running automation?
questions.ideal: I enable developer options and USB debugging so adb can connect. I turn the window, transition and animator animation scale to off to reduce flakiness, enable stay awake and remove screen lock so the screen never sleeps, allow install via USB, and disable battery optimization so the system does not kill the Appium server or app.

questions.q: How do you read element properties like text, enabled or checked in Appium, and how do they differ on Android and iOS?
questions.ideal: I use getText or getAttribute. On Android useful attributes are text, content-desc, resource-id, enabled, checked, selected and clickable. On iOS the attribute names differ, such as name, label, value, enabled and visible, and value holds switch state. So my page objects wrap attribute reads per platform instead of assuming the same names everywhere.

questions.q: How do you select a value from a dropdown, spinner or picker wheel in a mobile app?
questions.ideal: On Android a spinner opens a list, so I tap it, scroll the list if needed, and tap the option by text. On iOS a picker wheel can be set directly with sendKeys of the value, or with the mobile selectPickerWheelValue command. Date pickers vary by app, so I prefer setting values through the picker wheel or input field rather than complex swipes.

questions.q: How do you use the Appium server log to debug a failing test?
questions.ideal: The Appium server log shows every HTTP command, its endpoint, parameters and response. I run the server with log level debug and log timestamps, then look for the failing command and its error or stack trace. Session creation errors show which capabilities were rejected, and timing gaps show slow commands. I save the log as a CI artifact for every failed run.

questions.q: In Appium 2, what are drivers and plugins, and how do you install them?
questions.ideal: In Appium 2 the core server ships without platforms. Drivers like uiautomator2 or xcuitest are installed with appium driver install, and plugins that change server behaviour, such as the images or gestures plugin, with appium plugin install, then enabled with --use-plugins. Extensions live in APPIUM_HOME and are updated with appium driver update, so CI pins versions.

questions.q: How do you find an element in a long, lazily loaded list that is not on screen yet?
questions.ideal: Lists like RecyclerView only render visible rows, so the element does not exist until scrolled. On Android I use UiScrollable scrollIntoView through the android uiautomator locator. Otherwise I loop with mobile scrollGesture or swipe, re find the element after each scroll because views are recycled, and stop after a max scroll count or when the end of list repeats.

questions.q: When would you use UiSelector, iOS predicate strings or iOS class chain locators instead of XPath?
questions.ideal: Accessibility id and resource id are first choice. When those are missing, native locators beat XPath. On Android a UiSelector through the android uiautomator strategy can match text, description or scroll. On iOS predicate strings filter by attributes like label CONTAINS, and class chain walks the hierarchy. Both run natively, so they are much faster than XPath, which builds the whole page source.

questions.q: How do you push files to a device, pull logs from it and use the clipboard in Appium tests?
questions.ideal: pushFile sends a base64 encoded file to a device path, for example an image into the sdcard pictures folder so an upload test can pick it from the gallery, and pullFile fetches files such as app logs. setClipboardText and getClipboardText let me test copy and paste. On iOS paths use the app container, for example the bundle id plus documents folder.

questions.q: How do you automate a flow that moves between your app and another app, like the browser or settings?
questions.ideal: I call activateApp with the other app package or bundle id, such as Chrome or Settings, interact with it, then activateApp with my own package to return. queryAppState confirms whether an app is running in foreground or background. Deep links or Android intents also open specific screens. The session stays the same, only the active app changes.

questions.q: Which timeout capabilities do you tune in Appium, such as newCommandTimeout, and why?
questions.ideal: newCommandTimeout decides how long the server waits for the next command before ending the session, so I raise it while debugging with breakpoints. adbExecTimeout and uiautomator2ServerLaunchTimeout help on slow devices or CI emulators, and wdaLaunchTimeout helps iOS. Without tuning, sessions get killed or fail to start on slow farms, which looks like random flakiness.

questions.q: How do you test a mobile app in different languages, locales and right to left layouts?
questions.ideal: I set the language and locale capabilities, or change device settings, so the app starts in that locale. Locators must not rely on visible text, so I use ids and keep expected strings in translation resource files. I check truncation and overflow for long languages, right to left mirroring for Arabic, and date format, currency and number formatting per region.

questions.q: What are the Appium mobile execute methods, and give some examples you have used.
questions.ideal: Drivers expose extra features through executeScript with mobile: commands, for example mobile shell to run adb shell commands, mobile deepLink, mobile clickGesture or swipeGesture, and mobile startActivity. They are driver specific, so Android and iOS have different sets. Some, like mobile shell, need the server started with relaxed security or allow insecure for that feature.

questions.q: Your hybrid or mobile web test fails because of a Chromedriver version mismatch. How do you fix it?
questions.ideal: Appium uses Chromedriver to drive Chrome and WebViews, and it must match the Chrome or Android System WebView version on the device. I check the WebView version, then either set chromedriverExecutable to the matching binary, point to a chromedriver directory, or start the server with chromedriver autodownload allowed. Pinning device WebView versions on farms prevents repeat mismatches.

questions.q: Why can an element be found but isDisplayed returns false or a click fails in a mobile app?
questions.ideal: findElement only proves the element exists in the hierarchy. It can still be off screen, covered by an overlay or keyboard, or mid animation, so isDisplayed is false or the tap lands elsewhere. I wait for visibility and clickable state, scroll it into view, dismiss overlays and keyboard, and avoid clicking on presence alone.

questions.q: How do you automate Android hardware and system keys like back, home and the recent apps button?
questions.ideal: I use pressKey with an AndroidKey code, such as BACK, HOME or APP_SWITCH for recent apps, or driver.navigate().back(). openNotifications pulls down the notification shade for checks. Testing the back button matters because it can skip screens or lose data. On iOS there is no back key, so I tap the navigation bar back button instead.

questions.q: Your Android tests hang for seconds at every findElement because the app has continuous animations. How do you fix it?
questions.ideal: UiAutomator2 waits for the UI to be idle before each action, and endless animations like a Lottie loader never go idle. I lower waitForIdleTimeout through the settings API with updateSettings, disable animation scale on the device, and ask developers for a test build flag that stops decorative animations. That removes multi second waits per command.

questions.q: Your iOS suite is very slow and page source takes seconds. How do you speed up element lookup?
questions.ideal: XPath forces XCUITest to build a full snapshot of the hierarchy, which is slow on big screens. I replace XPath with accessibility id first, then class chain or predicate locators. I ask developers to add accessibilityIdentifier values, tune settings like snapshotMaxDepth or excluded attributes, and avoid calling page source in loops.

questions.q: What do you need to configure to run Appium tests in parallel on several local devices?
questions.ideal: Each session needs its own udid and unique ports, systemPort for UiAutomator2, wdaLocalPort for iOS WebDriverAgent, chromedriverPort or mjpegServerPort for WebViews and video. One server can host many sessions or I run multiple servers. In the framework I keep the driver in a ThreadLocal and map each thread to one device so tests never share sessions.

questions.q: How do you connect Appium nodes to Selenium Grid 4 to share devices across a team?
questions.ideal: Selenium Grid 4 can relay sessions to Appium servers. Each node gets a TOML config file with a relay section pointing at the Appium URL and stereotypes listing device capabilities. The router and session queue accept requests, and the distributor matches capabilities to free devices. This gives one endpoint for the team and scales shared devices without hardcoding udids.

questions.q: How would you automate a feature that scans a QR code or uses the camera?
questions.ideal: Real cameras cannot see a test screen, so I inject images. Android emulators support a virtual scene or custom image as camera input, and many cloud device farms offer camera image injection. Where that is not possible, developers add a test hook or deep link that passes the decoded QR payload, and I test the scanner itself with a small manual check.

questions.q: How do you test error states and edge cases in a mobile app that depend on backend responses?
questions.ideal: I point the app at a mock server like WireMock through a base url config in a debug build, or route traffic via a proxy such as mitmproxy to rewrite responses. Stubs return 500 errors, timeouts, empty states and odd payloads. On Android the debug network security config must trust the proxy certificate. This makes rare edge cases repeatable.

questions.q: Your proxy cannot see app traffic because of SSL pinning. How do you deal with it in testing?
questions.ideal: Pinning rejects the proxy certificate, which is the intended security. For testing I ask for a debug or test build flavor with pinning disabled or a network security config that trusts user certificates. Tools like Frida or objection can bypass it on rooted devices for security testing. I still verify that the production release build keeps pinning enabled.

questions.q: How do you test a mobile app on tablets, foldables and split screen modes?
questions.ideal: Large screens use different layouts, so I run key flows on tablet and foldable emulators. I test fold and unfold, split screen multi window and rotation because each causes a configuration change and activity recreation, which can lose state. I check responsive layout breakpoints with screenshots, and confirm typed data and scroll position survive the change.

questions.q: When would you write a custom Appium plugin, and how does it work?
questions.ideal: A plugin is a Node.js npm package that extends BasePlugin and can intercept or override any command, or add new routes. I would write one for cross cutting behaviour like extra logging, auto waits, self healing locators or a custom command for test data. It is installed with appium plugin install and enabled with use plugins, so test code stays clean.

questions.q: How do you automate a login that opens Google sign in or an OAuth page in a custom tab or system browser?
questions.ideal: OAuth often opens a Chrome custom tab or system browser outside my app context. I switch to the browser context or activate the browser app, sign in with a dedicated test account, and wait for the redirect deep link back. For most tests I bypass it with token injection or API login, keeping one end to end test for the real flow.

questions.q: Would you build an in house device lab or use a cloud device farm? Explain the trade offs.
questions.ideal: An in house device lab gives fast, cheap runs and access to internal networks, but needs maintenance of USB hubs, battery swelling, OS updates and staff. A cloud farm like BrowserStack offers wide device coverage instantly but costs per minute and raises security and data privacy questions. I often combine a small local lab for PR checks with cloud for the wider matrix.

questions.q: What quality gates would you set before a mobile release goes to the app stores?
questions.ideal: Before submission the build must pass automated regression, smoke on a device matrix and performance budgets for app size and startup time. Beta via TestFlight or the Play Console tracks the crash free rate in Crashlytics. Then a staged rollout releases to small percentages while monitoring. Because store apps cannot roll back, risky features ship behind a feature flag or kill switch.

questions.q: How would you design testing for an offline first mobile app that syncs when connectivity returns?
questions.ideal: I toggle airplane mode or network conditions, create and edit records offline, then reconnect and verify the sync queue uploads them. I test conflict resolution when the same record changed on server and device, app kills mid sync, and flaky reconnects. I validate the local database and server for data integrity, checking no duplicates and no data loss.

questions.q: Tests pass locally but fail on the cloud device farm. How do you investigate?
questions.ideal: I compare environment differences first, the exact device model, OS version and capabilities on the farm. Farms add latency and network routes, so internal APIs may need a tunnel and timeouts may be too tight. I download video, device logs and Appium logs to find the failing step, then reproduce on the same device remotely and isolate one variable at a time.

questions.q: How do you protect test data and credentials when using shared public device clouds?
questions.ideal: Shared devices may be reused by other customers, so I only use synthetic data and test accounts, never real customer data. Credentials come from a vault at runtime. I enable device cleanup or wipe after sessions, or pay for private dedicated devices for sensitive apps. Internal APIs go through a secure tunnel, and I check data residency and compliance terms with security.

questions.q: For a new mobile project, how would you choose between Appium, Maestro, Detox, Espresso and XCUITest?
questions.ideal: Espresso and XCUITest are fastest and most stable but platform specific and owned by developers. Detox is grey box and great for React Native. Maestro uses simple YAML flows with built in waits, good for quick end to end checks. Appium is cross platform and language agnostic, fitting QA teams with Java skills. I pick by team skills, app tech, speed and flakiness, often mixing layers.

questions.q: How do you test a mobile app whose screens are driven by server configuration and A/B experiments?
questions.ideal: Screens come from server JSON, so I validate the contract with schema tests on the backend and renderer tests on the client. In automation I force each experiment variant or remote config through overrides or test users pinned to a variant, so results are deterministic. Because combinations explode, I choose high risk combinations and verify unknown components degrade gracefully.

questions.q: How do you prepare your app and test suite for a new major Android or iOS release?
questions.ideal: I read release notes for behaviour changes, deprecations and new privacy permissions, then install developer preview or beta builds on devices and emulators. I add a CI lane running the regression suite against the beta. I update Xcode and the Appium driver early because they often break. Raising targetSdkVersion is tested separately since it activates new restrictions.

questions.q: How would you detect crashes and ANRs automatically during your Appium runs instead of only seeing generic failures?
questions.ideal: I add an after test hook that checks queryAppState and scans logcat for FATAL EXCEPTION and ANR entries, plus iOS crash logs. If found, the failure is tagged as app crash with the stack trace attached instead of element not found. I also link the run to Crashlytics or Firebase crash reporting so developers see the same crash in their tools.

questions.q: How would you build scalable, self hosted Android emulator infrastructure for CI?
questions.ideal: I run headless emulators inside Docker Android containers, which need KVM hardware acceleration, so I use bare metal or nested virtualization capable cloud instances. Kubernetes orchestrates emulator pods with Appium per pod. Quick boot snapshots keep warm emulators ready, cutting startup time. I track cost per run against device farm pricing, keeping real devices for final checks.

questions.q: What are load, stress, spike, soak and scalability testing?
questions.ideal: Load testing checks behaviour at expected users. Stress testing pushes beyond limits to find the breaking point. Spike testing applies sudden surges. Soak or endurance testing runs long to find memory leaks. Scalability testing checks how performance changes as resources grow.

questions.q: Which metrics do you measure in performance testing, and what do percentiles tell you?
questions.ideal: Key metrics are response time, throughput, error rate, concurrent users and server resource use such as CPU and memory. Percentiles like p95 and p99 show what the slowest users experience, which the average hides.

questions.q: Explain the main JMeter components: thread group, samplers, listeners, assertions, timers and config elements.
questions.ideal: A thread group defines users, ramp up and loops, samplers send requests, assertions validate responses, timers add think time, config elements like CSV Data Set supply data, controllers add logic and listeners show results, though heavy listeners should be avoided during runs.

questions.q: How do you design a realistic workload model for a performance test?
questions.ideal: Use production analytics or logs to find the critical business flows, their transaction mix and peak load, convert it into arrival rate or concurrent users with think time and pacing, use unique parameterised data, ramp up to a steady state and compare against agreed SLAs.

questions.q: What are correlation and parameterization in performance scripts, and how do you handle dynamic values like session ids?
questions.ideal: Correlation extracts dynamic server values like session IDs or CSRF tokens from a response using regex or JSON extractors and passes them to later requests. Parameterisation replaces hard coded data such as users with values from a CSV so a recorded script replays correctly under load.

questions.q: How do you generate very high load, and what is distributed testing in JMeter, k6 or Gatling?
questions.ideal: Run tests in non GUI mode and distribute load across several load generators, for example a JMeter controller with agents or k6 and Gatling in the cloud, while monitoring the generators so they do not become the bottleneck and making sure bandwidth is enough.

questions.q: Response times degrade at 500 users. How do you find the bottleneck?
questions.ideal: Correlate response time against load with monitoring or APM, then check each tier: CPU, memory, disk and network, database slow queries, indexes, connection pools and locks, application thread pools, garbage collection and heap, and profile the code with thread dumps. Fix the biggest bottleneck first and retest.

questions.q: How do you include performance testing in an agile CI/CD pipeline and set pass or fail criteria?
questions.ideal: Run small performance smoke tests on every build and larger tests nightly with tools like k6 or JMeter, compare against a baseline, set thresholds on percentiles and error rate as quality gates, show trends on Grafana dashboards and use a production like environment so results are meaningful.

questions.q: What are think time and pacing, and why do they matter in a load test?
questions.ideal: Think time is the pause a real user takes between actions, and pacing is the gap between iterations of the whole script. Without them virtual users hammer the server unrealistically and the throughput or request rate is wrong. In JMeter you add a constant or random timer to model realistic user behaviour.

questions.q: What is ramp up time, and how do you choose it for a test?
questions.ideal: Ramp up is the time taken to start all virtual users or threads gradually. A gradual ramp up allows warm up of caches and JIT and shows at which load response times degrade. After it the test holds a steady state for the main duration, then ramp down. A very short ramp up turns the test into a spike test.

questions.q: What is the difference between concurrent users and simultaneous users?
questions.ideal: Concurrent users are logged in with active sessions but spread their actions with think time. Simultaneous users hit the same request at the same moment. To test that you use a rendezvous point in LoadRunner or a synchronizing timer in JMeter, which holds each virtual user until a group is ready and then releases them together.

questions.q: How do you record a script in JMeter, and what do you clean up afterwards?
questions.ideal: Use the HTTP Test Script Recorder as a proxy on a port, set the browser to that proxy and install the JMeter root CA certificate for HTTPS. Alternatively use the BlazeMeter extension or convert a HAR file. Filter out static resources and third party calls, then cleanup by renaming samplers, grouping transactions and adding correlation and think time.

questions.q: What is the difference between client side and server side performance?
questions.ideal: Server side performance is how fast the backend, APIs and database respond under load, which JMeter measures. Client side performance is what the browser does after that: downloading assets, executing JavaScript and rendering. Page load time includes both plus network latency. Tools like Lighthouse and DevTools analyse the client side.

questions.q: What is a baseline in performance testing, and how is it different from a benchmark?
questions.ideal: A baseline is a reference point of your own application measured under known load in the same environment, used to detect regression between releases. A benchmark compares against an industry standard, SLA or competitor. Baselines need consistent environment, data and scripts, and repeat runs to make sure the numbers are stable.

questions.q: How do you gather non functional requirements before starting a performance test?
questions.ideal: I gather NFRs from stakeholders and the product owner, and validate them with production logs and analytics. Key items are the SLA response time at a percentile like p95, peak load in the peak hour, the transaction mix, error tolerance and expected growth. Vague goals like fast must become numbers before scripting.

questions.q: Why should JMeter tests be run in non GUI mode, and how do you do it?
questions.ideal: The GUI is meant for script creation and debugging only; it consumes memory and resources and distorts results at load. Run from the command line with jmeter -n -t script -l results.jtl, disable heavy listeners like View Results Tree, and generate the HTML report dashboard with the -e and -o options from the JTL file.

questions.q: What is Little's Law, and how do you use it to plan a load test?
questions.ideal: Little's Law says concurrent users equal throughput multiplied by response time plus think time. If the target is 50 requests per second with 2 seconds response time and 8 seconds think time, you need 500 users. I use the formula to calculate users and pacing so the test hits the required throughput.

questions.q: Explain the important settings of CSV Data Set Config in JMeter.
questions.ideal: CSV Data Set Config reads test data rows into variable names split by a delimiter. Sharing mode controls whether all threads share one file pointer or each thread group gets its own. Recycle on EOF restarts the file, while stop thread on EOF ends the thread when data runs out, which is important when each login or order needs unique data and no duplicate.

questions.q: Which JMeter logic controllers do you use most, and why?
questions.ideal: The transaction controller groups requests into one business transaction for reporting. The if controller adds conditions, the loop controller repeats steps and the throughput controller sends a percentage of users to a flow. The once only controller is used to login once per thread, the module controller allows reuse of fragments and the runtime controller limits duration.

questions.q: What are the main concepts of a k6 test script?
questions.ideal: k6 scripts are written in JavaScript. Options define virtual users and duration, or stages for ramping up and down. Scenarios with executors choose open or closed models. Checks validate responses without stopping the test, while thresholds are pass or fail criteria like p95 under 500 ms. You execute with k6 run from the CLI, which suits CI.

questions.q: What are the main building blocks of a Gatling simulation?
questions.ideal: A Gatling simulation class defines the HTTP protocol, one or more scenario chains of requests with pauses, and an injection profile like ramp users or constant users per second. Feeders supply test data, checks validate and extract values, and the DSL is available in Scala, Java or Kotlin. Gatling produces a detailed HTML report after the run.

questions.q: What is the difference between an open and a closed workload model?
questions.ideal: In a closed model a fixed number of users loop with think time, so when the server slows the request rate drops. In an open model new requests arrive at a fixed arrival rate regardless of response times, like real internet traffic. Closed models can hide problems through coordinated omission. Use constant arrival rate in k6 or the arrivals thread group or throughput shaping timer in JMeter.

questions.q: How do you read and analyse a JMeter HTML dashboard report?
questions.ideal: In the HTML dashboard I first check the error rate and error types, then percentiles like p90, p95 and p99 per transaction rather than averages. The Apdex score summarises user satisfaction. Over time graphs show if response time rises with active threads, and whether throughput in transactions per second flattens, which signals saturation.

questions.q: What do the HTTP Cookie Manager, Cache Manager and Header Manager do in JMeter?
questions.ideal: The cookie manager stores and sends cookies per thread like a browser, keeping session cookies such as JSESSIONID. The cache manager simulates browser caching of static content. The header manager adds headers like content type or an Authorization bearer token. Together with embedded resources and parallel downloads they make virtual users behave like real browsers.

questions.q: How do you detect a memory leak during performance testing?
questions.ideal: Run a long soak test and monitor heap usage and garbage collection. A healthy heap shows a sawtooth that returns to the same level after full GC; a memory leak shows an increasing trend and longer GC pauses until out of memory. Take a heap dump and analyse it in Eclipse MAT or a profiler like VisualVM to find the objects growing.

questions.q: How do you confirm that the database is the bottleneck and help fix it?
questions.ideal: Correlate response time with database metrics, then check the slow query log, AWR or pg_stat_statements for top queries. Review the execution plan for full table scans and missing index. Also check connection pool exhaustion and locks or blocking sessions. Share the evidence with developers and retest after each fix.

questions.q: How do APM tools help you during a load test?
questions.ideal: An APM tool such as Dynatrace, AppDynamics or New Relic shows each business transaction with distributed tracing across services, so you see which call or query is slow. Code level hotspots point to exact methods. It also shows infrastructure CPU and memory, and you correlate all of it with the load test timeline to explain degradation.

questions.q: How do you use thread dumps to analyse a slow or hung Java application under load?
questions.ideal: Take multiple dumps with jstack at intervals of a few seconds. Look for many blocked threads waiting on the same lock, a deadlock, or a thread pool exhausted with all workers waiting on a database or external call. For high CPU, map the busiest thread from top -H to its stack in the thread dump.

questions.q: How do you performance test a microservices application with many dependencies?
questions.ideal: Test each microservice in isolation at component level, using service virtualization with WireMock stubs for downstream dependencies, so you know each capacity. Then run end to end tests of key journeys. Distributed tracing shows which service adds latency, and the slowest service or shared resource usually defines overall throughput.

questions.q: How do you handle OAuth tokens and logins when running a large load test?
questions.ideal: Generate an OAuth access token once per user in a setup thread group or once only controller rather than logging in on every iteration, and store it in a variable or shared property. Handle expiry by calling the refresh token flow. Check rate limit rules on the identity provider so the auth server does not become a fake bottleneck.

questions.q: How can caching make your performance results misleading, and how do you control it?
questions.ideal: If every user requests the same item, the cache hit ratio is unrealistically high and results look great. Use parameterization with unique data matching production patterns, decide whether to test warm cache or cold cache, and include a warm up period. Also know whether the CDN and database buffer cache are in scope so results are not skewed.

questions.q: How do you make sure the load generator itself is not the bottleneck?
questions.ideal: Monitor the load generator CPU, memory and network bandwidth during the test. Increase JMeter heap with Xmx, remove heavy listeners like View Results Tree, use non GUI mode and efficient extractors. If CPU stays above 70 percent, scale out with distributed testing across more generators, otherwise the injector adds false latency.

questions.q: How do you use performance test results for capacity planning?
questions.ideal: Capacity planning starts with a forecast of growth and peak load. Tests find the throughput per instance at acceptable utilization, for example CPU below 70 percent. Divide projected peak by per instance capacity and add headroom of 30 to 50 percent. Then choose horizontal scaling or vertical scaling and estimate cloud cost.

questions.q: How would you prepare an e-commerce site for a big festive sale with ten times normal traffic?
questions.ideal: Model peak load from previous sales and run load, spike test and soak tests in a production like environment. Validate autoscaling and pre warm servers, push static content to a CDN and caching layers, and add rate limiting or a waiting room queue. Use feature flags for graceful degradation of non critical features and run a war room with live monitoring during the sale.

questions.q: When and how would you run performance tests in production safely?
questions.ideal: Production is the only true environment, so some teams test there carefully. Prefer shadow traffic or replay, and synthetic monitoring of key journeys. For real load tests choose an off peak window, limit blast radius with a kill switch and abort criteria, mark test data for cleanup, and get change approval from stakeholders and the operations team.

questions.q: Your test passed but production was slow at the same load. What could explain it?
questions.ideal: Common causes are environment differences in sizing or configuration, smaller data volume in the test database, and a workload model with the wrong traffic mix. Third party dependencies may have been mocks, network latency and CDN paths differ, and caching was warmer in tests. I compare each factor, fix the model and rerun to close the gap.

questions.q: How do you test and validate autoscaling behaviour of an application?
questions.ideal: Run a step and spike load and verify scale out happens at the configured metrics, such as CPU threshold or custom metrics like queue depth. Measure how long new instances take, including cold start and warm up, and whether errors appear meanwhile. Then reduce load to validate scale in and cooldown, and check cost and maximum instance limits.

questions.q: What is the difference between performance testing and performance engineering?
questions.ideal: Performance testing measures behaviour under load late in the cycle. Performance engineering builds performance in from architecture design review, setting a performance budget per service, profiling code, catching anti patterns like N plus one queries, and shift left testing in CI. It continues with production monitoring feeding back into design and capacity decisions.

questions.q: How do you measure and improve front end performance at scale?
questions.ideal: Track Core Web Vitals: LCP for loading, CLS for layout shift and INP for interaction to next paint. Use Lighthouse in CI for lab data and real user monitoring for field data across devices. Improve by reducing bundle size and JavaScript, compression, image optimisation, lazy loading and CDN caching.

questions.q: How do you report performance test results to managers and stakeholders?
questions.ideal: Start with an executive summary with a clear pass fail against each SLA and a go no go risk view. Show percentiles such as p95 instead of averages, trends and comparison with the previous baseline in simple graphs. List bottlenecks and findings with evidence, then concrete recommendations with owners and expected impact.

questions.q: Why should you add assertions to a load test script, and what would you check?
questions.ideal: Without assertions a server can return an error page or login page with status 200, and the tool counts it as success, giving false positives and great looking but wrong response times. I add response assertions on status code and body content, like expected text or JSON field, plus occasional duration assertions. Keep them light because heavy assertions load the generator.

questions.q: What is the difference between hits per second, requests per second and transactions per second?
questions.ideal: Hits per second counts every request to the server, including embedded resources like images, CSS and scripts. Requests per second is similar for APIs. Transactions per second counts complete business transactions, such as a login or checkout, that may contain many requests. Requirements are usually stated as transactions, while servers and load balancers see hits, so reports should show both throughput views.

questions.q: What is a transaction in a performance test script, and how do you create one in JMeter?
questions.ideal: A transaction groups the requests behind one user action, such as login or add to cart, so we measure its end to end response time. In JMeter I wrap the requests in a Transaction Controller, optionally with generate parent sample, and use a clear naming convention like 01_Login. Reports then show business level timing, which stakeholders understand.

questions.q: What are the main phases of a performance testing project?
questions.ideal: First gather requirements and NFRs, then a test plan with workload model and scope. Next script development with correlation, then environment setup and test data. Execution starts with a small smoke run, followed by load, stress and soak runs while monitoring. Finally analysis of results, bottlenecks and a report with recommendations, then retests after fixes.

questions.q: Why does the test environment matter so much for performance testing, and what should match production?
questions.ideal: Results are only valid in a production like environment. Hardware and instance size, configuration such as pool sizes and JVM settings, data volume, and network topology including load balancers should match. If the environment is half size, scaling results linearly is risky, so we document the ratio and clearly limit what we extrapolate.

questions.q: How would you choose between JMeter, LoadRunner, k6 and Gatling for a project?
questions.ideal: JMeter is free, mature and GUI based with many plugins. LoadRunner is commercial with a cost but supports many protocols like Citrix and SAP. k6 uses JavaScript and is developer friendly with easy CI integration. Gatling has a Scala or Java DSL and efficient engine. I decide by protocol support, team skills, budget and CI integration.

questions.q: What is a smoke or shakeout run before a load test, and why do you do it?
questions.ideal: Before the full test I run a smoke or shakeout with a few users for a short time. It validates the scripts, correlation and assertions, checks test data is ready, confirms monitoring dashboards collect metrics, and that the environment is stable. Finding a broken script here saves wasting an expensive full scale test window.

questions.q: Which server side resources do you monitor during a load test, and why?
questions.ideal: Client metrics show symptoms, server metrics show causes. I monitor CPU utilization, memory and heap, disk IO, and network bandwidth on every tier, plus thread and connection pools, and database query time and locks. Correlating a response time jump with a saturated resource, like CPU at ninety five percent, points to the bottleneck.

questions.q: What is the difference between elapsed time, latency and connect time in JMeter results?
questions.ideal: Elapsed time is from sending the request to receiving the last byte. Latency is time to first byte, so it includes server processing. Connect time is the TCP and SSL handshake, which is included in latency. Elapsed minus latency is download time. High connect time suggests network or keep alive issues, while high latency points to the backend.

questions.q: What is the difference between variables and properties in JMeter, and how do you pass values from the command line?
questions.ideal: Variables are local to each thread, for example extracted tokens or user defined variables. Properties are global and shared by all threads. From the command line I pass -Jhost=value and read it with the __P function, often with a default. This lets one script run against different environments, user counts and durations without editing it.

questions.q: How do you drive a test at a fixed target throughput instead of a fixed number of users?
questions.ideal: To hit a target TPS I use the Constant Throughput Timer or the Throughput Shaping Timer plugin, combined with the Concurrency or Arrivals Thread Group. There must be enough threads, otherwise the target cannot be reached when responses slow down. In k6 the constant arrival rate executor does this natively, which is an open model.

questions.q: Which JMeter plugins and advanced thread groups do you use, and why?
questions.ideal: I install the Plugins Manager first, usually via the command line for CI. The Ultimate Thread Group and Concurrency Thread Group give flexible stepped load profiles, and the Arrivals Thread Group gives an arrival rate model. Custom graphs like transactions per second and response times over time help analysis. I keep plugin versions pinned so tests are reproducible.

questions.q: Why is JSR223 with Groovy preferred over BeanShell in JMeter, and when do you script?
questions.ideal: JSR223 with Groovy compiles and caches scripts, so it is much faster than BeanShell, which is interpreted every time and burns generator CPU. I use a JSR223 preprocessor or postprocessor for custom logic like building signatures, parsing complex JSON or conditional data. I enable cache compiled script and avoid inlining variables in the script text, passing them as parameters.

questions.q: What is Locust and how is a Locust test structured?
questions.ideal: Locust is a Python load testing tool. I define a class extending HttpUser with methods marked by the task decorator, weighted to set the mix, and a wait time such as between one and three seconds as think time. It runs with a web UI dashboard or headless in CI, and scales distributed with a master and many workers.
