It is multi paradigm, supporting object oriented and functional styles, and has a rich standard library plus many third party libraries.

questions.q: What are list and dictionary comprehensions, and when should you avoid them?
questions.ideal: A list comprehension builds a list in one expression, like squares of numbers with an if clause as a filter. A dict comprehension builds a dictionary the same way. They are usually faster than loops. Avoid deeply nested ones that hurt readability, and use a generator expression with parentheses when the data is large, since it is lazy and saves memory.

questions.q: What is the difference between is and == in Python?
questions.ideal: == checks equality of values using the eq dunder method, while is checks identity, meaning both names point to the same object with the same id. Comparisons to None should use is None. Small integers and some strings are cached through interning, so is may appear to work for them, but it is unreliable for value comparisons.

questions.q: How does exception handling work in Python, including else, finally and custom exceptions?
questions.ideal: Code in try runs, and except catches specific exception types; avoid bare except. The else block runs only if no exception occurred, and finally always runs for cleanup. You raise errors with raise, and create a custom exception by subclassing Exception. Using raise from keeps exception chaining so the original cause appears in the traceback.

questions.q: What are modules and packages in Python, and what does if name equals main do?
questions.ideal: A module is a single py file, and a package is a directory of modules, traditionally marked by an init.py file. You use import or from import, and Python searches sys path and PYTHONPATH. The check if name equals main runs code only when the file is executed directly as a script, not when it is imported by another module.

questions.q: Why do we use virtual environments in Python, and how do you manage dependencies?
questions.ideal: A virtual environment created with venv gives each project isolation, so different projects can use different package versions without conflicts. After you activate it, pip installs packages only there. Dependencies are listed in requirements.txt with pinning of versions for reproducible installs. Tools like Poetry, Pipenv, uv or Conda add lock files and easier management.

questions.q: How do you work with strings in Python: slicing, immutability and formatting?
questions.ideal: Strings are immutable, so methods like replace, strip and split return new strings. Slicing uses start, stop and step, with negative index support, so step minus one reverses a string. f-strings are the modern formatting method. Use join to build strings from lists efficiently, and encode and decode to convert between unicode text and bytes.

questions.q: What are lambda functions, map, filter and reduce in Python?
questions.ideal: A lambda is an anonymous function limited to a single expression, often used as a key function in sorted. map applies a function to each item, filter keeps items where the function returns true, and reduce from functools combines items into one value. In modern Python a comprehension is often clearer than map and filter.

questions.q: Explain classes, init, self, inheritance and super in Python.
questions.ideal: A class defines objects; init is the initializer that sets attributes, and self refers to the current instance. Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and override parent methods, and super calls the parent implementation. Python supports multiple inheritance, resolving methods through the MRO, the method resolution order computed by C3 linearization, which super follows.

questions.q: What is the difference between instance methods, classmethod and staticmethod?
questions.ideal: An instance method takes self and works with instance data. A classmethod, marked with the decorator, takes cls and works with the class, so it is used for factory methods or alternative constructors like from json. A staticmethod takes neither and has no access to class or instance state; it is a utility helper grouped in the class.

questions.q: What are context managers in Python, and how do you write one?
questions.ideal: A context manager is used with the with statement to set up and clean up resources like files, locks or database connections. A class implements enter and exit, where exit receives any exception and can suppress it. The contextlib contextmanager decorator lets you write one as a generator with a single yield. Cleanup is guaranteed even when errors occur.

questions.q: What is the difference between an iterable, an iterator and a generator?
questions.ideal: An iterable is any object with iter that returns an iterator, like a list. An iterator implements next and raises StopIteration when exhausted, and can be consumed only in one pass. A generator is an easy way to build an iterator using yield, producing values lazily, which saves memory for large or infinite sequences.

questions.q: What is the mutable default argument problem in Python, and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal: Default arguments are evaluated once at function definition time, not on each call. If the default is a mutable list or dict, the same object is shared and changes persist across calls, causing surprising bugs. The fix is to use None as the default and create a new object inside the function when the argument is None.

questions.q: Explain Python scope rules, closures, and the global and nonlocal keywords.
questions.ideal: Python resolves names with LEGB: local, enclosing, global and builtin. A closure is an inner function that remembers variables from its enclosing scope, which is how decorators work. To assign to a module variable inside a function use global, and to modify an enclosing variable use nonlocal. Beware late binding of loop variables in closures.

questions.q: How are type hints used in Python, and are they enforced at runtime?
questions.ideal: Type hints annotate parameters and return values using the typing module, with Optional, Union and generics like list of int or TypeVar. They are not enforced at runtime by the interpreter; a static checker such as mypy or Pyright catches errors before running. Libraries like Pydantic and FastAPI do use them for runtime validation and documentation.

questions.q: How does FastAPI use Pydantic models and dependency injection?
questions.ideal: FastAPI uses Pydantic BaseModel classes to declare request bodies, so it handles validation and returns 422 errors automatically, and a response model controls serialization. Depends provides dependency injection for database sessions, authentication and shared logic. It generates OpenAPI docs with Swagger UI from type hints, and supports async def endpoints on ASGI.

questions.q: How does asyncio work, and what happens if you call blocking code inside a coroutine?
questions.ideal: asyncio runs a single threaded event loop that schedules coroutines defined with async def. await yields control while waiting for IO, so many IO bound tasks run concurrently, and gather or create task runs them together. Blocking calls like time sleep or sync database drivers freeze the whole loop, so use async libraries or move them to run in executor or asyncio to thread.

questions.q: What are descriptors in Python, and how does property use them?
questions.ideal: A descriptor is an object that defines get, set or delete and controls attribute access when stored on a class. property is a built in descriptor that turns methods into managed attributes with getters and setters. A data descriptor defines set and takes priority over instance attributes. ORMs like Django use descriptors for model fields, validation and lazy loading.

questions.q: How do you optimise Django ORM queries?
questions.ideal: Detect the N plus one problem with Django debug toolbar or query logging. Use select related for foreign key joins and prefetch related for many to many and reverse relations. Fetch only needed columns with only, defer or values. Add indexes on filtered fields and check explain plans. Use bulk create and bulk update for batches instead of saving in loops.

questions.q: How do you run background tasks with Celery, and how do you make them reliable?
questions.ideal: Celery sends tasks through a broker like Redis or RabbitMQ to worker processes. For reliability configure retry with exponential backoff, make tasks idempotent since they may run twice, and use acks late so a crashed worker does not lose tasks. Pass IDs rather than large objects, set time limits, and use Celery beat for periodic jobs. Monitor queues with Flower.

questions.q: How do you package and publish a Python library or service properly?
questions.ideal: Modern packaging uses pyproject.toml to declare metadata and dependencies with a build backend like setuptools, Hatch or Poetry. You build a wheel and sdist and publish to PyPI or a private index like Artifactory. Applications use a lock file for reproducible installs, libraries use flexible ranges, versions follow semantic versioning, and entry points create console scripts.

questions.q: How do you find and fix a memory leak in a long running Python process?
questions.ideal: Leaks usually come from unbounded global caches, lists that keep growing, or reference cycles holding objects. Use tracemalloc and compare snapshot diffs to find allocation sites, or tools like memray, objgraph and Pympler. The gc module can show uncollected objects. Fix by bounding caches, clearing references, and using weakref for back references or observer patterns.

questions.q: How do you protect a Django or Flask application against common web attacks?
questions.ideal: Use the ORM or parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection. Templates auto escape output against XSS, and Django CSRF middleware blocks cross site request forgery. Keep the secret key and credentials in environment variables or a vault, not code. Enforce HTTPS with secure cookies, use strong authentication with password hashing like bcrypt or Argon2, and turn off debug in production.

questions.q: What are dataclasses and slots in Python, and when would you use them?
questions.ideal: A dataclass removes boilerplate by generating init, repr and eq from annotated fields. frozen makes instances immutable and hashable, and default factory in field handles mutable defaults. slots replaces the per instance dict, using less memory and speeding attribute access for many objects. Use Pydantic when you need validation, and namedtuple or attrs for alternatives.

questions.q: How do you deploy and scale a FastAPI service for high traffic?
questions.ideal: Run FastAPI as an ASGI app with Uvicorn workers, often managed by Gunicorn, with workers matching CPU cores. Containerize it and use horizontal scaling with replicas on Kubernetes behind a load balancer or ingress. Use an async database driver like asyncpg with a properly sized connection pool, add Redis caching for hot reads, and offload heavy work to background queues.

questions.q: You need to process a 50 GB CSV file in Python on a machine with 8 GB RAM. How do you do it?
questions.ideal: Never load it whole. Stream it with a generator or the csv module, or read csv in pandas with chunksize, processing and aggregating each chunk. Select only needed columns and efficient dtypes to save memory. Use multiprocessing for CPU heavy steps, or tools like Polars lazy mode, DuckDB or Dask that handle out of core data. Convert to Parquet for later columnar reads.

questions.q: How do you run database schema migrations with zero downtime in a Python service?
questions.ideal: Use Alembic or Django migrations with the expand contract pattern. First expand with backward compatible changes like adding a nullable column, so old and new code both work during a rolling deployment. Backfill data in batches to avoid long locks. Switch reads and writes in code, and only later contract by dropping old columns. Test migrations on production sized data.

questions.q: Design a caching strategy for a read heavy Python API.
questions.ideal: Use cache aside with Redis or Memcached: read from cache, fall back to the database and populate with a TTL. Invalidate or use write through on updates to limit staleness. Small, static data can use an in process lru cache. Prevent stampede with locks or early refresh, and add HTTP caching with ETag and Cache Control headers so clients and CDNs help too.

questions.q: How would you secure and rate limit a public Python API?
questions.ideal: Authenticate with OAuth2 and short lived JWTs and enforce scopes. Apply rate limiting per key using Redis or the gateway. Strict input validation with Pydantic rejects bad payloads. Store keys in secrets management like Vault or a cloud secrets manager. Run dependency scanning with pip audit and Bandit in CI, enforce HTTPS, and keep audit logging and monitoring for abuse.

questions.q: How do you make a Python microservice observable in production?
questions.ideal: Use structured logging in JSON with structlog or the logging module, including a correlation id or trace id on each line. OpenTelemetry auto instrumentation provides distributed tracing across Django, FastAPI, requests and database calls. Expose Prometheus metrics for latency and errors, send exceptions to Sentry for error tracking, and add a health check endpoint for orchestrators.

questions.q: How would you break up a large Django monolith as the team grows?
questions.ideal: Start by making the monolith modular, organizing Django apps around domain boundaries and removing cross app imports and shared database coupling. Define API contracts between modules. Then extract services incrementally with the strangler fig approach, beginning with parts that change often or scale differently. Use events on a message queue for data sync, and keep monitoring to compare behavior.

questions.q: A Python service in production hangs with no errors. How do you debug it?
questions.ideal: First capture what it is doing: py-spy dump shows thread stacks of a live process without restarting it, and faulthandler can dump tracebacks on a signal. strace or gdb help at the system level. Common causes are a deadlock between locks, a blocking call to a network or database with no timeouts, or a stuck event loop. Fix by adding timeouts everywhere.

questions.q: How do range, enumerate and zip help you write cleaner loops in Python?
questions.ideal: Range produces a lazy sequence of numbers without building a list in memory. Enumerate gives the index and value together, so you avoid manual counters. Zip walks several iterables in parallel and returns pairs, stopping at the shortest unless strict is set in Python 3.10. Using these is more pythonic and readable than indexing with range of len.

questions.q: How do you read and write files safely in Python?
questions.ideal: You call open with a mode such as r for read, w for write which truncates, a for append, and b for binary. Using the with statement context manager makes sure the file is closed even on errors. Always pass an encoding like utf 8. Iterating line by line saves memory for big files, and pathlib Path gives cleaner path handling.

questions.q: What is truthiness in Python, and how should you check for None?
questions.ideal: In Python every object has truthiness. Falsy values include None, False, zero and empty containers like an empty list, string or dict; everything else is truthy, which you can test with bool. To check for None, use is None or is not None, because None is a singleton and identity is clearer. Writing if not x treats zero and empty as false too, which may be a bug.

questions.q: What is PEP 8, and which tools help enforce Python code style?
questions.ideal: PEP 8 is the official Python style guide. It recommends four spaces of indentation, snake case naming for functions and variables, CapWords for classes, a reasonable line length and clean imports. Teams enforce it automatically with a formatter like Black or Ruff format and a linter like Ruff, Flake8 or Pylint, typically through pre commit hooks and CI.

questions.q: What is the difference between sort and sorted in Python, and how do you sort by a custom key?
questions.ideal: List sort sorts in place and returns None, while sorted works on any iterable and returns a new list. Both take a key function, such as a lambda or operator itemgetter, to sort by a field, and reverse equals True for descending order. Python sorting is stable, so you can sort by secondary then primary key.

questions.q: How do get, setdefault and defaultdict help when working with dictionaries?
questions.ideal: Indexing a dict with a missing key raises KeyError. The get method returns None or a default value instead. Setdefault returns the value and inserts the default if missing. A defaultdict from collections creates default values automatically, such as a list for grouping. Iterating with items gives keys and values together, and dicts keep insertion order.

questions.q: How does division work in Python, and why does 0.1 plus 0.2 not equal 0.3?
questions.ideal: A single slash is true division and always returns a float, while double slash is floor division rounding down, and percent gives the modulo remainder. Floating point numbers are stored in binary, so 0.1 plus 0.2 is slightly off. Compare with math isclose, use round for display, and use the decimal module for money.

questions.q: What is tuple unpacking in Python, and how do you use star expressions?
questions.ideal: Unpacking assigns items of an iterable to several names in one line, like a, b equals pair. It lets you swap variables without a temp, and functions return multiple values as a tuple that you unpack. A star expression collects the rest, as in first, star rest. If counts do not match, Python raises ValueError about too many values.

questions.q: How do you work with JSON in Python?
questions.ideal: The json module converts between JSON text and Python objects. json loads parses a string into a dict or list, and load reads from a file. json dumps serializes to a string and dump writes to a file, with indent for pretty output. Types like datetime are not serializable by default, so you pass a default function or custom encoder.

questions.q: What do break, continue and pass do, and what is the else clause on a loop?
questions.ideal: Break exits the loop immediately, continue skips to the next iteration, and pass is a no op placeholder where syntax needs a statement. A for or while loop can have an else clause that runs only when the loop finishes without break, which is handy for search loops: if nothing was found the else branch handles it.

questions.q: What useful types does the collections module provide?
questions.ideal: The collections module has Counter for counting items and most common, deque for fast appends and pops at both ends which suits queues, namedtuple for lightweight immutable records with field names, defaultdict for automatic defaults, OrderedDict with move to end for LRU style logic, and ChainMap to layer several dicts such as config defaults and overrides.

questions.q: What are some useful itertools functions, and why are they memory efficient?
questions.ideal: Itertools functions return lazy iterators, so they process items one at a time with little memory. Chain joins iterables, islice slices any iterator, groupby groups consecutive items so you must sort first, and product, permutations and combinations generate combinatorics. Count, cycle and accumulate help too. Python 3.12 adds batched for chunking.

questions.q: How do lru_cache, partial and wraps from functools help you?
questions.ideal: The functools lru cache decorator gives memoization: results are cached by arguments, which must be hashable, with maxsize to bound memory. Partial creates a new function with some arguments fixed. Wraps is used inside custom decorators to keep the original function name and docstring. Be careful caching methods, because the cache keeps self alive.

questions.q: How should you use the logging module in a Python application?
questions.ideal: Use the logging module instead of print. Each module creates a logger with getLogger of name. Levels like debug, info, warning and error control verbosity. Handlers send records to console or files, and a formatter adds time and context, often JSON. Configure once at startup with dictConfig. Use logger exception inside except blocks to include the stack trace.

questions.q: How do abstract base classes work in Python, and how do they differ from protocols?
questions.ideal: The abc module provides ABC and the abstractmethod decorator. A subclass must implement every abstract method, otherwise trying to instantiate it raises TypeError. This enforces an interface contract through explicit inheritance. A typing Protocol instead uses structural typing, so any class with matching methods fits without being a subclass, checked by static type checkers.

questions.q: How do you structure a larger Flask application?
questions.ideal: Use an application factory, a create app function, so you can build apps with different config for tests. Split features into blueprints with their own routes. Initialise extensions like SQLAlchemy with init app inside the factory, which also avoids circular imports. Config classes per environment and the test client make testing easy.

questions.q: What are best practices when calling external HTTP APIs with requests or httpx?
questions.ideal: Always set a timeout, because requests has none by default and a call can hang forever. Reuse a Session or httpx Client for connection pooling. Add retries with backoff through urllib3 Retry or tenacity for idempotent calls. Call raise for status to check the status code. For asyncio code, use httpx AsyncClient instead of blocking requests.

questions.q: What is the difference between str and repr in Python?
questions.ideal: The str method returns a readable, user friendly string and is used by print and f strings. The repr method returns an unambiguous developer string for debugging, ideally one that could recreate the object, and is shown in the shell and in containers. If str is not defined, Python uses repr as fallback, so define repr first.

questions.q: What are structural pattern matching and the walrus operator in modern Python?
questions.ideal: Python 3.10 added match case, structural pattern matching that matches on shape, not just values. Patterns can destructure sequences, mapping and class patterns, capture variables, and use an if guard. The walrus operator from 3.8 is an assignment expression that assigns inside an expression, such as while chunk walrus read, avoiding repeated calls.

questions.q: What are metaclasses in Python, and when would you use one?
questions.ideal: A metaclass is the class of a class; by default it is type, which handles class creation. A custom metaclass can modify classes as they are created, for example a registry of plugins, validation, or how ORM frameworks like Django models build fields. Today init subclass and class decorators cover most needs more simply, so metaclasses are rarely needed.

questions.q: How does multiple inheritance work in Python, and what is the MRO?
questions.ideal: The method resolution order, MRO, defines the lookup order of classes, computed with C3 linearization so each class appears once and the diamond problem is resolved predictably. Super follows the MRO, not just the parent, so cooperative methods should all call super and accept kwargs. Multiple inheritance is mostly used for small mixins like logging or serialization.

questions.q: How do sessions and the 2.0 style work in SQLAlchemy, and what are common pitfalls?
questions.ideal: SQLAlchemy has an engine with a connection pool and a session implementing unit of work, tracking changes until commit or rollback. 2.0 style uses select statements with session execute. Use one session per request, closed in a finally or dependency. Lazy loading causes N plus 1 queries, so use selectinload or joinedload. Async sessions must not be shared across tasks.

questions.q: What is the difference between WSGI and ASGI, and how do you choose server workers?
questions.ideal: WSGI is the synchronous interface used by Flask and classic Django, served by Gunicorn with sync or thread workers. ASGI is asynchronous and supports websockets and long lived connections, used by FastAPI and Django async, served by Uvicorn, often under Gunicorn with Uvicorn workers. Worker count usually starts near two times cpu cores plus one, tuned with load tests.

questions.q: How do you use mypy, Protocols and generics to type check a Python codebase?
questions.ideal: Mypy or Pyright run static checks in CI. Adoption is gradual typing, adding hints to new and core modules, then enabling strict mode per package. Protocol enables structural typing, so you type duck typed interfaces without inheritance. Generics with TypeVar, or the new 3.12 syntax, keep containers and functions precise. Types catch bugs early and document code.

questions.q: What are Django signals, and why do many teams avoid them?
questions.ideal: Django signals like post save and pre save let a receiver run when models change. They decouple apps, but logic becomes hidden and hard to trace, they are skipped by bulk update and bulk create, and they run inside the transaction, so sending emails should use transaction on commit. Many teams prefer explicit calls in a service layer.

questions.q: What are the free threaded build and other recent performance changes in Python 3.13?
questions.ideal: Python 3.13 offers an experimental free threaded build that removes the GIL, letting threads run Python code in parallel on many cores. C extensions must be updated to be thread safe, and single thread performance is a bit lower. 3.13 also adds an experimental JIT, and subinterpreters give another parallelism path. Recent versions are also generally faster.

questions.q: How do you handle transactions and concurrency in Django?
questions.ideal: Wrap related writes in transaction atomic so they commit or roll back together; nested blocks create a savepoint. To avoid a race condition use select for update to lock rows, or F expressions to update counters in the database atomically. Use on commit to trigger tasks only after success, and know your database isolation level.

questions.q: What changed in Pydantic v2, and how do you use validators and settings?
questions.ideal: Pydantic v2 moved validation to pydantic core written in Rust, making it much faster. Validators became field validator and model validator for cross field rules, and dict became model dump for serialization. BaseSettings moved to the pydantic settings package and loads typed config from environment variables and dotenv files, failing fast at startup.

questions.q: How do you make thousands of concurrent HTTP calls with asyncio without overwhelming services?
questions.ideal: Use an async client like httpx or aiohttp with one shared session. Create tasks with gather or a TaskGroup, but wrap each call in an asyncio Semaphore to limit concurrency to a safe number. Set timeouts, handle exceptions per task so one failure does not cancel everything, and respect the server rate limit with backoff on 429 responses.

questions.q: Design a reliable webhook delivery system in Python for thousands of customers.
questions.ideal: Events are written to a durable queue, and workers deliver with short timeouts. Each payload carries an event id for idempotency and an HMAC signature for verification. Failures get retries with exponential backoff over hours, then go to dead letter storage with alerts and auto disable. Per customer isolation and rate limits stop one slow endpoint delaying everyone.

questions.q: How would you upgrade a large service from an old Python version to Python 3.12?
questions.ideal: First improve test coverage on critical paths. Audit dependencies for compatibility and upgrade libraries. Run CI matrix tests on both versions with tox or nox, and turn deprecation warnings into errors to find removed APIs like distutils. Roll out incremental changes with canary deployments, comparing errors and performance benchmarks before full switch.

questions.q: How would you design a multi tenant SaaS backend in Django?
questions.ideal: Options are a shared schema with a tenant id column, schema per tenant using Postgres schemas, or a database per tenant. Shared schema is cheapest but needs strong isolation, so every query is scoped through a tenant aware manager and row level security to prevent leakage. Middleware handles tenant resolution from domain or token. Quotas address noisy neighbor problems.

questions.q: How would you build real time notifications for a million users with Python?
questions.ideal: Use an ASGI async stack such as FastAPI or Django Channels for websockets. Each server holds many connections, and horizontal scaling uses a pub sub layer like Redis or NATS to fan out messages to the node holding each user. The load balancer supports long lived connections. Heartbeat pings detect dead sockets, clients reconnect with backoff, and backpressure drops or buffers for slow clients.

questions.q: How do you serve an ML model behind a Python API with strict latency requirements?
questions.ideal: Load the model once at startup and warm it. Inference is CPU bound, so run it in separate processes or a thread pool, never blocking the event loop. Dynamic batching improves GPU throughput, and ONNX or quantization reduces latency. Cache repeated inputs, keep payloads small, and load test p99 latency. Specialised servers like Triton fit very high load.

questions.q: How do you build a reliable Kafka consumer service in Python?
questions.ideal: Use confluent kafka in a consumer group so partitions spread across instances. Disable auto commit and do a manual offset commit after processing, giving at least once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent. Handle rebalance callbacks cleanly, send poison messages to a dead letter topic, and monitor consumer lag. Scale by adding partitions and processes.

questions.q: How do you use feature flags for safe releases in a Python service?
questions.ideal: Feature flags separate deploy from release. You ship code behind a flag, then do a gradual rollout by percentage or targeting segments such as internal users. A kill switch turns off a bad feature instantly. Flags also power AB testing experiments. Use a flag service or library with fast local evaluation, and schedule cleanup to avoid flag debt.

questions.q: How do you keep a large Python codebase healthy as many teams contribute?
questions.ideal: Enforce linting and formatting with Ruff in pre commit and CI, and type checking with mypy. Keep a test pyramid with good coverage on core logic. Define module boundaries and check them with import linter. Use codeowners for ownership and clear code review rules. Automate dependency updates with Renovate or Dependabot to avoid painful upgrades.

questions.q: Customers upload CSV files with millions of rows into your Django app. How do you design the import?
questions.ideal: Accept the upload to object storage and run a background job with Celery. Read in streaming chunks, run validation, and collect row errors into an error report rather than failing everything. Write with bulk create or Postgres COPY, using upsert on conflict to stay idempotent and allow resume from a checkpoint. Expose progress and status to the user.

questions.q: How do you use yield from and generator pipelines to process data streams in Python?
questions.ideal: A generator pipeline chains small generators, each reading from the previous one, so items flow lazily on demand with constant memory, like reading lines, filtering and parsing a huge log. Yield from lets one generator delegate to a sub generator and pass through its values and return value. Generators can receive values with send and stop with close, and once exhausted raise StopIteration.

questions.q: How would you add full text search to a Django or FastAPI product catalog with millions of items?
questions.ideal: For moderate needs, Postgres full text search with tsvector and a GIN index works well. At millions of items with faceted filters, relevance ranking and autocomplete, use Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. Keep the index in sync through change data capture or events after commits, support zero downtime reindex with aliases, and tune relevance with boosting and analyzers.

questions.q: What are the key features of Go, and how do slices differ from arrays?
questions.ideal: Go is a compiled, statically typed, garbage collected language with simple syntax and built in concurrency. Arrays have a fixed size, slices are dynamic views over a backing array with length and capacity, and append may reallocate.

questions.q: How does error handling work in Go, and what are defer, panic and recover?
questions.ideal: Go returns errors as values that you check explicitly and wrap with fmt.Errorf and %w, inspecting with errors.Is and errors.As. defer schedules cleanup in LIFO order, and panic and recover are only for unrecoverable situations.

questions.q: Explain goroutines, channels, the sync package and how Go avoids data races.
questions.ideal: Goroutines are lightweight threads managed by the Go scheduler. Channels pass data between them, buffered or unbuffered, select waits on several, and sync.Mutex and WaitGroup coordinate. Detect data races with the race detector and use context for cancellation.

questions.q: How do interfaces work in Go, and what are the empty interface and embedding?
questions.ideal: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly by having the methods, with no implements keyword. The empty interface any holds any value and needs type assertions. Go prefers composition through struct embedding, and pointer versus value receivers affect the method set.

questions.q: Describe worker pools, fan out fan in, and how to prevent goroutine leaks.
questions.ideal: A worker pool runs a fixed number of goroutines reading jobs from a channel, fan out distributes work and fan in merges results. Prevent leaks by giving every goroutine an exit path through context cancellation or a done channel, and use errgroup to manage them.

questions.q: How do you build a production REST or gRPC service in Go: routing, middleware, graceful shutdown and config?
questions.ideal: Use net/http or a router like chi or gin with middleware for logging, auth and panic recovery, set server timeouts, shut down gracefully on signals with Server.Shutdown and a context, load config from the environment, and use gRPC with protobuf for internal services.

questions.q: How do you profile and optimise a Go service? Mention pprof, escape analysis and allocations.
questions.ideal: Use pprof for CPU and heap profiles, benchmarks and go tool trace, reduce allocations and GC pressure with preallocated slices, strings.Builder and sync.Pool, understand escape analysis, and look for lock contention.

questions.q: How do you structure and test Go projects: packages, dependency injection, table driven tests and mocks?
questions.ideal: Organise by packages with cmd and internal directories, depend on small interfaces so dependencies can be faked, write table driven tests with subtests, measure coverage, run with the race detector, and use testcontainers for integration tests.

questions.q: How do maps work in Go, and what are their common pitfalls?
questions.ideal: A map is a hash table created with make or a map literal. Reading a key that does not exist returns the zero value, so use the comma ok idiom to check existence, and delete removes keys. Writing to a nil map panics. Iteration order is random. Maps are not thread safe for concurrent writes; use a mutex or sync Map.

questions.q: What is the difference between value receivers and pointer receivers in Go?
questions.ideal: Methods are attached to struct types through receivers. A value receiver works on a copy, so changes do not affect the caller, and is fine for small immutable types. A pointer receiver can modify the original and avoids copying large structs. The choice also affects the method set, which decides whether a value or only a pointer satisfies an interface. Be consistent per type.

questions.q: How do Go modules manage dependencies?
questions.ideal: A module is defined by go.mod, which lists the module path and required dependency versions, while go.sum stores checksum values for integrity. go get adds or upgrades dependencies and go mod tidy removes unused ones. Versions follow semantic versioning, and a major version of v2 or above changes the import path. You can use vendoring or a module proxy.

questions.q: How do you declare variables in Go, and what are zero values?
questions.ideal: You use var with an optional type, or short declaration with colon equals, which uses type inference and works only inside a function scope. Every variable gets a zero value if not initialized: zero for numbers, empty string, false, and nil for pointers, slices and maps. const declares constants. An unused variable is a compile error in Go.

questions.q: How do pointers work in Go, and how are they different from C pointers?
questions.ideal: A pointer holds a memory address. The ampersand operator gets the address of a variable and the star operator dereferences it. new allocates a zeroed value and returns a pointer. Unlike C, Go has no pointer arithmetic, and memory is garbage collected, so returning a pointer to a local variable is safe because it escapes to the heap. Dereferencing a nil pointer panics.

questions.q: How does Go handle strings, bytes and runes?
questions.ideal: A string is an immutable sequence of bytes, usually UTF 8 encoded. len returns the number of bytes, not characters. A rune is an int32 representing a Unicode code point. Using for range over a string decodes UTF 8 and yields runes, while indexing gives bytes. Convert to a byte slice to modify data, and use strings Builder for efficient building.

questions.q: How do packages and visibility work in Go?
questions.ideal: Every file belongs to a package. Names starting with a capital letter are exported and visible to other packages, while lowercase names are unexported and private to the package. An internal package can only be imported by code under its parent directory. An init function runs automatically when the package loads. Go forbids circular import cycles between packages.

questions.q: What are the main commands in the Go toolchain?
questions.ideal: go build compiles a single static binary, go run compiles and runs, and go test runs tests. go fmt enforces standard formatting and go vet finds suspicious code. Go can cross compile easily by setting GOOS and GOARCH, for example building a Linux binary on a Mac, which makes deployment in containers very simple.

questions.q: How does the select statement work in Go?
questions.ideal: select waits on multiple channels operations and blocks until one is ready. If several are ready, it picks one at random. A default case makes it non blocking. Adding a case on time After implements a timeout, and a case on the context Done channel handles cancellation. select inside a for loop is the core pattern for event handling goroutines.

questions.q: What is the difference between buffered and unbuffered channels, and what happens when you close a channel?
questions.ideal: An unbuffered channel is synchronous: a send blocks until a receiver takes the value. A buffered channel has capacity, so sends block only when full. Only the sender should close a channel. Sending on a closed channel causes a panic, while receiving returns the zero value with ok false. range over a channel reads until it is closed.

questions.q: What is the context package used for in Go?
questions.ideal: context carries cancellation, a deadline or timeout, and request scoped values across API boundaries. It is passed as the first parameter for propagation through calls to databases and HTTP clients. WithTimeout and WithCancel return a cancel function you must call to avoid a goroutine leak. Goroutines watch the Done channel to stop. Use values only for request metadata, not optional parameters.

questions.q: When do you use Mutex, RWMutex, atomic, WaitGroup and Once in Go?
questions.ideal: A Mutex protects shared state, usually with defer Unlock. An RWMutex allows many readers or one writer for read heavy data. The atomic package handles simple counters without locks. A WaitGroup waits for a group of goroutines to finish, and sync Once runs initialization exactly once. Go prefers channels to share memory by communicating, but locks are fine for simple state.

questions.q: How do you wrap and inspect errors in modern Go?
questions.ideal: Wrap errors with fmt Errorf using percent w to add context while keeping the original. errors Is checks whether any error in the chain matches a sentinel error such as sql ErrNoRows, and errors As extracts a specific custom error type. This lets callers make decisions without parsing strings, while logs still show the full context.

questions.q: How do generics work in Go, and when should you use them?
questions.ideal: Since Go 1.18, functions and types can take type parameters in square brackets, restricted by constraints. any allows all types, comparable allows equality, and custom constraints are interfaces listing types. Use generics to remove duplication in data structures and utilities like Map or Filter, but prefer plain interfaces when behaviour, not type, varies.

questions.q: How do slices work internally in Go, and what are the pitfalls of append?
questions.ideal: A slice is a header with a pointer to a backing array, a length and a capacity. append adds elements in place if capacity allows, otherwise it triggers reallocation into a new, larger array. Slices sharing a backing array can overwrite each other unexpectedly, so use copy or a full slice expression when you need independence, and always use the value append returns.

questions.q: How do you work with JSON in Go?
questions.ideal: The encoding json package uses Marshal to convert structs to JSON and Unmarshal to parse JSON. Only exported fields with capital letters are included. Struct tags set the JSON field name, and omitempty skips empty values. For HTTP bodies or large inputs, use json NewDecoder for streaming, and you can disallow unknown fields for strict validation.

questions.q: Explain the Go scheduler and the GMP model.
questions.ideal: The Go scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads using the GMP model: G is a goroutine, M is a machine or OS thread, and P is a logical processor holding a run queue. GOMAXPROCS sets the number of Ps. Idle Ps use work stealing from others. When a goroutine blocks in a syscall, the P moves to another M, and asynchronous preemption stops long running goroutines.

questions.q: How does the Go garbage collector work, and how can you tune it?
questions.ideal: Go uses a concurrent tri color mark and sweep garbage collector that runs alongside the program with short stop the world pauses, optimized for low latency. A write barrier keeps marking correct while code runs. GOGC controls how much the heap grows before the next cycle, and GOMEMLIMIT sets a soft memory limit. Reducing allocations is the best tuning.

questions.q: How do you detect and fix data races in Go?
questions.ideal: A data race occurs when goroutines access the same memory concurrently and at least one writes without synchronization. Run the race detector with the race flag in go test and CI, which reports conflicting accesses with stack traces. Fix it by establishing happens before through a mutex, channels or atomic operations, or by not sharing the data at all.

questions.q: How do you limit concurrency and apply backpressure in Go?
questions.ideal: Limit concurrency with a buffered channel used as a semaphore, a fixed worker pool, or errgroup with SetLimit, which also cancels the context on the first error. The x time rate package provides a token bucket rate limiter. For backpressure, use a bounded queue and reject or return 429 when it is full, which is load shedding instead of unbounded goroutines.

questions.q: How do you use database/sql correctly in Go?
questions.ideal: database sql manages a connection pool, tuned with SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns and SetConnMaxLifetime. Use QueryContext with a context for timeouts and parameterized placeholders or prepared statements to avoid SQL injection. Always defer rows Close and check rows Err, otherwise connections leak. Libraries like sqlx, pgx or GORM add convenience on top.

questions.q: What are good practices for designing interfaces in Go?
questions.ideal: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so keep them small, like io Reader and io Writer with one method. Define interfaces on the consumer side where they are used, not next to the implementation. The idiom is accept interfaces, return structs. This makes testing with mocks easy. Avoid interface pollution, meaning premature interfaces with one implementation and no need.

questions.q: What happens when a goroutine panics, and how do you handle it safely?
questions.ideal: A panic in any goroutine that is not recovered will crash the whole program, and a recover in main does not catch panics in other goroutines. Each goroutine needs its own defer with recover if panics are possible. HTTP servers use recovery middleware per handler. Prefer returning errors and use errgroup to collect them, keeping panic for truly unexpected bugs.

questions.q: How do you write benchmarks and fuzz tests in Go?
questions.ideal: Benchmarks are functions taking testing B that loop b N times, run with go test bench and benchmem to show allocations. benchstat compares results statistically between changes. Fuzzing uses testing F with a seed corpus, and the engine generates inputs to find crashes or edge cases. httptest provides a test server and recorder for HTTP handlers.

questions.q: Design a high throughput Kafka event processor in Go.
questions.ideal: Consumers in a consumer group each own partitions. To keep ordering per key, route messages by key to a fixed worker pool of goroutines through bounded channels, giving backpressure. Use batching for database writes. Commit offsets only after processing succeeds for at least once delivery with idempotent handlers. On SIGTERM, graceful shutdown stops fetching, drains workers and commits final offsets.

questions.q: Design a URL shortener service in Go that handles very high read traffic.
questions.ideal: Use id generation with a counter or Snowflake style IDs and base62 encoding for short codes. Storage is a key value or SQL database with an index on the code. Since reads dominate, add Redis caching and in memory LRU in stateless Go services behind a load balancer for horizontal scaling. Return a 301 or 302 redirect, and send click analytics asynchronously to a queue.

questions.q: Goroutine count keeps growing in a production Go service. How do you investigate and fix it?
questions.ideal: Track runtime NumGoroutine as a metric to confirm the goroutine leak, then capture the goroutine profile from debug pprof to see where goroutines are blocked, often on a channel send or receive with no partner, or a network call without timeout. Fix by passing context for cancellation, adding timeouts, and closing channels properly. Use goleak in tests to prevent regressions.

questions.q: How would you build a Kubernetes operator in Go?
questions.ideal: An operator extends Kubernetes with a CRD describing desired state and a controller built with controller runtime or Kubebuilder. Informers watch resources and cache them, triggering a reconcile loop that compares desired and actual state and makes changes. Reconcile must be idempotent and requeue on errors. It updates status conditions and uses a finalizer to clean up external resources.

questions.q: A Go service keeps getting OOMKilled in Kubernetes. How do you troubleshoot it?
questions.ideal: Compare container limits from the cgroup with RSS and Go heap metrics. Capture a pprof heap profile to find retained allocations or a leak, such as growing caches or goroutines. Go does not know container limits by default, so set GOMEMLIMIT a bit below the limit so the GC works harder before OOM, and tune GOGC. Then fix the code and right size requests.

questions.q: How do you build a resilient HTTP client in Go for calling unreliable downstream services?
questions.ideal: Never use the default client without timeouts: set client timeout and pass a context deadline per request. Tune the Transport for connection reuse with keep alive and idle connections, and always close response bodies. Add retries only for idempotent requests or with an idempotency key, using exponential backoff with jitter. A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service and fails fast.

questions.q: How do you add observability to Go microservices?
questions.ideal: Use structured logging with slog, zap or zerolog, including the trace id. OpenTelemetry instruments HTTP and gRPC for tracing with spans, relying on context propagation through every call. Expose Prometheus metrics via client golang for latency histograms and error counts. Enable pprof endpoints securely for profiling, and use continuous profiling in production.

questions.q: How do you structure a large Go codebase so it stays maintainable?
questions.ideal: Organize by domain, keeping business logic independent of transport and storage, similar to clean or hexagonal architecture with ports and adapters defined as small interfaces. Use internal packages to hide implementation details. Keep dependency direction one way to avoid import cycles. In a monorepo choose between one module or multi module carefully, and apply API versioning for public packages.

questions.q: How do loops work in Go, and what does range return for different types?
questions.ideal: Go has only the for loop, which also acts as a while or an infinite loop. Range iterates slices and arrays giving index and value, strings giving byte index and rune, maps giving key and value in random order, and channels giving values until closed. The value is a copy, so modifying it does not change the slice element.

questions.q: How does the switch statement in Go differ from switch in C or Java?
questions.ideal: In Go each switch case has an automatic break, so there is no accidental fall through; you must write fallthrough explicitly. A case can list multiple values separated by comma. Cases can be any expression, and a tagless switch with no condition replaces long if else chains. A type switch checks the dynamic type of an interface.

questions.q: How do constants and iota work in Go?
questions.ideal: Constants are declared with const and evaluated at compile time. Untyped constants have high precision and adapt to the type where used. Iota is a counter that starts at zero and increments on each line in a const block, used to build enum style values or bit flags with a shift. Go has no enum keyword, so this is the idiom.

questions.q: How does type conversion work in Go, and why are there no implicit conversions?
questions.ideal: Go requires explicit conversion, such as float64 of x, even between int and int64; there is no implicit conversion, which avoids hidden bugs. Converting a larger to a smaller integer can cause overflow or truncation silently. To turn numbers into text use strconv Itoa or Atoi, because string of an int gives a rune character instead.

questions.q: How do multiple return values and named results work in Go functions?
questions.ideal: Go functions can return multiple values, commonly a result and an error that callers check. Named results declare return variables, useful for documentation and modifying results in defer, but naked return in long functions hurts readability. The blank identifier underscore ignores a value. The comma ok idiom returns a value plus a boolean for map lookups and type assertions.

questions.q: What is the difference between new and make in Go?
questions.ideal: New allocates memory for any type, sets it to the zero value, and returns a pointer. Make is only for slice, map and channel types and returns an initialized, ready to use value, not a pointer, setting up internal structures like length, capacity or buffer. A nil map from new cannot be written to, so maps need make or a literal.

questions.q: What are closures in Go, and how did loop variable capture change in Go 1.22?
questions.ideal: An anonymous function becomes a closure when it captures variables from its outer scope by reference. Before Go 1.22, the loop variable was shared across iterations, so goroutines started in a loop often saw the same variable value. Since Go 1.22, each iteration gets a new per iteration variable, fixing that classic bug.

questions.q: What are variadic functions in Go, and how do you pass a slice to one?
questions.ideal: A variadic function takes any number of arguments of one type using three dots before the type, and must be the last parameter. Inside the function it is a slice. To pass an existing slice you spread it with three dots after the argument, as in append of a, b dots. Println and append are common variadic examples.

questions.q: What is the difference between a type definition and a type alias in Go?
questions.ideal: A type definition such as type Celsius float64 creates a new distinct type that needs explicit conversion and can have its own methods. A type alias with an equals sign is just another name for the same type, sharing its method set. Aliases are mainly for refactoring and migration of types between packages without breaking callers.

questions.q: What is the init function in Go, and in what order is package initialization done?
questions.ideal: During package initialization, each package initializes its package variables, then runs its init functions, after all imported packages have initialized first, and finally main runs. A file can have several init functions. A blank import runs init only for side effects, like registering a database driver. Overuse of init makes code hard to test, so prefer explicit setup.

questions.q: Why can an interface holding a nil pointer not be equal to nil in Go?
questions.ideal: An interface value has two parts, a dynamic type and a dynamic value, and it is nil only when both are nil. If a function returns a typed nil pointer as an error interface, the type is set, so err not equal nil is true even though the pointer is nil. Return a literal nil for the error instead.

questions.q: How do type assertions and type switches work in Go?
questions.ideal: A type assertion extracts the concrete type from an interface, such as x dot of string. Without the comma ok form, a wrong assertion causes a panic; with ok you check safely. A type switch tests several possible dynamic types in one statement. These are needed with any values, but heavy use may suggest better interface design.

questions.q: What are common pitfalls with time After, timers and tickers in Go?
questions.ideal: Each time After call creates a timer; in older Go, calling it inside a select loop leaked timers until they fired, though Go 1.23 made unreferenced timers collectable. A ticker must be stopped with Stop or it keeps running. Use a single timer with reset in loops, and prefer context with a deadline for cancellation of operations.

questions.q: What is sync.Pool used for, and what are its caveats?
questions.ideal: Sync Pool lets you reuse temporary objects such as byte buffers, reducing allocations and gc pressure in hot paths. Objects may be cleared at any garbage collection, so it is not a cache or connection pool. Always reset objects before putting them back, and avoid storing very large buffers that keep memory high. Benchmark to confirm it helps.

questions.q: What is wrong with using http.Get or the default HTTP client in production Go code?
questions.ideal: The default client has no timeout, so a slow server can hang goroutines forever. Create a client with a timeout and a tuned transport for the connection pool, such as MaxIdleConnsPerHost, and reuse it. Always close the response body and read it fully so keep alive works. Use NewRequestWithContext so callers can cancel requests through context.

questions.q: Why are io.Reader and io.Writer so important in Go?
questions.ideal: Io Reader and io Writer are small interfaces with one method each, so files, network connections, buffers, gzip and HTTP bodies all implement them. This allows composition, wrapping readers like bufio or gzip, and streaming data with io Copy without loading everything into memory. It is the core example of small interfaces in Go.

questions.q: What does the embed directive do in Go, and when is it useful?
questions.ideal: The go embed directive includes static files such as templates, HTML assets, migrations or config into the binary at compile time. You embed into a string, byte slice or an embed FS for directories, then serve it with http FS. This yields a single binary deployment with no extra files to ship, at the cost of rebuilding to change assets.

questions.q: How do build tags and cross compilation work in Go?
questions.ideal: Build constraints, the go build comment line, include files only for certain tags, OS or architecture, and file suffix names like linux or windows do the same. They are used for platform code or integration tests behind a tag. Cross compilation just sets GOOS and GOARCH, which works easily when CGO ENABLED is zero, producing static binaries.

questions.q: What is errgroup, and how does it improve on a plain WaitGroup?
questions.ideal: Errgroup from x sync runs goroutines like a WaitGroup but also collects the first error. With WithContext, the context is cancelled as soon as any goroutine fails, so the others stop early. SetLimit bounds the number of concurrent goroutines. Wait returns the first error, which makes parallel calls much cleaner than WaitGroup plus manual error channels.

questions.q: How does structured logging work with the log slog package in Go?
questions.ideal: Go 1.21 added log slog for structured logging with key value attributes. A handler formats output, such as the JSON handler or text handler, and supports levels like debug, info and error. Logger With adds fields such as request id to every line. It is designed for performance with few allocations, and other libraries can plug in as handlers.

questions.q: What does the Go memory model guarantee, and how do atomics fit in?
questions.ideal: The Go memory model defines when a write is visible to a read through happens before relations created by synchronization like channel sends and receives, mutex unlock and lock, and sync atomic operations. Without them, a data race exists and the compiler or CPU reordering means no visibility guarantees. Atomics are sequentially consistent but work only for single values.

questions.q: What are the costs and risks of using cgo and the unsafe package?
questions.ideal: Cgo calls have overhead compared to Go calls, break easy cross compilation and static binary builds, and C memory is invisible to the garbage collector. The unsafe package bypasses type and memory safety, risking crashes and breaking on Go version changes, hurting portability. Use them only where needed, isolate them, and benchmark the gains.

questions.q: How does reflection work in Go, and when should you avoid it?
questions.ideal: The reflect package inspects types at runtime with TypeOf and ValueOf, used by encoding json, ORMs and validators to read struct tags. Reflection is slow, loses compile time type safety and can cause runtime panic on wrong kinds. Prefer interfaces, generics or code generation, and keep reflection in libraries, not business logic.

questions.q: How do you handle streaming, deadlines and errors in gRPC services written in Go?
questions.ideal: gRPC uses protobuf contracts and supports unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streams. Clients set a deadline via context, which propagates across services. Servers return status codes such as NotFound or Unavailable for retries. Interceptors add logging, auth and metrics. Streams need flow control and should check context cancellation.

questions.q: What is profile guided optimization in Go, and how do you use it?
questions.ideal: Profile guided optimization takes a CPU profile from pprof, ideally a representative production profile, saved as default.pgo in the main package. The compiler then makes better inlining and devirtualization decisions for hot paths, typically giving a few percent improvement in CPU. Profiles should be refreshed periodically as code changes.

questions.q: What are range over function iterators in Go 1.23?
questions.ideal: Go 1.23 added range over function iterators. An iterator is a function that takes a yield callback, typed as iter Seq or Seq2. The for range loop calls it, and yield returns false when the loop has an early break, so the iterator stops. This gives a standard, lazy way to iterate custom collections, used by new slices and maps helpers.

questions.q: What is false sharing, and how can struct layout affect Go performance?
questions.ideal: False sharing happens when goroutines on different cores update separate variables that sit on the same cache line, causing cache line ping pong and contention. Adding padding to put hot counters on separate lines fixes it. Struct layout also matters for alignment: ordering fields from largest to smallest reduces padding and memory size.

questions.q: How do you prevent a cache stampede in a Go service?
questions.ideal: A cache stampede happens when a hot key expires and many requests hit the database at once. The singleflight package lets only one goroutine load a key while duplicate requests wait for its result. Adding jitter to expiry spreads refreshes, serving stale values while refreshing in background helps, and a lock per key is another option.

questions.q: How do you write integration tests for a Go HTTP service with a real database?
questions.ideal: For integration tests, use httptest to run the handler with a test server, and testcontainers to start a real Postgres in Docker with migrations and fixtures applied. Separate slow suites with build tags or testing Short. Register t Cleanup for teardown, use t Parallel with isolated schemas or transactions, and run them in CI alongside unit tests.

questions.q: How do you build small, secure container images for Go services?
questions.ideal: Use a multi stage build: compile in a golang image, then copy only the static binary, built with CGO ENABLED zero, trimpath and ldflags to strip symbols, into distroless or scratch. Include CA certificates and time zone data if needed, and run as a non root user. The image is tiny with a small attack surface.

questions.q: Design a high performance in memory key value cache in Go.
questions.ideal: I would split the map into sharding by key hash, each shard with its own RWMutex to reduce lock contention. Eviction uses LRU or a sampled approach, with TTL expiry checked lazily plus a background sweeper. To reduce gc pressure, avoid pointers in large maps by storing values in byte arenas, like bigcache. Keep a memory limit and validate with benchmarks.

questions.q: How would you design a Go server handling a million concurrent WebSocket connections?
questions.ideal: Goroutines are cheap, but a million connections with two goroutines each and buffers is heavy, so minimise per websocket connection memory with small or pooled buffers, or use an epoll based event loop library. Raise file descriptors ulimit and kernel limits. Use heartbeat pings to drop dead peers, and horizontal scaling behind a load balancer with a pub sub layer between nodes.

questions.q: Design a distributed job queue and scheduler in Go.
questions.ideal: Jobs are stored in a durable queue such as Postgres with skip locked or Redis. A worker pool claims jobs with a lease or visibility timeout, giving at least once delivery with acknowledgement on completion. Failed jobs get retries with backoff then dead letter. Handlers must be idempotent. Support priorities, delayed and cron scheduling, and graceful shutdown that finishes leases.

questions.q: A Go service has high p99 latency under load but low CPU. How do you find the cause?
questions.ideal: Low CPU with high latency suggests waiting, not computing. I would enable the mutex profile and block profile to find lock contention, capture a goroutine profile to see where goroutines are stuck, and use the execution trace for scheduler delays. Often the cause is a global lock, a small connection pool, or blocking IO on a slow downstream.

questions.q: Your team wants to rewrite a Python service in Go for performance. How do you decide and execute?
questions.ideal: First measure: profile the existing service to see if the bottleneck is language bound or due to IO and design. Weigh cost, risk and team skills. If justified, migrate incrementally with the strangler pattern, endpoint by endpoint, verifying parity with shadow traffic. Keep rollback through feature flag routing, and track latency and cost gains.

questions.q: How would you build an API gateway or reverse proxy in Go?
questions.ideal: Go httputil ReverseProxy gives the base. Add routing by host and path, middleware chains for authentication, rate limiting and request ids, and load balancing across backends with active health checks. Set timeouts on every hop and a circuit breaker for failing backends. Tune transport pools, and add observability with metrics and tracing. Config should reload without restart.

questions.q: How do you guarantee exactly once effects when processing payments in a Go service?
questions.ideal: True exactly once delivery is impossible, so aim for effectively once: at least once delivery with retries plus idempotency. Store an idempotency key with a unique constraint in the same database transaction as the state change. Publish events with the transactional outbox. Downstream payment providers also get the key. Daily reconciliation against provider reports catches anything missed.

questions.q: How do you evolve gRPC and protobuf APIs without breaking clients?
questions.ideal: Never change or reuse field numbers; when removing a field, mark its number and name reserved. Adding new optional fields is backward compatible because old clients ignore unknown fields. Use buf for lint and breaking change detection in CI. For incompatible redesigns, create versioned packages like v2 and serve both, marking old fields deprecated with a timeline.

questions.q: A Go service stops serving requests but does not crash. How do you debug it in production?
questions.ideal: I would grab a goroutine dump from debug pprof goroutine with debug equals two, or send SIGQUIT for a stack dump. Group goroutines by state to find many blocked on a mutex, an unread channel, or a network call without timeouts, which reveals deadlock or exhaustion. Fix with context deadlines and lock ordering, and add a liveness health check that detects it.

questions.q: How do you design and version a Go library that many teams depend on?
questions.ideal: Follow semantic versioning; a breaking change needs a major version with a v2 suffix in the import path. Keep a small API surface and hide details in an internal package. Use functional options or config structs so new settings stay backward compatible. Accept interfaces, return concrete types, and provide documentation with runnable examples in godoc.

questions.q: What is Ruby on Rails, and what do convention over configuration and MVC mean?
questions.ideal: Rails is a Ruby web framework following MVC, with convention over configuration so sensible defaults reduce setup, and DRY to avoid repetition. It ships generators, routing, ActiveRecord and gems managed by Bundler.

questions.q: What is the difference between a block, proc and lambda in Ruby, and what are symbols?
questions.ideal: A block is an anonymous chunk of code passed to a method. A proc is an object wrapping a block with lenient arguments, a lambda is stricter about arguments and returns from itself. Symbols are immutable unique identifiers, lighter than strings.

questions.q: Explain ActiveRecord associations, validations, callbacks and the N+1 query problem.
questions.ideal: ActiveRecord maps models to tables with associations like has_many and belongs_to, validations and callbacks. N+1 queries are solved with includes, preload or eager_load, detected with the Bullet gem.

questions.q: Walk through a Rails request cycle, and explain routing, strong parameters and CSRF.
questions.ideal: A request passes through Rack middleware to the router, which dispatches to a controller action. Strong parameters whitelist attributes against mass assignment, CSRF tokens protect forms, and the controller renders a view or JSON.

questions.q: How do you handle background jobs and caching in Rails?
questions.ideal: Use Active Job with Sidekiq backed by Redis for background work like email, make jobs idempotent with retries, and speed pages with fragment or Russian doll caching in Redis or Memcached with proper cache keys and expiry.

questions.q: How do you test Rails apps with RSpec or Minitest: factories, mocks and system tests?
questions.ideal: Use RSpec or Minitest with model, request and system specs, FactoryBot for data, doubles and WebMock or VCR for external calls, Capybara for browser flows, and track coverage in CI.

questions.q: A Rails app is slow in production. How do you find and fix bottlenecks?
questions.ideal: Measure with an APM or rack-mini-profiler, fix slow queries with EXPLAIN and indexes, remove N+1 queries, add caching, move slow work to background jobs, tune Puma workers and threads, paginate and use pluck, and watch memory and GC.

questions.q: How do you keep a large Rails codebase maintainable: service objects, engines, API design and security?
questions.ideal: Keep controllers and models thin with service objects and concerns, modularise with engines, version APIs and use serializers, run Brakeman and bundler-audit for security, enforce style with RuboCop and upgrade Rails and gems regularly.

questions.q: What are gems in Ruby, and what do Bundler, the Gemfile and Gemfile.lock do?
questions.ideal: A gem is a packaged Ruby library published on RubyGems. The Gemfile lists dependencies with a version constraint such as the pessimistic tilde operator. Bundler resolves them with bundle install and writes Gemfile.lock, which pins exact versions so every developer, CI and production run the same set. You commit the lock file for applications.

questions.q: What are migrations in Rails and how do you create and roll them back?
questions.ideal: A migration is a versioned Ruby class describing a schema change such as adding a table or column. You create one with rails generate migration, apply it with rails db migrate, and undo it with db rollback using the change or down method. Rails records each timestamp version in the schema_migrations table and dumps the result to schema.rb.

questions.q: What is a module in Ruby, and what is the difference between include and extend?
questions.ideal: A module groups methods and constants and also acts as a namespace. Used as a mixin, include adds its methods as instance methods, while extend adds them as class methods on the singleton. Ruby has no multiple inheritance, so modules share behaviour across classes. Enumerable is a classic example: define each and you get map, select and more.

questions.q: Explain each, map, select and reduce in Ruby with examples.
questions.ideal: These are Enumerable methods on arrays and hashes that take a block. Each iterates and returns the original collection. Map transforms every element into a new array. Select filters elements where the block is true, and reject does the opposite. Reduce, also called inject, accumulates a single value such as a sum. Chaining them keeps code short and readable.

questions.q: What are local, instance, class and global variables in Ruby?
questions.ideal: A local variable lives only inside its method or block scope. An instance variable starts with an at sign and belongs to one object. A class variable starts with a double at sign and is shared by the class and subclasses. A global variable starts with a dollar sign and is visible everywhere, so avoid it. A constant starts with an uppercase letter.

questions.q: What values are truthy and falsy in Ruby, and what is nil?
questions.ideal: In Ruby only nil and false are falsy; everything else is truthy, including zero, an empty string and an empty array, which surprises people from other languages. Nil is an object of NilClass that means no value. The safe navigation operator ampersand dot avoids NoMethodError on nil, and Rails adds blank and present for convenient checks.

questions.q: What do attr_accessor, attr_reader and attr_writer do in Ruby?
questions.ideal: Ruby objects hide their instance variables, so attr_reader generates a getter, attr_writer generates a setter, and attr_accessor generates both. They read and write the matching at-sign variable usually set in initialize, the constructor called by new. Exposing only readers keeps good encapsulation and you can keep other methods private.

questions.q: What are Rails environments and how is configuration managed across them?
questions.ideal: Rails runs in a named environment set by RAILS_ENV: development with reloading and verbose errors, the test environment for automated tests, and production with caching and eager loading. Each has a file under config environments and a section in database.yml. Secrets go in encrypted credentials with a master key or in environment variables, never in code.

questions.q: How do scopes, where, joins and pluck work in ActiveRecord queries?
questions.ideal: ActiveRecord builds lazy, chainable relation objects. Where adds conditions, joins adds an inner join, and order and limit control sorting and pagination. A scope is a named reusable query defined on the model. Pluck fetches only chosen columns as an array of values, avoiding object instantiation. The SQL runs only when results are actually needed.

questions.q: What are layouts, partials and helpers in Rails views?
questions.ideal: Views are ERB templates mixing HTML and embedded Ruby. The layout wraps every page and calls yield for the action content. A partial, a file starting with underscore, renders a reusable fragment and can take locals or a collection. A helper module holds presentation methods like formatting dates. Together they reduce duplication and keep views dry.

questions.q: How would you implement authentication in a Rails application?
questions.ideal: Most teams use Devise, or Rails has_secure_password which stores a bcrypt password digest. After login the user id goes into a signed, encrypted session cookie, and a before_action loads current_user and blocks anonymous access. For APIs we issue a JWT or API token instead of cookies. OmniAuth adds OAuth social login with Google or GitHub.

questions.q: Explain resourceful routes, nested routes and namespaces in Rails.
questions.ideal: Calling resources in routes.rb maps the seven RESTful actions such as index, show, create, update and destroy to a controller. Nested routes express ownership, like posts inside users, but should be kept shallow. A namespace groups controllers such as admin or api v1. Member and collection add custom actions, and rails routes lists every path helper.

questions.q: What is a polymorphic association in Rails, and when would you use it?
questions.ideal: A polymorphic association lets one model belong to multiple models through one interface, for example comments that can attach to posts or photos via commentable. The table stores a foreign key id column plus a type column with the class name. It is flexible, but the database cannot enforce referential integrity with a foreign key constraint.

questions.q: How does exception handling work in Ruby with begin, rescue, ensure and retry?
questions.ideal: Code goes in a begin block, and rescue catches specific exception classes, ideally StandardError subclasses, never bare Exception. Ensure always runs for cleanup like closing files. Retry reruns the block, usually with a counter. Raise throws an error and you can define a custom exception class. In Rails controllers rescue_from maps errors to responses.

questions.q: What is metaprogramming in Ruby? Explain send, define_method and method_missing.
questions.ideal: Metaprogramming means code that writes or changes code at runtime. Send calls a method by name, and public_send respects visibility. Define_method generates methods dynamically, as ActiveRecord does for attributes. Method_missing catches undefined calls for ghost methods, and you must also implement respond_to_missing. Monkey patching open classes is risky, so refinements scope such changes safely.

questions.q: How do you handle transactions and concurrent updates in Rails?
questions.ideal: Wrap related writes in a transaction so they commit or rollback atomically. For race conditions, optimistic locking adds a lock_version column and raises StaleObjectError if someone else saved first. Pessimistic locking uses lock or with_lock to issue SELECT FOR UPDATE. A unique index constraint in the database is the final safety net against duplicates.

questions.q: What is Rack, and how does middleware fit into a Rails application?
questions.ideal: Rack is the common interface between Ruby web servers like Puma and frameworks. An app is any object with a call method taking env and returning status, headers and body. Middleware wraps the app in a stack, each layer handling things like sessions or logging before passing on. You add one with config.middleware.use, for example Rack::Attack for throttling.

questions.q: What is the difference between includes, preload and eager_load in ActiveRecord?
questions.ideal: Preload always runs separate queries per association. Eager_load uses one left outer join single query. Includes chooses automatically and switches to eager_load when you add references or filter on the association. A counter cache stores association counts in a column to avoid count queries, and the Bullet gem detects N+1 and unused eager loading in development.

questions.q: What are common security vulnerabilities in Rails apps and how do you prevent them?
questions.ideal: Rails protects a lot by default but developers break it. Prevent SQL injection with placeholders instead of string interpolation. ERB escapes output to stop XSS, so avoid html_safe and raw on user input. Keep CSRF authenticity tokens on, use strong parameters against mass assignment, store secrets in credentials, and run Brakeman and bundler-audit in CI.

questions.q: How does Ruby manage memory and garbage collection, and how do you reduce allocations?
questions.ideal: Ruby uses a generational, incremental garbage collector with frequent minor GC for young objects and occasional major GC. Every object allocation costs, so we add the frozen string literal comment, reuse symbols, and use find_each to batch through large tables. Tools like memory_profiler and derailed_benchmarks reveal memory bloat and the hottest allocation sites.

questions.q: How does concurrency work in Ruby and Rails, considering the GVL, Puma threads and workers?
questions.ideal: CRuby has a GVL, so only one thread runs Ruby code at a time, but threads still help I/O bound work since the lock is released during I/O.
