Debug, used with colon question inside braces, is for developers and can be added with derive Debug. Pretty print with hash question formats nested structures over multiple lines. Implementing Display also gives you to_string automatically.

questions.q: What are rustup, rustc, cargo, clippy and rustfmt?
questions.ideal: Rustup installs and manages toolchains and channels like stable and nightly. Rustc is the compiler, but you usually drive it through Cargo, the build tool and package manager. Clippy is a linter with hundreds of lints that catch common mistakes and non idiomatic code. Rustfmt, run via cargo fmt, formats code consistently, and both typically run in CI.

questions.q: How does type inference work in Rust, and when do you need annotations or the turbofish?
questions.ideal: Rust infers local variable types from how they are used, but function signatures must be explicit. When the compiler cannot decide, as with parse or collect, you add a type annotation on the variable or use the turbofish, colon colon with angle brackets, like parse colon colon i32. It specifies the type parameter of a generic function directly.

questions.q: Where do values live in Rust, on the stack or the heap, and how do you put something on the heap?
questions.ideal: Values with known size at compile time live on the stack by default, which is fast. Data that grows, such as the buffers of String and Vec, live on the heap, with a pointer, length and capacity on the stack. Box new puts any value on the heap explicitly, useful for recursive types. When the owner goes out of scope, drop runs and the heap memory is freed.

questions.q: Why can you not index a Rust String by position, and how do you get characters?
questions.ideal: Rust strings are UTF-8, so one character can take several bytes, and indexing by position would be ambiguous or slow, so it is not allowed. Use chars to iterate Unicode scalar values, bytes for raw bytes, or a slice with a byte range, which panics if it is not on a char boundary. For user perceived characters you need grapheme segmentation from a crate.

questions.q: How do you write documentation in Rust, and what are doc comments?
questions.ideal: Doc comments start with triple slash for items, or slash slash bang for module level docs, and are written in Markdown. Cargo doc runs rustdoc to generate HTML documentation, and crates published to crates io get docs on docs rs. Code blocks in doc comments are examples that also run as doc tests, so documentation stays correct.

questions.q: When would you use thiserror versus anyhow for error handling in Rust?
questions.ideal: Thiserror is for libraries: it derives the Error trait for a custom error enum, so callers can match on specific variants. Anyhow is for application code, where you just need to propagate any error with the question mark operator and add context messages via context or with_context. A common pattern is thiserror in library crates and anyhow at the binary level.

questions.q: How do you work with Option and Result using combinators like map, and_then and unwrap_or?
questions.ideal: Combinators transform values without explicit match. Map changes the inner value, and_then chains operations that themselves return an Option or Result, and unwrap_or or unwrap_or_else supplies a default lazily. Ok_or converts an Option into a Result with an error. Chaining these, together with the question mark operator for early return, keeps error handling concise.

questions.q: What is Cow in Rust, and when is it useful?
questions.ideal: Cow, clone on write, is an enum holding either a borrowed reference or an owned value. A function can return Cow of str, giving back the borrowed input unchanged in the common case and allocating a new String only when modification is needed. This avoids allocation on the fast path. To_mut clones only when you first need to modify, and into_owned converts it.

questions.q: What does impl Trait mean in argument position and in return position?
questions.ideal: In argument position impl Trait is shorthand for an anonymous generic parameter accepting any type that implements the trait. In return position it returns an opaque single concrete type, hidden from the caller, which is how you return an iterator or closure without boxing. All return paths must produce the same type; otherwise you need Box dyn Trait.

questions.q: What is the difference between associated types and generic type parameters on a trait?
questions.ideal: An associated type, like Item on Iterator, is chosen once per implementing type, so a type has one implementation and callers do not specify it, which is ergonomic and helps inference. A generic parameter on the trait, like From of T, allows multiple implementations for different T on the same type. Use associated types when there is one natural output type.

questions.q: How do you overload operators in Rust?
questions.ideal: Operators are overloaded by implementing traits from std ops, like Add with its associated Output type, Sub, Mul, Neg and Index. Comparison uses PartialEq and PartialOrd, usually derived. For example implementing Add for a Money or Vector type lets you write a plus b. Rust does not allow custom operators, only these traits, which keeps code predictable.

questions.q: What is the HashMap entry API, and why is it better than get then insert?
questions.ideal: The entry API returns an Entry for a key, occupied or vacant, so you can write entry key or_insert zero and increment, a classic word count. It does a single lookup instead of a double lookup with get then insert, and avoids borrow checker conflicts from holding a reference while inserting. And_modify plus or_default handle update or insert cleanly.

questions.q: How do you add logging to a Rust application with log or tracing?
questions.ideal: The log crate is a facade with macros like info and error, and a backend such as env_logger prints them. The tracing crate is more powerful: it adds spans that capture context across async tasks, plus structured fields on events. A tracing subscriber formats output as text or JSON, and an env filter using RUST_LOG controls levels per module.

questions.q: How do you sort custom types in Rust, and what is the difference between Ord and PartialOrd?
questions.ideal: Ord means a total order, required by sort, BTreeMap and max. PartialOrd allows incomparable values, which is why floats like f64 only implement PartialOrd because of NaN. You can derive Ord, which compares fields in order, or use sort_by_key or sort_by with a closure. Sort is stable, while sort_unstable is faster and uses no extra memory.

questions.q: How do you collect an iterator of Result values into a single Result in Rust?
questions.ideal: Collect works through the FromIterator trait, and Result implements it, so an iterator of Result values can collect into a Result of Vec. It will short circuit on the first error and return it, otherwise you get all the successes. If you want to keep going and gather all errors, use partition to split successes and errors, then handle both lists.

questions.q: What are the Send and Sync traits in Rust, and why do Rc and RefCell not implement them?
questions.ideal: Send means a value can be moved to another thread, and Sync means a shared reference can be used from multiple threads. They are auto traits, implemented automatically when all fields qualify. Rc uses non atomic reference counts, so it is neither, and RefCell is not Sync because its borrow tracking is not thread safe. Arc with Mutex is the thread safe alternative.

questions.q: What is the typestate pattern in Rust, and how does PhantomData help?
questions.ideal: The typestate pattern encodes an object state as a generic parameter, such as Connection of Open or Closed, so invalid states and calls are rejected at compile time. Methods that change state consume self and return the new type, so a state transition cannot be skipped. PhantomData marks the unused marker type parameter; it is zero sized, so the pattern is zero cost at runtime.

questions.q: What are scoped threads in Rust, and why does thread::spawn require a static lifetime?
questions.ideal: Thread spawn requires a static lifetime and Send closures because the thread may outlive the caller, so you must move owned data or use Arc clones. Std thread scope, stable since Rust 1.63, creates scoped threads that are joined automatically before the scope ends, so they can safely borrow local variables and references without Arc.

questions.q: How does Rayon provide data parallelism in Rust?
questions.ideal: Rayon adds a parallel iterator, par_iter, so changing iter to par_iter spreads CPU bound work across cores. It uses a work stealing thread pool to balance tasks, and rayon join splits recursive work. Because closures must be Send and Sync, the compiler prevents a data race. It is for data parallelism, not for async IO, which belongs to Tokio.

questions.q: How do async functions in traits work in modern Rust, and what limitations remain?
questions.ideal: Since Rust 1.75 async fn in trait is stabilized, built on return position impl trait in traits. Before that, the async trait crate boxed each future with Box Pin, costing an allocation. Remaining limits: you cannot easily require the returned future to be Send for spawning, and such traits are not dyn compatible, so for dyn dispatch you still use boxing or the crate.

questions.q: What is the orphan rule in Rust, and how does the newtype pattern work around it?
questions.ideal: The orphan rule, part of coherence, says you can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is local to your crate, preventing conflicting impls. To implement a foreign trait on a foreign type, wrap it in a newtype, a tuple struct with one field. Newtypes are zero cost and also add type safety, like Meters versus Feet. Deref can expose inner methods.

questions.q: What are const generics in Rust, and where are they useful?
questions.ideal: Const generics let a generic parameter be a compile time value, usually a usize, written const N colon usize. They let you implement traits for arrays of any fixed size, and build types like a Matrix or a fixed capacity buffer whose dimensions are checked at compile time without heap allocation. Currently they mainly support integers, bool and char.

questions.q: What are Rust editions, and how do you migrate a crate to a new edition?
questions.ideal: Editions such as 2018, 2021 and 2024 let Rust introduce breaking changes like new keywords or changed closure capture rules, while staying backward compatible: crates of different editions interoperate in one build. You set the edition key in Cargo toml. To migrate, run cargo fix with the edition flag, which rewrites code automatically, then fix remaining warnings and bump the edition.

questions.q: How do you use property-based testing and fuzzing in Rust?
questions.ideal: Property based testing with proptest or quickcheck generates random inputs and checks invariants, like decode of encode equals the input, and shrinking reduces failures to a minimal case. Fuzzing with cargo fuzz uses libFuzzer coverage guidance to find crashes and panics, especially in parsers and unsafe code. Fuzz targets run continuously in CI or OSS Fuzz.

questions.q: How do you apply backpressure in async Rust using bounded channels and semaphores?
questions.ideal: Backpressure slows producers when a slow consumer cannot keep up. A Tokio bounded channel has a fixed capacity, so send awaits when the buffer is full, while an unbounded channel risks unlimited memory growth. A semaphore limits concurrent tasks or requests by handing out permits. Together they keep latency and memory predictable under load instead of crashing.

questions.q: A long-running Rust service slowly grows in memory. How do you investigate it?
questions.ideal: Rust prevents many bugs but leaks are still possible through Rc cycles, mem forget, Box leak, or an unbounded cache or queue that never evicts. Use heap profiling with dhat, heaptrack or jemalloc profiling to see what holds memory. Often RSS growth is fragmentation in the system allocator, so switching to jemalloc or mimalloc helps. Add bounds and metrics on caches and channels.

questions.q: How do you implement graceful shutdown in a Tokio based service?
questions.ideal: Listen for SIGTERM or ctrl c with Tokio signal handling. Then stop accepting new connections and notify tasks via a cancellation token or broadcast channel. Let in flight requests drain and await tasks with a JoinSet, but enforce a timeout so shutdown never hangs. Finally flush logs and metrics and close database pools. Axum and hyper support graceful shutdown hooks directly.

questions.q: How would you design a plugin system for a Rust application?
questions.ideal: Rust has no stable ABI, so loading a dynamic library with libloading is fragile and needs a C ABI or the abi stable crate. Compile time plugins via trait objects and Cargo features are simplest when you control the code. For third party plugins, WebAssembly with Wasmtime gives a sandbox with isolation and language independence, at some performance cost. Scripting engines are another option.

questions.q: How would you design zero-copy parsing for a high throughput protocol in Rust?
questions.ideal: Zero copy parsing returns structs with lifetimes that borrow slices of the input buffer instead of allocating new strings, avoiding allocation per field. Parser combinator crates like nom work well for this, and serde supports borrowed fields. The bytes crate provides reference counted shared buffers so slices can outlive a single read and move between tasks without copying.

questions.q: How would you speed up a Python codebase by writing performance-critical parts in Rust?
questions.ideal: First profile to find the hot path bottleneck. Then write that part in Rust with PyO3, exposing functions and classes as a Python extension, and build with Maturin, which produces wheels installable by pip for each platform. Release the GIL with allow_threads during heavy work so other Python threads run. Keep the interface coarse to reduce crossing overhead.

questions.q: How do you build and deploy Rust services as small, reproducible artifacts?
questions.ideal: Rust compiles to a single binary, and with the musl target you get a statically linked binary. Use a Docker multi stage build: compile in a Rust image with cargo build locked so Cargo lock pins versions for reproducible builds, then copy into a distroless or scratch image. Tune the release profile with LTO and strip for size, and use cross to cross compile for ARM.

questions.q: How should a production Rust service handle panics?
questions.ideal: Panics signal bugs, not expected errors, which should be Result. By default panics unwind and kill only the thread or Tokio task, which can leave a poisoned mutex. Panic abort in the release profile is smaller and fails fast, letting a supervisor like Kubernetes restart the crashed process. Catch unwind is used at FFI boundaries. Log panics with a panic hook and alert on them.

questions.q: When and how would you use Rust with WebAssembly?
questions.ideal: Rust compiles to WebAssembly with strong performance and no garbage collector, ideal for CPU heavy browser code such as image processing. Wasm bindgen generates JavaScript glue, and wasm pack builds npm packages. On the server side, WASI runs Wasm in edge platforms and plugin sandboxes. Watch bundle size by optimizing with wasm opt and avoiding heavy dependencies.

questions.q: How would you instrument a production Rust microservice for observability?
questions.ideal: Use the tracing crate with spans around requests and structured logs in JSON. Export spans with OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing across services. Expose metrics such as latency histograms, error counts and pool usage to Prometheus via the metrics crate. For async debugging of stuck tasks, tokio console shows task states. Propagate trace context through HTTP headers and message queues.

questions.q: How do you evolve serialized data formats in a Rust system without breaking older clients?
questions.ideal: Plan for backward and forward compatibility because a rolling deploy runs old and new versions together. With serde, new fields use serde default or Option, and avoid deny unknown fields so older readers ignore additions. Mark public enums non exhaustive and add an unknown catch all variant. For cross language contracts use Protobuf via prost or Avro with explicit versioning and never reuse field numbers.

questions.q: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP, and between UNION and UNION ALL in Oracle?
questions.ideal: DELETE is DML, can use WHERE and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is DDL, removes all rows quickly and cannot be rolled back. DROP removes the table itself. UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them and is faster.

questions.q: Explain inner, left, right and full outer joins, and what a self join is.
questions.ideal: An inner join returns matching rows, a left join returns all left rows with matches or nulls, a right join the reverse, and a full outer join all rows from both. A self join joins a table to itself, for example employees and managers.

questions.q: What are procedures, functions, packages and triggers in PL/SQL, and why use packages?
questions.ideal: A procedure performs actions, a function returns a value, a package groups related code in a specification and body with encapsulation and better performance, and a trigger fires automatically on DML. Handle errors in the exception block and use BULK COLLECT and FORALL for speed.

questions.q: What types of indexes exist in Oracle, and when is an index not used?
questions.ideal: B-tree indexes are the default, bitmap indexes suit low cardinality columns, function based indexes index expressions and composite indexes cover several columns. An index may be ignored when a function is applied to the column, there is an implicit conversion, the leading column is not used or selectivity is low.

questions.q: How do you tune a slow Oracle SQL query? Mention explain plan, statistics, hints and AWR.
questions.ideal: Read the execution plan with EXPLAIN PLAN or DBMS_XPLAN, keep optimizer statistics current, check index use and join methods, use bind variables to avoid hard parsing, use hints sparingly, and analyse with AWR, ASH, SQL Tuning Advisor or TKPROF.

questions.q: Explain the Oracle architecture: SGA, PGA, background processes, redo and undo.
questions.ideal: The instance has memory (SGA with buffer cache and shared pool, plus a private PGA per session) and background processes like DBWR, LGWR, SMON and PMON. Redo logs record changes for recovery, undo holds old values for rollback and read consistency, and the database is datafiles, control files and redo logs.

questions.q: Explain Oracle backup and recovery with RMAN, archivelog mode and Data Guard.
questions.ideal: Run in ARCHIVELOG mode and use RMAN for full and incremental hot backups, then restore and recover to a point in time using archived redo. Data Guard keeps a standby for disaster recovery and failover, and flashback undoes logical mistakes quickly.

questions.q: Users report hanging sessions. How do you diagnose locks, deadlocks and wait events in Oracle?
questions.ideal: Query V$SESSION and V$LOCK to find the blocking session and its SQL, usually an uncommitted transaction holding a row lock, check wait events through ASH or AWR, review deadlock traces for ORA-00060, kill the session if needed and fix the application to commit sooner and lock in a consistent order.

questions.q: What is the difference between CHAR, VARCHAR2, NUMBER, DATE and TIMESTAMP in Oracle?
questions.ideal: CHAR is fixed length and blank padded, while VARCHAR2 is variable length and saves space for strings. NUMBER stores numerics with precision and scale. DATE holds date and time to the second, TIMESTAMP adds fractional seconds and optional time zone, and CLOB or BLOB store large text or binary objects.

questions.q: How do NVL, NVL2, COALESCE, NULLIF and DECODE work in Oracle?
questions.ideal: NVL replaces a null with a given value, NVL2 returns one value when the expression is not null and another when it is null. COALESCE returns the first non null argument. NULLIF returns null when two values are equal. DECODE is Oracle if then else logic, and the standard CASE WHEN expression is more readable and flexible.

questions.q: What are ROWID and ROWNUM, and how do you get the top N rows in Oracle?
questions.ideal: ROWID is the physical address of a row and the fastest way to access it. ROWNUM is a pseudocolumn assigned before ORDER BY, so for top N you sort in an inline view subquery and filter ROWNUM outside. From 12c you can write FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY with OFFSET, or use ROW_NUMBER for per group ranking.

questions.q: What is a sequence in Oracle, and how is it different from an identity column?
questions.ideal: A sequence generates unique numbers through NEXTVAL and CURRVAL, usually for surrogate primary keys. CACHE improves performance but means gaps after rollback or restart, so sequences never guarantee gap free numbers. INCREMENT BY, START WITH and CYCLE control behaviour. From 12c an identity column defined GENERATED ALWAYS uses a hidden sequence automatically.

questions.q: What constraints are available in Oracle, and what does it mean to disable or defer a constraint?
questions.ideal: Oracle supports NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY with options like ON DELETE CASCADE, and CHECK conditions. Constraints can be disabled for bulk loads and enabled later, with NOVALIDATE skipping existing rows. A DEFERRABLE constraint set to deferred is checked at commit time instead of per statement, useful for circular references.

questions.q: What are synonyms in Oracle, and when do you use public versus private synonyms?
questions.ideal: A synonym is an alias for an object such as a table, view or package. A private synonym belongs to one schema, while a public synonym is visible to all users. They let applications reference objects without a schema prefix or hide a database link to a remote object, but users still need grants and privileges to access the underlying object.

questions.q: What is a view in Oracle, and can you run DML through a view?
questions.ideal: A view is a stored query acting as a virtual table, used to simplify queries and for security by hiding columns or rows. A simple view on a single table without aggregates is updatable. A complex view with joins, GROUP BY or DISTINCT usually needs an INSTEAD OF trigger for DML. WITH CHECK OPTION and WITH READ ONLY control changes.

questions.q: Explain COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT in Oracle, and what happens with an implicit commit.
questions.ideal: A transaction starts with the first DML. COMMIT makes changes permanent, ROLLBACK undoes them, and SAVEPOINT marks a point so you can ROLLBACK TO it for a partial rollback. Any DDL statement causes an implicit commit before and after it, and a normal session exit also commits, while an abnormal end rolls back the open transaction.

questions.q: Explain implicit cursors, explicit cursors, cursor FOR loops and REF cursors in PL/SQL.
questions.ideal: Oracle opens an implicit cursor for every DML and SELECT INTO, with attributes like SQL%ROWCOUNT and SQL%FOUND. An explicit cursor is declared then OPEN, FETCH and CLOSE, checking %NOTFOUND and %ISOPEN, and can take parameters. A cursor FOR loop opens and closes automatically. A REF cursor or SYS_REFCURSOR is a pointer used to return a result set to Java or another caller.

questions.q: How does exception handling work in PL/SQL? Explain predefined, user defined exceptions and RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR.
questions.ideal: Predefined exceptions like NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS are raised automatically. User defined exceptions are declared and fired with RAISE, and PRAGMA EXCEPTION_INIT maps an Oracle error number to a name. RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR sends a custom error between 20000 and 20999 to the caller. Use SQLCODE and SQLERRM for logging, and in WHEN OTHERS log then reraise rather than swallow errors, otherwise unhandled exceptions propagate to the outer block.

questions.q: How do you write a hierarchical query in Oracle, for example an employee manager tree?
questions.ideal: Use START WITH to pick the root, such as the employee with no manager, and CONNECT BY PRIOR employee_id = manager_id to walk down. LEVEL gives depth, SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH builds the path, and ORDER SIBLINGS BY sorts within each level. NOCYCLE with CONNECT_BY_ISCYCLE handles loops. The ANSI alternative is a recursive WITH clause, the recursive CTE.

questions.q: What is the MERGE statement in Oracle, and where would you use it?
questions.ideal: MERGE performs an upsert in one statement. You merge INTO a target USING a source table or query, joined ON a match condition. WHEN MATCHED updates existing rows and can also delete with a DELETE WHERE clause, and WHEN NOT MATCHED inserts new rows. It is common in ETL loads from a staging table into a data warehouse and avoids row by row logic.

questions.q: What is a materialized view, and explain refresh options like complete, fast and on commit.
questions.ideal: A materialized view stores the query result physically, unlike a normal view. Complete refresh rebuilds it fully, while fast refresh applies only changes using a materialized view log on the base table. Refresh can happen ON COMMIT or ON DEMAND through DBMS_MVIEW or a schedule. Query rewrite lets the optimizer use a summary materialized view automatically for reporting queries.

questions.q: What is the mutating table error ORA-04091, and how do you solve it?
questions.ideal: ORA-04091 occurs when a row level trigger queries or modifies the same table that fired it, because the table is in the middle of changing. Fixes include a compound trigger in 11g that gathers rows in a collection during the row section and processes them in the after statement section, or package variables with statement level triggers. An autonomous transaction hides the error but gives wrong results, so avoid it.

questions.q: What are the PL/SQL collection types: associative arrays, nested tables and VARRAYs?
questions.ideal: Associative arrays, also called INDEX BY tables, are key value structures that exist only in PL/SQL. Nested tables are unbounded, can be sparse after deletes and can be stored in columns and queried with the TABLE operator. VARRAYs have a fixed maximum size and keep order. Methods like COUNT, EXISTS, EXTEND and DELETE manage them, and they are the targets of BULK COLLECT and FORALL.

questions.q: When do you use dynamic SQL in PL/SQL, and how do you avoid SQL injection with EXECUTE IMMEDIATE?
questions.ideal: Dynamic SQL is needed when the statement is known only at runtime, such as DDL or a variable table name. EXECUTE IMMEDIATE runs it, with INTO for results and the USING clause for bind variables. Never concatenate user input, which causes SQL injection, and validate object names with DBMS_ASSERT or a whitelist. DBMS_SQL handles cases with an unknown number of columns.

questions.q: Explain table partitioning in Oracle: range, list, hash, interval, and local versus global indexes.
questions.ideal: Range partitioning splits by value ranges such as dates, list by discrete values, hash spreads rows evenly, and interval creates new range partitions automatically. Composite schemes add subpartitions. Partition pruning lets queries scan only relevant partitions. Local indexes are partitioned with the table and easy to maintain, while global indexes can become unusable after a drop partition. Exchange partition and dropping old partitions make archiving fast.

questions.q: What is an autonomous transaction in PL/SQL, and what are valid and risky uses?
questions.ideal: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION makes a procedure run as an independent transaction that must commit or roll back itself. Its classic use is error logging or an audit log that survives even when the main transaction rolls back. Risks include a self deadlock when it touches rows locked by the parent, and misuse to hide the mutating table error, which breaks consistency.

questions.q: How do you process millions of rows efficiently in PL/SQL with BULK COLLECT and FORALL?
questions.ideal: Row by row loops cause a context switch between the PL/SQL and SQL engines for every row. BULK COLLECT fetches in batches using the LIMIT clause to control PGA memory, and FORALL sends DML in bulk. SAVE EXCEPTIONS continues past bad rows and reports them through SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS. Avoid committing too often, and prefer a single set based SQL statement whenever possible.

questions.q: How does the Oracle cost based optimizer choose a plan, and what are bind peeking and adaptive cursor sharing?
questions.ideal: The cost based optimizer estimates cost from statistics, histograms and cardinality estimates and picks the cheapest plan. With bind peeking it looks at the bind value on first execution, which can give a bad plan for skewed data. Adaptive cursor sharing marks cursors bind sensitive then bind aware and creates new child cursors per value range. In 12c adaptive plans can also switch join methods at runtime.

questions.q: Explain nested loop, hash join and sort merge join in an Oracle execution plan, and when each is chosen.
questions.ideal: A nested loop join suits small row sources, looping over the driving table and probing the other through an index. A hash join builds a hash table on the smaller input in PGA memory and probes it, best for large equality joins. A sort merge join sorts both inputs and merges, useful for range or non equality conditions. Hints like USE_NL or USE_HASH force choices.

questions.q: What causes ORA-01555 snapshot too old, and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal: ORA-01555 occurs when a long running query needs old undo for read consistency but that undo was already overwritten. Fixes include increasing the undo tablespace and undo_retention, using RETENTION GUARANTEE, tuning the query to run faster, and avoiding fetch across commit where a loop commits while reading the same table. Delayed block cleanout after big loads can also trigger it.

questions.q: Explain tablespaces, segments, extents, blocks and the high water mark in Oracle.
questions.ideal: A tablespace is a logical container made of datafiles. Each table or index is a segment, made of extents, which are contiguous groups of blocks, the smallest unit of I/O. The high water mark is the highest block ever used, and full table scans read up to it even after deletes. ALTER TABLE SHRINK SPACE or MOVE reclaims space. Locally managed tablespaces with ASSM are standard.

questions.q: What flashback features does Oracle offer, and how would you recover an accidentally deleted set of rows?
questions.ideal: Flashback query with AS OF TIMESTAMP reads old data using undo, so deleted rows can be inserted back from it. FLASHBACK TABLE TO TIMESTAMP rewinds a table if row movement is enabled. FLASHBACK DROP restores a dropped table from the recycle bin. Flashback version query shows row history, and flashback database rewinds the whole database to a restore point using flashback logs. All depend on undo retention.

questions.q: Explain Oracle RAC architecture, cache fusion and how you handle performance problems in RAC.
questions.ideal: RAC runs multiple instances on separate nodes over shared storage, usually ASM. Cache fusion ships blocks between instances over the private interconnect. Performance issues show as global cache waits like gc buffer busy, often from hot blocks or sequences, fixed with sequence CACHE NOORDER, partitioning and services that route workload to specific nodes. SCAN listeners handle load balancing and TAF or application continuity provide failover.

questions.q: Explain the Oracle multitenant architecture with CDB and PDB, and its benefits for consolidation.
questions.ideal: A container database CDB holds the root and seed plus many pluggable databases PDB that share one instance, memory and background processes, which improves consolidation. PDBs can be cloned quickly for provisioning, refreshed, or unplugged and plugged into a newer CDB for fast upgrade. Resource Manager limits CPU and I/O per PDB for isolation, and users are either common across containers or local to one PDB.

questions.q: How would you migrate a large Oracle database to new hardware or a new version with minimal downtime?
questions.ideal: Choose by size and downtime. Data Pump expdp and impdp suits smaller databases. Transportable tablespaces with incremental backups suit cross platform moves. Data Guard switchover or RMAN DUPLICATE work for same platform. For near zero downtime, GoldenGate replicates changes until cutover. Always rehearse in testing, validate row counts and performance, and keep a rollback plan, such as reverse replication.

questions.q: After an upgrade a critical query suddenly picks a bad plan. How do you stabilize it?
questions.ideal: Confirm the plan regression by comparing current and historical plans in AWR through DBA_HIST_SQLSTAT. The quickest fix is to load the old good plan into a SQL plan baseline with SPM, or accept a SQL profile from the SQL Tuning Advisor. Check whether statistics changed and restore old stats if needed, and test pending statistics in future. OPTIMIZER_FEATURES_ENABLE or hints are fallback options.

questions.q: How do you secure sensitive data in Oracle? Explain VPD, TDE, data redaction and auditing.
questions.ideal: Virtual Private Database adds row level security predicates through policies. Transparent Data Encryption encrypts tablespaces or columns at rest with keys in a wallet or keystore. Data redaction masks values like card numbers at query time. Unified auditing records sensitive actions. Apply least privilege roles, use Database Vault to restrict even DBA access to application data, and enable network encryption with TLS.

questions.q: Design a nightly PL/SQL batch that loads 50 million rows into a reporting table within a short window.
questions.ideal: Load files through an external table into a staging table, then insert with the APPEND hint for direct path, parallel DML and NOLOGGING to reduce redo, followed by a backup. Build the data in a separate table and use partition exchange to swap it in instantly. Disable or rebuild indexes after the load, use DML error logging with LOG ERRORS, and design restartability with checkpoints.

questions.q: How do you change the structure of a large, busy table in Oracle without downtime?
questions.ideal: DBMS_REDEFINITION copies the table into an interim table with the new structure while DML continues, then sync_interim_table catches up and finish_redef_table swaps them with only a brief lock. Many changes are now online DDL, such as adding a column with a default or building an index ONLINE. For application code, edition based redefinition with editions lets old and new versions run side by side for a zero downtime upgrade.

questions.q: Users get ORA-04031 errors. How do you diagnose and fix shared pool memory problems?
questions.ideal: ORA-04031 means the shared pool cannot allocate a contiguous chunk, usually from fragmentation caused by heavy hard parsing of literal SQL. Check V$SGASTAT and the shared pool advisory, fix the application to use bind variables, or set CURSOR_SHARING to FORCE as a stopgap. Size memory through SGA_TARGET with ASMM or MEMORY_TARGET with AMM, pin large packages with DBMS_SHARED_POOL KEEP, and flush only in emergencies.

questions.q: What is the DUAL table in Oracle, and when do you use it?
questions.ideal: DUAL is a dummy table owned by SYS with one row and one column. You select from it when you need to evaluate an expression or function that is not tied to a real table, such as SELECT SYSDATE FROM DUAL, calling a sequence NEXTVAL, or testing a calculation. Since 23ai the FROM DUAL clause is optional.

questions.q: What is the Oracle data dictionary, and what is the difference between USER, ALL and DBA views?
questions.ideal: The data dictionary is read only metadata about objects. USER views like USER_TABLES show objects you own, ALL views show everything accessible to you, and DBA views show the entire database but need a privilege such as SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE. Dynamic performance views like V$SESSION, often called V dollar views, show live instance activity rather than stored definitions.

questions.q: What is the difference between a user and a schema in Oracle?
questions.ideal: In Oracle a user is an account that can log in, and the schema is the collection of objects that user owns, with the same name. CREATE USER creates both; you grant CREATE SESSION to log in and a quota on a tablespace to store objects. From 19c you can create a schema only account with no authentication, accessed through proxy or grants.

questions.q: How do TO_CHAR, TO_DATE and TO_NUMBER work, and why should you avoid relying on implicit conversion?
questions.ideal: TO_CHAR formats a date or number as text, TO_DATE parses a string into a date and TO_NUMBER parses numbers, each with a format mask like YYYY-MM-DD. Relying on implicit conversion depends on NLS_DATE_FORMAT settings, so code breaks across sessions, and conversion applied to a column can stop an index being used and force a full scan.

questions.q: Which Oracle string functions do you use most, such as SUBSTR, INSTR, REPLACE and TRIM?
questions.ideal: SUBSTR extracts part of a string, INSTR returns the position of a substring, REPLACE swaps text, and TRIM, LTRIM and RTRIM remove spaces or characters. UPPER, LOWER and INITCAP change case, often for case insensitive comparisons. LENGTH returns character count, and concatenation uses CONCAT or the double pipe operator. Note that in Oracle an empty string is treated as NULL.

questions.q: What is the Oracle listener and tnsnames.ora, and how does a client connect to the database?
questions.ideal: The listener is a process, managed with lsnrctl, that accepts client connections on a port, usually 1521, and hands them to the instance by service name. Clients resolve a net service name through tnsnames.ora or use easy connect with host, port and service. Common errors are ORA-12541 no listener and ORA-12514 when the service name is not registered.

questions.q: Why can a NOT IN subquery return no rows when the subquery contains a NULL?
questions.ideal: NOT IN compares the value against every subquery value, and comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN under three valued logic, so the whole condition is never true and you get no rows. The fix is to use NOT EXISTS, which handles NULLs correctly, or add an IS NOT NULL filter inside the subquery. Oracle may also convert NOT EXISTS into an efficient anti join.

questions.q: What is the difference between system privileges, object privileges and roles in Oracle?
questions.ideal: System privileges such as CREATE SESSION or CREATE TABLE allow actions across the database, while object privileges such as SELECT or INSERT on a specific table allow access to one object. A role groups privileges so you grant once to many users. WITH ADMIN OPTION and WITH GRANT OPTION allow passing them on, REVOKE removes them, and you follow least privilege.

questions.q: What are %TYPE and %ROWTYPE in PL/SQL, and why are they useful?
questions.ideal: %TYPE anchors a variable to a column data type, and %ROWTYPE declares a record matching a table row or cursor. Because the declaration is anchored, when a column type or size changes the PL/SQL code adapts after recompilation, reducing maintenance. %ROWTYPE is convenient to fetch into a whole row from a cursor without declaring each variable separately.

questions.q: Which tools do you use to work with Oracle, such as SQL*Plus and SQL Developer, and what are they good for?
questions.ideal: SQL*Plus is the command line client used for scripts, spool output and DBA tasks on servers. SQL Developer is a free graphical tool for writing queries, debugging PL/SQL, viewing explain plans and using Data Modeler. SQLcl is a modern command line with history and formatting. Some teams also use Toad. Autotrace in these tools shows the plan and statistics for a statement.

questions.q: What is a global temporary table in Oracle, and how does ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS differ from PRESERVE ROWS?
questions.ideal: A global temporary table has a permanent definition but data private to each session. ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS clears the rows at the end of the transaction, while ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS keeps them until the session ends. It generates less redo and undo, especially with temporary undo. From 18c private temporary tables, prefixed ORA$PTT, have even the definition private to the session.

questions.q: How do you concatenate values from many rows into one comma separated string in Oracle?
questions.ideal: LISTAGG aggregates values into one string with a delimiter, using WITHIN GROUP ORDER BY to control order, combined with GROUP BY per group. If the result exceeds the VARCHAR2 limit you get ORA-01489, so use ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE. From 19c LISTAGG supports DISTINCT to remove duplicates. Older code used XMLAGG or custom aggregate functions instead.

questions.q: What do ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS do in Oracle reporting queries?
questions.ideal: These extend GROUP BY. ROLLUP produces hierarchical subtotals and a grand total, for example by region then country. CUBE produces subtotals for all combinations of the columns. GROUPING SETS lets you list exactly which groupings you want in one pass. The GROUPING or GROUPING_ID function tells you whether a NULL is a real value or a subtotal row.

questions.q: What is a pipelined table function in PL/SQL, and when would you use it?
questions.ideal: A pipelined table function returns rows with PIPE ROW as they are produced, and you query it with the TABLE operator like a table. It needs a collection type of an object type. Because rows stream to the caller instead of building a full collection in memory, it suits ETL transformation chains, and PARALLEL_ENABLE allows parallel execution.

questions.q: What are external tables in Oracle, and how do they compare with SQL*Loader?
questions.ideal: An external table, defined with ORGANIZATION EXTERNAL, lets you query a flat file such as CSV directly with SQL through the ORACLE_LOADER access driver and a directory object. It is read only but can be joined and loaded with INSERT SELECT, even in parallel. SQL*Loader is a separate client utility, better for loading files from a client machine with control files.

questions.q: How do you schedule jobs in Oracle using DBMS_SCHEDULER, and how is it better than DBMS_JOB?
questions.ideal: DBMS_SCHEDULER creates jobs with CREATE_JOB and a calendar repeat_interval such as FREQ=DAILY. It separates programs, schedules and jobs, supports chains of dependent steps, external scripts, windows and resource plans, and records history in DBA_SCHEDULER_JOB_RUN_DETAILS. DBMS_JOB is legacy, with limited interval syntax and logging, and is now converted to scheduler jobs internally.

questions.q: How do you use regular expressions in Oracle SQL, for example to validate or extract data?
questions.ideal: Oracle provides REGEXP_LIKE to validate patterns such as emails in a WHERE clause or check constraint, REGEXP_SUBSTR to extract a match, REGEXP_REPLACE to clean text, plus REGEXP_INSTR and REGEXP_COUNT. They are powerful but cost more CPU than simple functions like INSTR or LIKE, so on large tables consider performance and use simpler functions when they work.

questions.q: How do PIVOT and UNPIVOT work in Oracle?
questions.ideal: PIVOT turns rows into columns by applying an aggregate such as SUM for each value in a fixed IN list, for example months becoming columns. UNPIVOT does the reverse, turning columns into rows. The IN list must be known in advance, so a dynamic set of columns needs dynamic SQL or PIVOT XML. Before 11g the same result was done with CASE or DECODE.

questions.q: What causes ORA-04068 existing state of packages has been discarded, and how do you avoid it?
questions.ideal: ORA-04068 happens when a package with global variables holds package state in a session and the package is recompiled, for example during deployment. Pooled sessions then fail on the next call. You avoid it by keeping no global state, moving constants into a separate package, using PRAGMA SERIALLY_REUSABLE, retrying once, or deploying with edition based redefinition.

questions.q: How do you load a large batch where some rows fail without the whole statement rolling back?
questions.ideal: DML error logging adds LOG ERRORS INTO an error table created with DBMS_ERRLOG, usually ERR$ prefixed, and REJECT LIMIT UNLIMITED. Bad rows are written to the error table with the error message, and the good rows load instead of a statement level rollback. In PL/SQL the equivalent is FORALL with SAVE EXCEPTIONS and reading SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS.

questions.q: What is the Oracle result cache, and when can it help or hurt?
questions.ideal: The result cache stores query or PL/SQL function results in the shared pool so repeated calls return without re-execution. You enable it with the RESULT_CACHE hint or the function result cache clause. Any DML on dependent tables causes invalidation, so it suits read mostly lookup tables. On frequently changing data it hurts through constant invalidation and latch contention.

questions.q: How do you trace a slow session in Oracle with 10046 trace and TKPROF?
questions.ideal: You enable SQL trace, also called event 10046, with DBMS_MONITOR.SESSION_TRACE_ENABLE including waits and binds. The raw trace file shows every call, wait events and bind values. TKPROF formats it into per statement parse, execute and fetch counts with elapsed and CPU times, plus row source plans, so you see exactly where time goes. Tools like Method R or trcsess combine traces.

questions.q: How does parallel query work in Oracle, and what problems can it cause?
questions.ideal: Parallel execution splits a large operation, typically a full scan of large tables, among PX server processes managed by a query coordinator. The degree of parallelism comes from the table, a PARALLEL hint or auto DOP, and parallel DML must be enabled in the session. Overuse exhausts CPU and PX servers, causing downgraded queries, so control it with resource manager and statement queuing.

questions.q: What table compression options exist in Oracle, and what are their trade offs?
questions.ideal: Basic compression works only for direct path loads. Advanced row compression, formerly OLTP compression, also compresses during normal DML but needs the Advanced Compression license. Hybrid columnar compression on Exadata gives the highest ratio for warehouse data. Benefits are storage savings and less IO; costs are CPU overhead and, for HCC, slow single row updates.

questions.q: What are histograms in Oracle statistics, and how can they cause or fix bad plans?
questions.ideal: A histogram describes data distribution for skewed columns, using frequency, top frequency or hybrid types. Without one, the optimizer assumes even distribution and gets cardinality estimates wrong. DBMS_STATS creates them through METHOD_OPT, often based on column usage. Combined with bind peeking, histograms can make plans flip between bind values, which adaptive cursor sharing tries to handle.

questions.q: What is the index clustering factor, and why might Oracle ignore an index that seems perfect?
questions.ideal: The clustering factor counts how many table block visits a full index scan needs. If rows are stored in the same order as the index, it is near the number of table blocks; if scattered, near the number of rows. A high value makes the index range scan cost high, so the optimizer prefers a full table scan. Fixes include attribute clustering or setting TABLE_CACHED_BLOCKS.

questions.q: What is the difference between row chaining and row migration, and how do you fix them?
questions.ideal: Row chaining happens when a row is too large for one block, so it spans blocks. Row migration happens when an update makes a row grow and it no longer fits, so it moves and leaves a pointer. Both cause extra IO, visible in the table fetch continued row statistic. Fix migration with higher PCTFREE and ALTER TABLE MOVE; chaining needs bigger blocks or redesign.

questions.q: An application gets ORA-01000 maximum open cursors exceeded. How do you troubleshoot it?
questions.ideal: ORA-01000 means a session hit the OPEN_CURSORS parameter limit. Usually it is a cursor leak where the application does not close statements or result sets, often missing a finally block or try with resources. Query V$OPEN_CURSOR grouped by SQL to find the leaking statement. Raising the parameter only delays it; fixing close calls is the real solution. Do not confuse it with SESSION_CACHED_CURSORS.

questions.q: Why is calling a PL/SQL function from a SQL query on millions of rows slow, and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal: Each call from the SQL engine to the PL/SQL engine is a context switch, and on millions of rows the overhead dominates. Fixes are rewriting the logic in pure SQL, adding PRAGMA UDF, declaring the function inline using WITH FUNCTION, wrapping the call in a scalar subquery to get caching, marking it DETERMINISTIC, or using the function result cache for lookup style functions.

questions.q: How do you find which lines of a slow PL/SQL program consume the most time?
questions.ideal: DBMS_PROFILER gives line level timing, while the hierarchical profiler DBMS_HPROF reports time per subprogram with the call tree, separating SQL time from PL/SQL time, and plshprof turns it into HTML. Combine with SQL Monitor for heavy statements. Long term, add instrumentation such as logging start and end timing in batch code, for example with Logger or DBMS_APPLICATION_INFO.

questions.q: What is edition based redefinition, and how does it enable zero downtime application upgrades?
questions.ideal: Edition based redefinition lets two versions of editionable objects such as PL/SQL and views exist side by side in different editions. Tables are accessed through editioning views, and crossedition triggers keep old and new column structures in sync while both application versions run. Sessions move to the new edition gradually, giving a zero downtime online upgrade and easy rollback.

questions.q: How does Oracle GoldenGate replication work, and when would you choose it over Data Guard?
questions.ideal: GoldenGate uses an Extract process to capture changes from redo, writes them to trail files, and a Replicat applies them on the target. It is logical replication, so it supports heterogeneous targets, different versions, subsets of tables and bidirectional active active setups with conflict resolution. Data Guard is a block level physical standby, simpler and better for pure disaster recovery.

questions.q: What makes Exadata faster for Oracle workloads, and what should a developer know about it?
questions.ideal: Exadata pushes work to storage cells through smart scan offload, filtering rows and columns before sending them to the database. Storage indexes skip regions that cannot match, smart flash cache speeds IO, and hybrid columnar compression shrinks data. Smart scan needs full scan with direct path read, so some warehouse queries run faster after dropping indexes, while OLTP still relies on index access.

questions.q: How does Oracle Database In-Memory work, and how do you decide which tables to populate?
questions.ideal: Database In-Memory keeps a columnar copy of selected tables in the IM column store, sized with INMEMORY_SIZE, while the buffer cache keeps row format, so it is dual format with transactions unaffected. Analytic reporting queries scanning few columns over many rows benefit most. Choose tables based on heat map and analytic workloads, set population priority, and drop analytic indexes once in-memory scans replace them.

questions.q: How do you prove that a database upgrade or parameter change will not slow critical SQL?
questions.ideal: Capture the workload into a SQL tuning set, then use SQL Performance Analyzer to execute it before and after the change and compare elapsed time and plans for regressions. For full concurrency testing, Real Application Testing includes Database Replay, which captures production workload and replays it on the upgraded test system. Regressed statements are fixed with SQL plan baselines from the old plans.

questions.q: What is Oracle ASM, and how do disk groups and redundancy work?
questions.ideal: ASM is Oracle volume manager and file system for database files. Disks are grouped into disk groups, and ASM does striping across all disks and mirroring based on redundancy: external relies on storage RAID, normal keeps two copies and high three, placed in different failure groups. Adding or removing disks triggers an online rebalance controlled by the power setting.

questions.q: Commits are slow and AWR shows high log file sync waits. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.ideal: Log file sync is the wait for LGWR to write redo after a commit. Compare it to log file parallel write: if that is also high, storage latency is the problem, so move redo logs to fast disks. If writes are fast, there are too many commits, such as row by row commits in loops, so batch commits. CPU starvation of LGWR can also be a cause.

questions.q: Inserts into a table with a sequence based primary key suffer buffer busy and index split waits on RAC. How do you fix it?
questions.ideal: Monotonic sequence values all insert into the last leaf block, creating a hot right hand index with buffer busy waits and, on RAC, gc buffer busy and index contention. Fixes include a larger sequence cache, scalable sequences in 18c and later, a reverse key index (losing range scans), or a hash partitioned index that spreads inserts over several leaf blocks.

questions.q: How would you use Oracle Resource Manager to protect OLTP users from heavy reporting in a consolidated database?
questions.ideal: Resource Manager defines consumer groups, for example OLTP and reporting, mapped by service, user or module. A resource plan sets directives such as CPU shares, parallel degree limits and statement queuing. Runaway query rules can switch a session to a lower group or cancel a call after a time or IO threshold. In multitenant, CDB plans also allocate shares between PDBs.

questions.q: What are some important new features in Oracle Database 23ai for developers?
questions.ideal: Oracle 23ai introduces JSON relational duality views, which expose relational tables as updatable JSON documents, and AI vector search with a VECTOR data type and similarity indexes. It adds a native BOOLEAN data type, SQL domains for reusable column rules, IF NOT EXISTS in DDL, FROM DUAL optional, schema level privileges and lock free reservations.

questions.q: What is the CSS box model, and what is the difference between flexbox and grid?
questions.ideal: The box model is content, padding, border and margin, and box-sizing border-box includes padding and border in the width. Flexbox lays out in one dimension, grid in two. Semantic HTML and understanding specificity and the cascade keep CSS predictable.

questions.q: What is the difference between var, let and const, and what are closures and hoisting?
questions.ideal: var is function scoped and hoisted, let and const are block scoped with a temporal dead zone, and const cannot be reassigned. A closure is a function that remembers variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has returned.

questions.q: Explain the event loop, promises, async await and the microtask queue.
questions.ideal: JavaScript is single threaded with an event loop that runs the call stack, then microtasks such as promise callbacks, then macrotasks like setTimeout. async and await are syntax over promises, and Promise.all runs promises in parallel.

questions.q: What are event bubbling, capturing and delegation, and how do you improve DOM performance?
questions.ideal: Events capture down and then bubble up the DOM. Event delegation attaches one listener on a parent and uses event.target. Reduce reflow and repaint by batching DOM changes, and use debounce, throttle and requestAnimationFrame for frequent events.

questions.q: How do you improve page load performance and Core Web Vitals?
questions.ideal: Improve LCP, INP and CLS by optimising and lazy loading images in modern formats, code splitting and minifying bundles, compressing with gzip or Brotli, using a CDN and cache headers, deferring non critical scripts, inlining critical CSS and measuring with Lighthouse.

questions.q: What are XSS, CSRF and CORS, and how do you protect a frontend?
questions.ideal: XSS injects scripts, prevented by escaping output, avoiding innerHTML and using a CSP. CSRF abuses a logged in session, prevented with tokens and SameSite cookies. CORS controls cross origin requests through headers and preflight. Use HttpOnly secure cookies, HTTPS and audit dependencies.

questions.q: How do you build accessible web apps? Mention ARIA, semantic HTML and keyboard navigation.
questions.ideal: Use semantic HTML first, add ARIA only where needed, ensure full keyboard navigation with visible focus, provide alt text and labels, meet WCAG colour contrast, and test with a screen reader and tools like axe and Lighthouse.

questions.q: How do you architect a large frontend: state, components, micro frontends and testing?
questions.ideal: Build reusable components within a design system, keep state predictable with a store such as Redux or Zustand, consider micro frontends for independent team deployments, use TypeScript, lint and performance budgets, and test with Jest and Testing Library plus end to end tests.

questions.q: What is semantic HTML, and which HTML5 elements would you use to structure a page?
questions.ideal: Semantic HTML uses elements that describe meaning instead of generic div and span tags. A page uses header and footer, nav for navigation, main for primary content, article for standalone content, section for grouped content and aside for a sidebar. This improves SEO, accessibility for screen reader users and code readability, and it gives built in behaviour for free.

questions.q: What are the data types in JavaScript, and what is type coercion with == versus ===?
questions.ideal: JavaScript primitive types are string, number, boolean, undefined, null, symbol and bigint, and everything else is an object, including arrays and functions, held by reference. Double equals is loose equality that performs type coercion, so zero equals an empty string. Triple equals is strict equality checking type and value, so it is preferred. The typeof operator reports types, though typeof null returns object.

questions.q: What is the difference between display block, inline, inline-block and none, and visibility hidden?
questions.ideal: Block elements start on a new line and take full width. Inline elements flow on the same line and ignore width and height. Inline-block flows inline but respects width and height. Display none removes the element from layout so it takes no space, while visibility hidden hides it but still takes space, and opacity zero keeps it invisible but still clickable.

questions.q: How do you make a website responsive for mobile, tablet and desktop?
questions.ideal: Add the viewport meta tag, design mobile first, and use media queries with min width breakpoints to adapt layout for tablet and desktop. Use fluid widths with percentages and relative units, flexbox and grid for flexible layout, and responsive images with srcset and max width 100 percent. Test using browser devtools device mode and on real phones.

questions.q: Explain map, filter, reduce and forEach in JavaScript with examples.
questions.ideal: map transforms each element and returns a new array, for example doubling numbers. filter returns a subset matching a condition. reduce combines elements into a single value using an accumulator, like a sum. forEach just loops for side effects and returns nothing. map, filter and reduce leave the original unchanged, and find, some and every are related helpers.

questions.q: What is the difference between cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage?
questions.ideal: Cookies are small, around 4KB, sent with every request to the server and can have an expiry and an HttpOnly flag for security. localStorage stores about 5MB per origin and persists with no expiry. sessionStorage is similar but scoped to one tab and cleared when the session ends. Neither web storage is sent to the server or safe for sensitive tokens because scripts can read them.

questions.q: What is the difference between px, em, rem, percent, vh and vw in CSS?
questions.ideal: px is an absolute unit in CSS pixels. em is relative to the parent font size, so it compounds when nested, while rem is relative to the root font size on the html element and is predictable. Percent is relative to the parent. vh and vw are viewport units, one percent of the viewport height or width. Using rem respects the user font size for accessibility.

questions.q: How do you validate forms on the frontend, and why is server side validation still required?
questions.ideal: Use HTML5 validation attributes like required, pattern, minlength and type email, and add custom JavaScript validation on the submit event with preventDefault, or the constraint validation API with setCustomValidity. Show clear inline error messages linked to fields so they are accessible. Server side validation is still required because client checks are for user experience and can be bypassed easily, so they provide no security.

questions.q: How does the this keyword work in JavaScript, and what do call, apply and bind do?
questions.ideal: The value of this depends on the call. In a method call it is the object, in a plain call it is the global object or undefined in strict mode and with new the new instance. Arrow functions use lexical this. call and apply invoke a function with a chosen this, passing arguments individually or as an array, and bind returns a new function with this permanently set.

questions.q: Explain prototypal inheritance in JavaScript and how ES6 classes relate to it.
questions.ideal: Every object has an internal prototype link, accessed through __proto__ or Object.getPrototypeOf. When a property is missing, JavaScript walks up the prototype chain. Object.create sets a prototype directly, and constructor functions with new set it to Function.prototype. ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over this, with extends and super linking prototypes. hasOwnProperty checks own property versus inherited ones.

questions.q: How are arrow functions different from regular functions in JavaScript?
questions.ideal: Arrow functions have concise syntax with implicit return for a single expression. They have no own this but use lexical this from the enclosing scope, which suits callbacks. They have no arguments object, so you use rest parameters, and they cannot be used as a constructor with new. Avoid them as object methods or event handlers that need this to point to the element.

questions.q: How do you call a REST API with fetch, handle errors properly and cancel a request?
questions.ideal: fetch returns a promise that only rejects on a network error, not on HTTP errors, so check response ok or the status code yourself and throw. Use async await with try catch, call response json to parse the body, and set method, headers and a JSON body for POST. To cancel, pass an AbortController signal and call abort, for example when a component unmounts or on new searches.

questions.q: What are ES modules, and how do they differ from CommonJS?
questions.ideal: ES modules use import and export and are static, so bundlers can do tree shaking to remove unused code. They support named exports and a default export, and run in browsers with script type module and in Node. CommonJS uses require and module.exports, loads synchronously at runtime and is Node's older system. Dynamic import returns a promise and enables lazy loading and code splitting.

questions.q: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy in JavaScript, and how do you do each?
questions.ideal: A shallow copy duplicates only the top level, so nested objects are still shared by reference and mutation affects both; spread operator and Object.assign make shallow copies. A deep copy makes nested data independent. structuredClone is the modern built in way. JSON.parse of JSON.stringify works only for plain data and loses dates, functions and undefined. Libraries like lodash cloneDeep also work.

questions.q: How do you organise CSS in a large project? Explain BEM, preprocessors and CSS modules.
questions.ideal: BEM, block element modifier, is a naming convention that keeps selectors flat and avoids specificity conflicts. SASS or SCSS preprocessors add variables, mixins and nesting. CSS modules scope class names locally to a component so global clashes disappear. Other options are CSS in JS like styled components and utility first frameworks like Tailwind. Consistent conventions matter more than the tool.

questions.q: What happens in the browser from typing a URL until the page is rendered?
questions.ideal: The browser resolves the domain with DNS, opens a TCP connection with a TLS handshake, and sends an HTTP request. It parses the HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combining them into a render tree. Then it runs layout to compute positions, paint to fill pixels and composite layers to screen. Stylesheets and synchronous scripts are render blocking, so defer them when possible.

questions.q: What causes memory leaks in frontend apps, and how do you find them?
questions.ideal: Leaks happen when references keep unused objects alive, such as event listeners never removed, setInterval timers never cleared, detached DOM nodes held in variables, global variables, caches and closures. Find them in the devtools memory tab by taking a heap snapshot before and after an action and comparing retained objects. Fix with cleanup on unmount, removing listeners, clearing timers and using WeakMap for caches.

questions.q: What are web workers, and when would you use them in a frontend application?
questions.ideal: Web workers run JavaScript on a background thread so heavy computation, such as parsing large files, image processing or encryption, does not block the main UI thread and freeze the page. They communicate by postMessage message passing and have no DOM access. Transferable objects or SharedArrayBuffer avoid copying large data, and libraries like Comlink make the messaging feel like normal function calls.

questions.q: What is a service worker, and how does it make a Progressive Web App work offline?
questions.ideal: A service worker is a script that sits between the page and the network as a proxy for requests. Using the Cache API it can serve assets offline with strategies like cache first, network first or stale while revalidate. It has an install, activate and update lifecycle. With a web manifest the PWA becomes installable, and service workers also enable push notifications, requiring HTTPS.

questions.q: Compare polling, long polling, Server Sent Events and WebSockets for real time updates.
questions.ideal: Polling asks the server at an interval and is simple but wasteful. Long polling holds the request open until data arrives. Server Sent Events through EventSource stream one way from server to client with automatic reconnect, ideal for notifications or live scores. WebSockets are bidirectional full duplex, best for chat or collaboration, but need heartbeat, reconnect logic and scaling care with load balancer sticky sessions.

questions.q: How do you build smooth 60 fps animations on the web?
questions.ideal: Animate only transform and opacity, which the compositor can handle on the GPU without layout or paint. Avoid animating layout properties like top, left or width, which cause reflow each frame. Use CSS transitions or requestAnimationFrame for JavaScript animation, apply will-change carefully to promote a layer, and check the performance panel for jank, keeping each frame within the 16ms frame budget.

questions.q: Explain client side rendering, server side rendering, static site generation and hydration, and when to use each.
questions.ideal: Client side rendering renders in the browser, fine for dashboards but weaker for SEO and first paint. Server side rendering produces HTML per request, good for SEO and dynamic content but adds server cost and TTFB. Static site generation builds pages at build time, fastest for content sites, with incremental static regeneration refreshing them. Hydration attaches events to server HTML, and islands or streaming reduce it.

questions.q: How do you render a list or table with 100,000 rows without freezing the browser?
questions.ideal: Rendering 100,000 DOM nodes is far too many, so use virtualization, also called windowing, which renders only the visible rows in the viewport plus a small buffer and adjusts positions while scrolling. Libraries like react window or a virtual scroller help, and fixed row height is easiest, otherwise measure heights. Alternatives are server pagination or infinite scroll loading with Intersection Observer.

questions.q: How do you ensure your JavaScript and CSS work across older browsers?
questions.ideal: Define target browsers with browserslist, transpile modern syntax with Babel and add polyfills through core-js only for missing APIs. Autoprefixer with PostCSS adds vendor prefixes. Check support on Can I Use, use feature detection with CSS supports or checks in JavaScript, and follow progressive enhancement so core features work everywhere. Test on real devices or a service like BrowserStack.

questions.q: Design an autocomplete or search typeahead component for a large e-commerce site.
questions.ideal: Debounce input by about 300ms and require a minimum number of characters before calling the server ranking API. Cancel stale requests with AbortController to avoid a race condition showing old results, and cache previous queries. Support keyboard navigation with arrow keys and enter using the ARIA combobox pattern, highlight matching text, and handle loading, empty and error states. Track analytics for selected suggestions.

questions.q: How do you monitor errors and performance of a frontend in production?
questions.ideal: Use an error tracking tool like Sentry that captures window onerror and unhandledrejection events plus error boundary failures with a fallback UI. Upload source maps privately so minified stack traces become readable, and tag each event with release, browser and user context. Collect real user monitoring of web vitals, build dashboards and alerts on regressions, and apply sampling while scrubbing PII for privacy.

questions.q: How would you migrate a large jQuery application to a modern framework without stopping feature work?
questions.ideal: Use an incremental migration with the strangler pattern, not a big bang rewrite. Set up a modern bundler and build pipeline, then mount new framework components as islands inside existing jQuery pages, or move route by route. Use a bridge such as an event bus for shared state between old and new code. Protect behaviour with end to end regression tests and delete legacy code as areas are replaced.

questions.q: How do you build a frontend that supports multiple languages, including right to left scripts?
questions.ideal: Keep all strings in translation files referenced by keys, loaded with an i18n library and lazy loading locale bundles. Use the Intl API for number, date and currency formatting, and ICU message format for pluralization and gender. For right to left languages like Arabic set the dir attribute and use CSS logical properties such as margin-inline-start. Design for text expansion so layouts do not break.

questions.q: How would you implement feature flags and A/B testing in a frontend application?
questions.ideal: Feature flags are toggles fetched from remote config such as LaunchDarkly, Unleash or an in house service, letting you ship code dark and enable a gradual rollout by percentage or a canary group. For A/B testing assign each user a variant with consistent bucketing on user id so it stays sticky, send exposure and conversion events to analytics and judge significance. Schedule cleanup to avoid flag debt.

questions.q: How do you deploy a frontend so users never load broken or stale assets, and how do you roll back?
questions.ideal: Build assets with content hash filenames so they can use long immutable caching, which is cache busting by fingerprint. Serve index html with no cache so it always points to the latest assets. Upload new files before switching the HTML, an atomic deploy with versioned folders on the CDN, and keep old chunks so open tabs avoid chunk load errors. Rollback means pointing back to the previous version.

questions.q: Design an offline first web app, such as a field sales form, that syncs data when the network returns.
questions.ideal: Cache the app shell with a service worker and store data locally in IndexedDB so the app works fully offline. Writes go to an outbox sync queue, replayed with Background Sync or on online events, with a unique request id so retries are idempotent on the server. Define conflict resolution, such as last write wins, field level merge or user choice, and show clear status feedback about pending changes.

questions.q: Design a JavaScript widget, like a chat or payment button, that other companies embed on their websites.
questions.ideal: Ship a small async script tag loader from a CDN that lazily loads the rest to protect host performance and bundle size. Use an iframe for isolation and security of sensitive parts, communicating via postMessage with a strict origin check, or shadow DOM for style isolation so CSS leaks neither way. Avoid global pollution with a single namespace, and keep versioning backward compatible because you cannot redeploy the host pages.

questions.q: What is the difference between a normal script tag, async and defer?
questions.ideal: A normal script is parser blocking: HTML parsing stops while it downloads and runs. Async downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives, in no guaranteed execution order, which suits independent analytics. Defer downloads in parallel and runs in order after parsing, before DOMContentLoaded, which suits app code. Type module scripts are deferred by default.

questions.q: How does CSS specificity work, and how is the cascade resolved?
questions.ideal: The cascade picks the winning declaration by importance, specificity and then source order, where the later rule wins. Specificity counts inline style highest, then ID selectors, then class selectors, attributes and pseudo classes, then element selectors. !important overrides normal rules and should be avoided because it causes specificity wars. Keeping selectors flat with classes makes styles predictable.

questions.q: Explain static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky positioning in CSS.
questions.ideal: Static is the default flow. Relative offsets an element from its normal place and creates a reference for children. Absolute removes it from flow and positions it against the nearest positioned ancestor. Fixed positions against the viewport, staying put while scrolling. Sticky behaves relative until a scroll threshold, then sticks. Top, left and z-index apply to positioned elements.

questions.q: What is the difference between pseudo classes and pseudo elements in CSS?
questions.ideal: A pseudo class, written with a single colon, selects an element in a state or position, like hover, focus or nth-child. A pseudo element, written with a double colon, styles part of an element or inserts generated content, like ::before and ::after, which need the content property, plus ::first-line, ::placeholder and ::selection.

questions.q: How do you select and update elements in the DOM with plain JavaScript?
questions.ideal: Use querySelector or getElementById to find one element and querySelectorAll for many. Change text with textContent, which is safe, while innerHTML parses HTML and can cause XSS with user input. Use classList add, remove and toggle for styles, createElement with append or appendChild to add nodes, and addEventListener to react to events.

questions.q: How do destructuring, the spread operator and rest parameters work in JavaScript?
questions.ideal: Destructuring unpacks values from arrays and objects into variables, for example const name and age from user, with default values for missing ones. The spread operator expands an array or object, useful to copy or merge objects and arrays, though only shallowly. Rest parameters collect remaining arguments or properties into an array or object.

questions.q: What are truthy and falsy values, and how do optional chaining and nullish coalescing help?
questions.ideal: Falsy values are false, zero, empty string, NaN, null and undefined; everything else is truthy. Using the logical OR for defaults wrongly replaces zero or empty string, while nullish coalescing, the double question mark, only falls back for null or undefined. Optional chaining, question dot, safely reads nested properties, returning undefined instead of throwing.

questions.q: Which meta tags and head elements matter for mobile and SEO?
questions.ideal: The viewport meta tag makes mobile layouts scale correctly, and charset UTF-8 ensures text is decoded properly. A unique title and meta description help SEO and search snippets. Open Graph tags control social sharing previews, a canonical link avoids duplicate content, and the lang attribute on html helps search engines and screen readers.

questions.q: How do you use browser DevTools to debug a frontend problem?
questions.ideal: Open DevTools and use Elements to inspect the DOM and computed styles, Console for errors and logging, and Network to check requests, status codes and payloads. Sources lets you set a breakpoint or use the debugger statement and step through code. Performance and Lighthouse profile speed, and the Application tab shows storage and cookies.

questions.q: How do you add images properly to a web page for accessibility and performance?
questions.ideal: Always add alt text describing the image, or empty alt for decorative ones. Set width and height to reserve space and avoid layout shift. Use loading lazy for images below the fold, srcset and sizes to serve responsive images, modern formats like WebP or AVIF, and compress images to optimize download size.

questions.q: What is the difference between debounce and throttle, and where would you use each?
questions.ideal: Debounce delays a function until events stop for a set time, using a timer with setTimeout, so typing in a search input triggers one request after the user pauses. Throttle runs a function at most once per interval, which suits scroll and resize handlers. Both can fire on the leading or trailing edge, and both reduce wasted work and network calls.

questions.q: What are CSS custom properties, and how would you use them to implement dark mode?
questions.ideal: CSS custom properties are variables declared like --primary on :root and used with var. Unlike preprocessor variables they follow the cascade and inheritance and can change at runtime. For dark mode, redefine the color tokens under a prefers-color-scheme media query or a data-theme attribute set by JavaScript, so all components switch theme without changing their CSS.
