questions.q: What is the difference between Promise.all, allSettled, race and any?
questions.ideal: Promise.all runs promises concurrently and resolves with all results but fails fast on the first rejection. Promise.allSettled waits for every promise and reports each status, so one failure does not lose other results. Promise.race settles with the first settled promise, useful for timeouts. Promise.any resolves with the first fulfilled one, ignoring rejections unless all fail.

questions.q: What is the IntersectionObserver API, and what is it used for?
questions.ideal: IntersectionObserver notifies you asynchronously when an element enters or leaves the viewport or a container, with threshold and rootMargin options. It replaces expensive scroll events and getBoundingClientRect checks, improving performance. Common uses are lazy loading images, infinite scroll by observing a sentinel near the bottom, impression tracking and starting animations when visible.

questions.q: Why does a high z-index sometimes not work, and what is a stacking context?
questions.ideal: z-index only works on positioned elements or flex and grid children, and only within its stacking context. Properties like opacity below one, transform, filter or position with z-index on a parent ancestor create a new stacking context, so a child with z-index 9999 cannot escape above elements outside it. Fix by restructuring, rendering modals at body level, or using isolation isolate deliberately.

questions.q: When would you use Map, Set, WeakMap or WeakSet instead of plain objects and arrays?
questions.ideal: Map stores key value pairs with any key type, including objects, keeps insertion order and has a size property, which plain objects lack. Set stores unique values, making deduplication easy. WeakMap and WeakSet hold weak references to object keys, so entries do not prevent garbage collection, which avoids memory leaks when attaching metadata to DOM nodes.

questions.q: What does a bundler like webpack or Vite do, and what is tree shaking?
questions.ideal: A bundler such as webpack, Vite or Rollup resolves imports and combines modules into optimized files with minification and source maps. Tree shaking removes unused exports, which needs static ES modules and no side effects. Vite serves native ES modules in development with a fast dev server and hot module replacement, and uses Rollup or esbuild for production builds.

questions.q: How do package.json versions and lock files work, and why does it matter for builds?
questions.ideal: package.json lists dependencies with semver ranges: caret allows minor updates and tilde allows patch updates. The lock file, such as package-lock or yarn.lock, pins exact versions of the whole tree, so builds are reproducible. In CI use npm ci, which installs exactly from the lock file. Run npm audit for vulnerabilities and commit the lock file.

questions.q: How do you test frontend code, and what types of tests do you write?
questions.ideal: Write fast unit tests for logic with Jest or Vitest, component tests with Testing Library that query by role and text to test user behavior rather than implementation details, and a few end to end tests with Playwright or Cypress for critical journeys. Mock network calls with MSW. Follow the testing pyramid and focus coverage on risky code.

questions.q: How does client side routing work in a single page application?
questions.ideal: Client side routing intercepts link clicks and uses the History API pushState to change the URL without a page reload, then renders the matching view. The popstate event handles the back button. Hash routing is an older approach. Because a refresh or deep link requests the path from the server, the server fallback must rewrite unknown routes to index.html instead of returning 404.

questions.q: What is a Content Security Policy, and how do you roll it out without breaking the site?
questions.ideal: A Content Security Policy header restricts where scripts, styles and other resources can load from, a strong XSS mitigation. Directives like script-src control sources, and blocking inline scripts with no unsafe-inline is the main benefit, using nonces or hashes with strict-dynamic instead. Roll it out first in report-only mode, collect violation reporting, fix them, then enforce.

questions.q: How do you use code splitting and lazy loading to reduce bundle size?
questions.ideal: Code splitting breaks the bundle into chunks loaded on demand with dynamic import. Start with route based splitting so each page loads only its code, then lazy loading of heavy components like charts or editors. Separate a stable vendor chunk for better caching. Use a bundle analyzer to find large dependencies, and prefetch likely next routes to hide latency.

questions.q: How do you configure HTTP caching for HTML, JavaScript and images?
questions.ideal: Static assets get hashed filenames with a content hash, so they can use Cache-Control max-age one year immutable. HTML should use no-cache so browsers revalidate every time with ETag or Last-Modified and get 304 if unchanged, ensuring users get new asset references. A CDN can cache with s-maxage separately, and a deploy changes hashes to bust caches.

questions.q: How do you load web fonts without hurting performance or causing text to flash or shift?
questions.ideal: Without care, fonts cause FOIT, invisible text, or FOUT with layout shift when swapping. Use font-display swap or optional, preload critical fonts, serve WOFF2 and subsetting to only needed characters, and self host to avoid extra connections. Tune the fallback font with size-adjust and related descriptors so the swap does not shift layout.

questions.q: What are web components, and what are Shadow DOM and custom elements good for?
questions.ideal: Web components are browser standards: custom elements defined with customElements.define, Shadow DOM for style and DOM encapsulation, templates and slots for content projection. They are framework agnostic, so a design system or widget works in React, Angular or plain pages. Trade offs include harder styling from outside, server rendering complexity and form and accessibility integration.

questions.q: A search page sometimes shows results for an old query. Why does that happen, and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal: This is a race condition: responses arrive out of order, so a slow stale response for an old query overwrites the newer one. Fix it by cancelling the previous request with AbortController, tracking a request id and ignoring results that are not from the latest request, or ignoring results after cleanup in a component. Debounce also reduces how many requests are in flight.

questions.q: Where should a single page application store authentication tokens, and what are the trade offs?
questions.ideal: Tokens in localStorage are readable by any script, so XSS can steal them. An HttpOnly cookie hides the token from JavaScript but needs CSRF protection with SameSite and tokens. A common pattern keeps a short lived access token in memory and a refresh token with rotation in an HttpOnly cookie, or uses a backend for frontend, BFF, that holds tokens server side.

questions.q: How do you manage the performance and security impact of third party scripts like analytics, ads and chat widgets?
questions.ideal: Third party scripts often block the main thread and add long tasks and requests. Load them async or defer, lazy load widgets with a facade until the user interacts, or move them to a web worker using Partytown. Keep governance through audits of the tag manager, restrict sources with CSP, and use subresource integrity for static third party files.

questions.q: How do you debug a poor Interaction to Next Paint score?
questions.ideal: INP measures how fast the page visually responds to interactions, made of input delay, processing time and presentation delay. Find slow interactions from RUM field data using the web-vitals library, then reproduce them in the DevTools performance panel. Fix long tasks by making the event handler do less, deferring non urgent work, and breaking up work by yielding with scheduler.yield or setTimeout.

questions.q: Which modern CSS features have changed how you write layouts and styles?
questions.ideal: Container queries let components respond to their container size instead of the viewport. The :has selector works as a parent selector, styling an element based on its children. Cascade layers with @layer control precedence without specificity hacks. Native CSS nesting reduces preprocessor need, subgrid aligns nested grids, and clamp enables fluid typography and spacing.

questions.q: How would you build and roll out a design system and component library for many product teams?
questions.ideal: Start with design tokens for color, spacing and typography, then build accessible components documented in Storybook with usage guidelines. Publish with semantic versioning and a changelog, and support theming for multiple brands. Adoption needs governance with a core team, a contribution model, codemods for breaking changes and metrics on usage, rather than forcing teams to switch at once.

questions.q: Would you put many frontend apps and shared packages in a monorepo? How do you keep builds fast?
questions.ideal: A monorepo makes shared packages and atomic changes across apps easy and keeps versions consistent, unlike a polyrepo with versioning overhead. To keep builds fast use Nx or Turborepo with workspaces, running only affected projects through incremental builds and a remote cache. Define ownership with CODEOWNERS and module boundary rules so teams do not couple everything.

questions.q: How do you stop frontend performance from slowly getting worse as many teams ship features?
questions.ideal: Define a performance budget for bundle size and Core Web Vitals such as LCP, INP and CLS. Enforce it in the CI pipeline with size-limit and Lighthouse CI, failing the build or flagging regressions on pull requests. Track RUM field data on dashboards per page with clear ownership, and review trends regularly, because lab tests alone miss real device problems.

questions.q: Design the frontend for an infinite scrolling social media feed.
questions.ideal: Load pages with cursor based pagination triggered by an IntersectionObserver for infinite scroll, and use virtualization to keep the DOM small. Keep fetched pages in a cache so scroll restoration works on back navigation. Use optimistic updates for likes, show a new posts banner from polling or a WebSocket instead of shifting content, and lazy load images with reserved dimensions.

questions.q: How would you build real time collaborative editing, like Google Docs, in the browser?
questions.ideal: Concurrent edits must merge without conflict. Operational transformation uses a central server to transform operations, while CRDT libraries such as Yjs or Automerge merge changes in any order, which also supports offline editing and later sync. Changes stream over a WebSocket, presence shows other users cursors, and snapshots are persisted on the server for history and loading.

questions.q: A popular npm dependency in your app was compromised. How do you respond, and how do you reduce this risk in future?
questions.ideal: Identify affected builds from the lock file, remove or rollback to a safe or patched version, redeploy, and rotate secrets or credentials the build or app could expose, then check logs for abuse. To reduce supply chain risk, pin versions, use npm ci, run audits with Dependabot or Snyk, review new packages, minimize dependencies, and use CSP and SRI for runtime protection.

questions.q: How would you design data fetching and caching for a large single page application?
questions.ideal: Separate server state from client state. Use a query cache library like TanStack Query or SWR that gives deduplication of identical requests, stale while revalidate, retry and consistent loading and error states. Mutations trigger invalidation of affected queries or optimistic updates. Define query keys and conventions centrally, and use a typed API client so teams fetch consistently.

questions.q: A user opens your app in several tabs. How do you keep authentication and data in sync across tabs?
questions.ideal: Use the BroadcastChannel API or the storage event from localStorage to send messages between tabs, so logout or login in one tab updates all others. A shared worker or service worker can hold a single WebSocket connection, or tabs use leader election so only one connects. On visibilitychange or focus, refetch stale data so the visible tab is current.

questions.q: How would you build a web app that performs well for users on cheap phones and slow 3G networks?
questions.ideal: On low end devices, JavaScript parse and execution cost dominates, so set a strict JavaScript budget and ship HTML first with server side rendering and progressive enhancement. Use Brotli compression, adaptive images that honour Save-Data, and a service worker for caching and offline support. Test with CPU and network throttling and on real devices, not only fast laptops.

questions.q: After a release, some users see a blank white screen, only on older Safari. How do you investigate and prevent it?
questions.ideal: First rollback to restore service, then check error monitoring such as Sentry filtered by browser to find the syntax or API error. Often a new dependency shipped modern syntax not handled by the transpile step, or a missing polyfill outside the browserslist targets. Prevent it with correct browser support config, an error boundary fallback instead of a blank page, and cross browser testing on BrowserStack in CI.

questions.q: What is React, what is JSX, and what is the virtual DOM?
questions.ideal: React is a library for building UIs from components. JSX is HTML like syntax inside JavaScript. The virtual DOM is an in memory tree that React diffs to update only what changed in the real DOM. Data flows one way from parent props to children.

questions.q: What is the difference between props and state, and class versus functional components?
questions.ideal: Props are read only inputs from the parent, state is local data that triggers a re-render when it changes. Functional components with hooks are the modern approach and replace class components and their lifecycle methods. Share state by lifting it up.

questions.q: Explain useEffect, useMemo, useCallback and useRef, and the rules of hooks.
questions.ideal: useEffect runs side effects after render, controlled by its dependency array and a cleanup function. useMemo and useCallback memoise values and functions, useRef holds a mutable value or DOM node without re-rendering. Hooks must be called at the top level of components or custom hooks.

questions.q: Why are keys needed in lists, and what are controlled and uncontrolled components?
questions.ideal: Keys give list items a stable identity so React reconciles changes correctly, and indexes are a poor key when the list changes. A controlled input keeps its value in state, an uncontrolled input keeps it in the DOM and is read through a ref.

questions.q: When would you use Context, Redux or other state libraries, and how do you avoid prop drilling?
questions.ideal: Use local state by default, Context for low frequency shared values like theme, and Redux Toolkit or Zustand for complex global client state. Server data is better handled by React Query or SWR with caching. Use selectors and split contexts to avoid needless re-renders.

questions.q: How do you find and fix performance problems in React, such as unnecessary re-renders?
questions.ideal: Find hotspots with the React Profiler, prevent needless renders with React.memo, useMemo and useCallback, keep state close to where it is used, split code with lazy and Suspense, and virtualise long lists.

questions.q: Explain CSR, SSR, SSG and ISR, and when you would use Next.js.
questions.ideal: CSR renders in the browser, SSR renders per request on the server, SSG pre-renders at build time and ISR revalidates static pages over time. Next.js provides these with file based routing and server components, helping SEO and first load, followed by hydration on the client.

questions.q: How do you test and structure a large React application?
questions.ideal: Test behaviour with Jest and React Testing Library, mock APIs with MSW, cover critical flows end to end with Cypress or Playwright, use TypeScript, error boundaries and a feature based folder structure, and document components in Storybook as part of a design system.

questions.q: What are React Fragments, and why would you use them instead of a wrapper div?
questions.ideal: A component must return a single parent element. A Fragment, written as React.Fragment or the empty tag short syntax, groups children without adding an extra wrapper div to the DOM. This keeps markup clean and avoids breaking layout such as flexbox, grid or table rows. The long form lets you pass a key when rendering fragments in a list.

questions.q: What are the different ways to do conditional rendering in React?
questions.ideal: You can use an if statement with early return before the JSX, a ternary operator inside JSX for either-or output, or the logical and short circuit to show something only when true. Returning null renders nothing. Be careful with logical and on numbers, because a falsy zero is actually rendered as 0, so convert to a boolean first.

questions.q: How does event handling work in React, and what is a synthetic event?
questions.ideal: React uses camelCase props like onClick and you pass a function reference, not a call, often an arrow function when you need arguments. The handler receives a SyntheticEvent, a cross browser wrapper with a consistent API. You call preventDefault explicitly instead of returning false. React attaches listeners at the root and uses event delegation rather than adding a listener to each node.

questions.q: What is the children prop and how does component composition work in React?
questions.ideal: props.children holds whatever is placed between a component's opening and closing tags. React prefers composition over inheritance, so you build reusable wrapper components like a Card, Modal or layout that render children. For multiple areas you pass elements as named props, acting like slots, for example header and footer props, instead of extending classes.

questions.q: Why might calling setState twice in a row with count plus one only increase the count once?
questions.ideal: State updates are not applied immediately; React batches them and applies them on the next render. Inside the handler, count is a snapshot of the old value, so both calls compute the same stale result. Using an updater function like setCount with prev plus one reads the previous state each time, so both increments apply before the re-render.

questions.q: What are the common ways to style a React application?
questions.ideal: Options include a global stylesheet with className, which risks name conflicts; CSS Modules, which generate scoped class names; CSS in JS libraries like styled components or Emotion; inline styles using a style object for dynamic values; and utility first frameworks like Tailwind. Teams pick based on scoping needs, theming, performance and developer preference.

questions.q: What does a tool like Vite or Create React App do for a React project?
questions.ideal: Vite and Create React App set up the toolchain so you can start quickly. They transpile JSX and modern JavaScript using Babel or esbuild, run a dev server with hot module replacement for instant updates, and bundle code with webpack or Rollup. The production build minifies, splits and optimizes assets. CRA is now deprecated, so Vite or Next.js are preferred.

questions.q: How do you set default values for props and validate prop types in React?
questions.ideal: In function components, the modern way is default values in destructuring parameters; defaultProps is legacy for functions. PropTypes gives runtime warnings in development when a prop has the wrong type or a required prop is missing. Most teams now use TypeScript interfaces or types instead, which catch mistakes at compile time and mark props as optional or required.

questions.q: What does lifting state up mean in React, and when do you do it?
questions.ideal: When two sibling components need the same data, you move the state to their closest common parent. The parent passes the value down as props and passes a callback so children can request changes. This keeps a single source of truth and keeps siblings in sync. If lifting goes too far up, consider composition or Context.

questions.q: What is a custom hook, and when would you write one?
questions.ideal: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks, letting you reuse stateful logic across components, such as useFetch, useDebounce or useLocalStorage. Each component calling it gets its own independent state; it shares logic, not state. It must follow the rules of hooks, called at the top level and only from components or other hooks.

questions.q: How does client side routing work with React Router?
questions.ideal: React Router uses the browser history API to change the URL without a full page reload. You wrap the app in BrowserRouter or createBrowserRouter, define Routes with paths, and use Link or useNavigate to move. Dynamic segments are read with useParams. Nested routes render inside a parent layout through Outlet, and loaders can fetch data before rendering.

questions.q: How do you fetch data inside useEffect correctly, and how do you avoid race conditions?
questions.ideal: Call fetch inside useEffect with the right dependency array and track loading and error state. If the dependency changes quickly, responses can arrive out of order, a race condition. Return a cleanup function that uses an AbortController to cancel the request or sets an ignore flag so stale responses do not update state. Libraries like React Query handle this for you.

questions.q: What is an error boundary in React and what does it not catch?
questions.ideal: An error boundary is a class component implementing getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch to catch render errors in its child tree and show a fallback UI instead of a blank screen, while logging the error. It does not catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code like setTimeout or promises, or server rendering. The react error boundary library gives a hook friendly wrapper.

questions.q: When would you choose useReducer over useState?
questions.ideal: useReducer suits complex state with multiple related values or when the next state depends on the previous state in many ways. You dispatch an action with a type, and a pure reducer function returns the new state, which keeps update logic in one predictable place and makes it easy to unit test. For a simple toggle or input, useState is enough.

questions.q: How do you give a parent access to a child's DOM node, and what are forwardRef and useImperativeHandle?
questions.ideal: A parent creates a ref with useRef and passes it down. Function components needed forwardRef to forward that ref to an inner DOM node, for example to focus an input or scroll. useImperativeHandle lets the child expose a limited API of methods instead of the raw node. In React 19, ref can be passed as a normal prop without forwardRef.

questions.q: What is a React portal and when would you use one?
questions.ideal: createPortal renders children into a different DOM node, often document.body, while keeping them in the same React tree. It is used for modals, tooltips and dropdowns so parent overflow hidden or z-index stacking does not clip them. Events still bubble through the React tree, so a click inside the portal reaches React ancestors even though the DOM is elsewhere.

questions.q: Explain reconciliation and the diffing algorithm in React, including Fiber.
questions.ideal: Reconciliation compares the new element tree with the previous one. The diffing heuristic assumes different element types produce different trees, so it remounts them, while same types are updated in place, and keys identify list items. Fiber splits work into units so the render phase is interruptible and can prioritize urgent updates, and the commit phase then applies changes to the DOM in one go.

questions.q: How do you implement code splitting and lazy loading in React?
questions.ideal: Code splitting breaks the bundle into chunks so the initial load is smaller. React.lazy with a dynamic import loads a component only when needed, wrapped in Suspense with a fallback spinner. The best starting point is route based splitting, plus heavy widgets like charts or editors. You can preload or prefetch chunks on hover, and check bundle size with an analyzer.

questions.q: What are useTransition and useDeferredValue, and what problem do they solve?
questions.ideal: With concurrent rendering in React 18, you can mark updates as non urgent. startTransition from useTransition wraps a heavy state update, like filtering a big list, so urgent updates such as typing stay responsive, and isPending shows a loading hint. useDeferredValue gives a lagging copy of a value to render expensive parts later. They solve input lag without debounce hacks.

questions.q: Why use a library like React Query or SWR instead of storing API data in Redux?
questions.ideal: API data is server state: it is shared, can become stale and must be refetched. React Query or SWR provide caching, deduplication of duplicate requests, stale while revalidate background refetch, retries and cache invalidation after a mutation, plus optimistic updates. Putting this in Redux means writing all that by hand, so Redux or Zustand is kept for client state.

questions.q: What is a stale closure in React hooks and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal: A stale closure happens when a callback captured an old value from an earlier render, for example a setInterval inside useEffect with an empty dependency array that always sees count as zero. Fixes include adding the value to the dependency array as the exhaustive deps lint rule suggests, using a functional update with prev, or storing the latest value in a useRef.

questions.q: Compare higher order components, render props and hooks for sharing logic.
questions.ideal: A higher order component wraps a component and injects props, good for cross cutting concerns like auth, but causes wrapper hell and prop naming collisions. Render props pass a function that returns UI, which is flexible but deeply nested. Custom hooks share logic without extra components or collisions, so they are now preferred, while HOCs remain in some libraries.

questions.q: How would you handle large, complex forms in React with good performance and validation?
questions.ideal: For large forms I use React Hook Form, which relies on uncontrolled inputs registered through refs, so typing does not re-render the whole form, unlike Formik controlled state. Validation is defined with a schema in Zod or Yup and shared with the backend types, showing field errors on blur or submit. Field arrays handle dynamic fields, and submission handles server error messages.

questions.q: How do you make a React application accessible?
questions.ideal: Use semantic HTML such as real button elements and labels linked with htmlFor, and alt text for images. Everything must work with the keyboard, with visible focus and proper focus management, like trapping focus in a modal and returning it after closing. Add ARIA attributes only when semantics are missing. Test with a screen reader and tools like axe, Lighthouse and eslint plugin jsx a11y.

questions.q: What are React Server Components and how do they differ from server side rendering?
questions.ideal: React Server Components run only on the server, can be async and fetch from a database directly, and send zero JavaScript for themselves, reducing bundle size. SSR instead renders client components to HTML and then hydrates them. Interactive parts are marked use client, and props passed from server to client must be serializable. In Next.js App Router they work with streaming through Suspense.

questions.q: How would you split a large React product into micro frontends, and what are the trade offs?
questions.ideal: Micro frontends let autonomous teams build and independently deploy parts of the app, usually with webpack Module Federation or single spa. React should be a shared singleton to avoid duplicate copies. A shared design system keeps UI consistent, and communication uses events or clear contracts. Trade offs are operational complexity, version drift and performance overhead, so I only use it when team scale justifies it.

questions.q: How would you build and maintain a shared React component library for many teams?
questions.ideal: I start with design tokens for color, spacing and typography so theming is consistent, then build accessible primitives. Each component is documented in Storybook with usage guidance and tested with unit and visual regression tests like Chromatic. The package is published with semver versioning and a changelog, supports tree shaking, and has a contribution process and deprecation policy so teams can upgrade safely.

questions.q: What causes hydration mismatch errors in SSR apps and how do you fix them?
questions.ideal: Hydration attaches React to server rendered HTML, and a mismatch occurs when the first client render differs. Common causes are Date or Math.random values, reading window or localStorage during render, and invalid HTML nesting. Fix it by rendering browser only content after mount in useEffect, using dynamic import with ssr false in Next.js, or suppressHydrationWarning for small unavoidable differences like timestamps.

questions.q: What security risks do you consider in a React application?
questions.ideal: React escapes output by default, but XSS still happens through dangerouslySetInnerHTML or javascript URLs, so I sanitize with DOMPurify. Tokens in localStorage can be stolen by XSS, so I prefer httpOnly cookies with CSRF protection such as SameSite and tokens. A content security policy limits scripts, secrets never go in the bundle, and npm audit plus lockfiles reduce supply chain risk.

questions.q: How would you migrate a large legacy React codebase with class components to modern React and TypeScript?
questions.ideal: I migrate incrementally rather than a big rewrite. First add tests around critical flows to catch regression. TypeScript is enabled with allowJs so files convert gradually, tightening strict mode later. New code uses function components and hooks, and class components are converted when touched. Codemods automate upgrades like React version changes and lifecycle renames, and progress is tracked with lint rules.

questions.q: How do you measure and monitor frontend performance of a React app in production?
questions.ideal: I track Core Web Vitals from real user monitoring, not just lab Lighthouse scores: LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness and CLS for layout stability, using the web vitals library sent to tools like Sentry or Datadog. Regressions trigger alerts and performance budgets in CI. For slow interactions I reproduce them and use the React Profiler and browser performance panel to find the cause.

questions.q: How would you make a React web app work offline as a progressive web app?
questions.ideal: A progressive web app uses a service worker, usually generated with Workbox, to cache assets and API responses with the right caching strategy: cache first for static files, network first or stale while revalidate for data. A web app manifest makes it installable. Offline edits are saved in IndexedDB and replayed with background sync, and users get a refresh prompt when a new version is deployed.

questions.q: What does React StrictMode do, and why do effects sometimes run twice in development?
questions.ideal: StrictMode is a development only wrapper that helps find bugs. It renders components twice and mounts, unmounts and remounts effects to expose impure rendering and missing cleanup functions. Side effects that break under this double invoke would cause bugs later. It has no effect in the production build, so extra calls only happen in dev mode.

questions.q: What is one way data flow in React, and how does a child send information back to its parent?
questions.ideal: React uses one way, unidirectional data flow: the parent passes data down to the child through props, which are read only. The child cannot modify props directly. To send information back, the parent passes a callback function as a prop, and the child calls that handler with the new value so the parent updates its own state.

questions.q: What are the main rules of writing JSX, such as naming and attributes?
questions.ideal: JSX must return a single root element or a fragment. Attributes use camelCase, so class becomes className and onclick becomes onClick. Component names must start with a capital letter so React knows they are components. JavaScript expressions go inside curly braces, and every tag must be closed, with self closing tags for elements like img and input.

questions.q: Why should you not mutate state directly in React, and how do you update arrays and objects correctly?
questions.ideal: React decides to re render by comparing references, so mutating state keeps the same reference and the update may be skipped. Instead treat state as immutable and create a new copy: use the spread operator for objects, and map, filter or spread for arrays instead of push or splice. A new reference tells React something changed and lets memoization work.

questions.q: What is the difference between useEffect with no dependency array, an empty array, and an array with values?
questions.ideal: With no dependency array the effect runs after every render. With an empty array it runs once on mount, and its cleanup runs on unmount. With values in the array it runs on mount and whenever those values change. Missing a dependency causes stale values, so the eslint hooks rule helps keep dependencies correct.

questions.q: What does it mean that a React component should be pure, and what side effects should not happen during rendering?
questions.ideal: A pure component returns the same output for the same props and state, like a pure function. During render you should not cause side effects such as fetching data, changing global variables, setting timers or mutating the DOM. Those belong in an event handler or useEffect. Purity keeps rendering predictable and lets React safely re render, pause or repeat work.

questions.q: How do you use environment variables in a React app, and what should never be put in them?
questions.ideal: Environment variables live in a dot env file and are read at build time, for example import meta env with the VITE prefix, or REACT_APP in Create React App. They are bundled into the JavaScript, so they are public and visible in the browser. Never put secrets like private API keys there; keep them on a backend server or proxy.

questions.q: How do you debug a React application using React DevTools and the browser?
questions.ideal: React DevTools adds a Components tab to inspect the component tree, and view or edit props and state and hooks. The Profiler records renders and shows why and how long each component rendered, and highlight updates shows re renders. Combined with console log, breakpoints and the debugger statement in browser tools, you can trace bugs quickly.

questions.q: What is dangerouslySetInnerHTML, and why is it risky?
questions.ideal: By default React escapes text, which protects against XSS. dangerouslySetInnerHTML inserts a raw HTML string directly into the DOM, bypassing that escaping. If the HTML comes from untrusted user input, an attacker can inject scripts, causing cross site scripting. Only use it for trusted content, and sanitize it first with a library like DOMPurify.

questions.q: How do mounting, updating and unmounting work in function components?
questions.ideal: A component mounts when it first renders into the DOM, updates when its state, props or context change and it re renders, and unmounts when removed. In function components useEffect handles all three: the effect runs after mount, reruns on updates based on its dependency array, and the returned cleanup function runs before the next effect and on unmount.

questions.q: What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect, and when would you use the layout version?
questions.ideal: useEffect runs after the browser paints, so it does not block the screen. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM changes but before paint. Use it when you must measure the DOM, like dimensions for a tooltip position, and update before the user sees anything, avoiding a flicker. Because it blocks paint, keep it small and prefer useEffect by default.

questions.q: How does React.memo work, and when does it fail to prevent re-renders?
questions.ideal: React.memo wraps a component and skips re rendering when its props are the same by shallow comparison. It fails when the parent passes a new object, array or inline function each render, since that is a new reference. Stabilise them with useCallback and useMemo. Memo also does not stop re renders caused by the component's own state or context changes.

questions.q: How do you test React components with React Testing Library?
questions.ideal: React Testing Library tests behavior from the user perspective rather than implementation details. You render the component, query elements with getByRole or label text, simulate interactions with userEvent, and assert on what appears. For async UI use findBy or waitFor. Tests run in Jest or Vitest, and you mock network calls with MSW, the mock service worker.

questions.q: How would you build a search input that calls an API only after the user stops typing?
questions.ideal: I would debounce the input: store the text in state, and in a useEffect start a setTimeout of around 300 milliseconds before calling the API, with a cleanup that calls clearTimeout so typing resets the delay. I also cancel older requests with an AbortController to avoid race conditions from stale responses, and wrap it in a reusable useDebounce custom hook.

questions.q: What is automatic batching in React 18, and what does flushSync do?
questions.ideal: Batching groups several state updates into a single render. Before React 18 batching happened only in event handlers; with createRoot in React 18 it is automatic everywhere, including promises, setTimeout and native events, giving fewer renders. If you need the DOM updated immediately, for example before measuring or scrolling, flushSync forces the update to apply synchronously.

questions.q: What is Suspense in React, and how is it used for loading states?
questions.ideal: Suspense lets a component wait for something and show a fallback such as a spinner meanwhile. It started with React lazy for code splitting and now supports data fetching through frameworks, the use hook, or libraries like React Query in suspense mode. You can nest boundaries to control which parts load together, and pair them with an error boundary for failures.

questions.q: How do you type props, state, events and hooks when using TypeScript with React?
questions.ideal: Define a props interface or type alias for each component, and type children as ReactNode. useState usually infers types but you pass a generic for unions or null. Events use types such as ChangeEvent of HTMLInputElement or MouseEvent. useRef takes the element type, and generic components let reusable lists or tables stay type safe with TypeScript.

questions.q: What is the useId hook used for in React?
questions.ideal: useId generates a unique, stable ID for a component instance. It is mainly for accessibility, linking a label to an input with htmlFor or connecting aria attributes like aria describedby. It produces the same ID on the server and client, so it avoids hydration mismatches with SSR. It should not be used for list keys.

questions.q: How does file based routing work in the Next.js App Router?
questions.ideal: In the Next.js App Router, folders inside the app directory define routes, and a page file makes a route public. Layout files wrap child routes and stay mounted for nested layouts. Dynamic segments use square brackets, like a slug. Special files such as loading, error and not found give Suspense fallbacks and error boundaries automatically.

questions.q: What is useSyncExternalStore and when do you need it?
questions.ideal: useSyncExternalStore lets components subscribe safely to an external store that lives outside React, like a browser API such as online status or a custom store. You give it a subscribe function and a getSnapshot function. It prevents tearing, where concurrent rendering shows inconsistent values in different components. State libraries like Zustand and Redux use it internally.

questions.q: How do you implement optimistic UI updates in React, and how do you handle failures?
questions.ideal: Optimistic UI updates the screen immediately, before the server confirms, so the app feels instant. In React Query you update the cache in onMutate, save the previous value, and rollback in onError, then invalidate to refetch the real data. React 19 also offers useOptimistic. On failure you revert and show an error so the user knows the action did not save.

questions.q: How would you render a list of fifty thousand rows in React without slowing the page?
questions.ideal: Rendering fifty thousand rows creates too many DOM nodes. Instead use virtualization, also called windowing, with libraries like react window or TanStack Virtual. Only the visible rows in the viewport plus a small overscan buffer are rendered, and rows are recycled as you scroll. Combine with memoized rows, fixed or measured heights, and pagination or infinite scroll for the data.

questions.q: What are Server Actions in Next.js and React, and what should you watch out for?
questions.ideal: Server Actions are async functions marked with use server that run on the server and can be called from forms or components, handling mutations without writing API routes. Forms work with progressive enhancement even without JavaScript. Because they are public endpoints, you must still do validation, for example with Zod, and authorization checks, then revalidate the path or cache after changes.

questions.q: What are the important new features in React 19?
questions.ideal: React 19 adds Actions, async transitions that manage pending and error states. useActionState handles form state, useOptimistic shows optimistic values, and the use hook reads promises and context. Ref is now a normal prop, so forwardRef is rarely needed, and components can render document metadata like the title. The React compiler, released alongside, auto memoizes components.

questions.q: How does Redux Toolkit simplify Redux, and what is RTK Query?
questions.ideal: Redux Toolkit removes boilerplate. createSlice generates the reducer and actions together, and Immer lets you write mutating syntax while keeping updates immutable. configureStore sets up middleware and DevTools by default. RTK Query adds an API slice for data fetching and caching, with automatic loading states, cache invalidation via tags, and generated hooks, similar to React Query.

questions.q: What causes memory leaks in React applications and how do you find them?
questions.ideal: Memory leaks usually come from effects without cleanup: event listeners never removed, setInterval timers never cleared, and WebSocket or store subscriptions not unsubscribed, plus closures holding big objects or global caches that grow. Always return a cleanup function. To find them, take heap snapshots in the Chrome DevTools memory tab, repeat an action, and compare retained objects.

questions.q: How do you analyze and reduce the JavaScript bundle size of a React app?
questions.ideal: Start with a bundle analyzer or source map explorer to see what is large. Replace heavy dependencies, for example moment with date fns, and import only needed functions so tree shaking works. Use code splitting with lazy and dynamic import per route. Serve gzip or brotli compression, and enforce a performance budget with a size limit check in CI.

questions.q: How do you handle authentication in a React single page app, including token storage and protected routes?
questions.ideal: After login the backend issues tokens. Storing a JWT in localStorage exposes it to XSS, so prefer an httpOnly cookie, or keep the access token in memory with a refresh token in an httpOnly cookie for silent refresh. A protected route component redirects unauthenticated users to login, but real authorization must always be enforced server side in the backend.

questions.q: How would you implement infinite scrolling in React?
questions.ideal: Place a sentinel element at the end of the list and watch it with an IntersectionObserver; when visible, fetch the next page. Use cursor based pagination from the API and React Query useInfiniteQuery to manage pages and loading state. Prevent duplicate requests, show a spinner, add virtualization for huge lists, and offer a load more button for accessibility.

questions.q: What is the React Compiler, and how does it change the way teams write memoization?
questions.ideal: The React Compiler is a build time tool that applies automatic memoization, so most manual useMemo, useCallback and React memo calls become unnecessary. It only works when code follows the rules of React, meaning pure components and no mutation of props or state, so teams enable its ESLint plugin first. Adoption is incremental, opting in directory by directory and verifying with profiling.

questions.q: How would you design a caching and revalidation strategy in a Next.js App Router application?
questions.ideal: I classify pages by freshness. Marketing and catalog pages use static rendering with time based revalidate, served from the CDN edge. Data that changes on events uses tags and on demand revalidation with revalidateTag from a webhook or Server Action. Personalized pages that depend on cookies use dynamic rendering or no store, so user data is never cached for everyone.

questions.q: Explain streaming server rendering with Suspense and selective hydration.
questions.ideal: With streaming, the server sends HTML in chunks instead of waiting for all data. Suspense boundaries render fallbacks first, so time to first byte and first paint improve, and slow data sections stream in later. Selective hydration hydrates boundaries independently and gives priority to the part the user interacts with, such as a click, avoiding one big blocking hydration.

questions.q: How would you roll out a risky frontend change safely to millions of users?
questions.ideal: I put the change behind feature flags using a service like LaunchDarkly or an internal system, then do a gradual rollout: internal users, then one percent canary, then larger percentages. Monitoring tracks error rate, Web Vitals and business metrics, with a kill switch for instant rollback without redeploy. It can double as an A/B test, and we plan cleanup to avoid flag debt.

questions.q: How would you choose between a Vite single page app, Next.js and React Router framework mode for a new product?
questions.ideal: For an internal dashboard behind login a Vite SPA is simplest. For public content needing SEO and fast first load, choose Next.js or React Router framework mode, formerly Remix, for SSR. I weigh hosting and deployment needs, such as Vercel versus self hosted Node, data loading patterns, team skills and experience, ecosystem maturity and vendor lock in.

questions.q: How would you share code between a React web app and a React Native mobile app?
questions.ideal: I use a monorepo with shared packages for business logic, API clients, validation, hooks and state, which port easily. UI components differ, since web uses DOM elements and React Native uses native views, so I keep platform specific files or use React Native Web or Expo Router for universal components. Design tokens are shared while respecting each platform's navigation conventions.

questions.q: How would you build a real time collaborative editor, like Google Docs, in React?
questions.ideal: Use WebSockets for real time sync and a CRDT library such as Yjs or Automerge, or operational transform, so concurrent edits merge without conflicts. Presence shows other users' cursors. The document lives in the CRDT, not React state, and components subscribe narrowly to avoid excess re renders. CRDTs also support offline edits that sync on reconnect.

questions.q: How would you architect a React app that must be white-labeled for many clients with different branding?
questions.ideal: I would build once and load tenant config at runtime by domain. Branding is expressed as design tokens mapped to CSS variables, so a theme swaps colors, fonts and logos without rebuilding, and also supports dark mode. Feature flags enable features per client. Components never hard code colors, and each theme is checked for accessibility and contrast.

questions.q: How would you implement internationalization in a large React application?
questions.ideal: I use a library like react i18next or FormatJS react intl, with translation keys in per locale message files that are lazy loaded as locale bundles. ICU message format handles plurals and gender, and the Intl API formats dates, numbers and currency. I support right to left layouts with CSS logical properties, and add checks for missing keys in CI.

questions.q: How do you optimize images in a React or Next.js application?
questions.ideal: Images are often the largest assets. In Next.js the Image component handles image optimization automatically: responsive srcset and sizes, modern formats like WebP and AVIF, and lazy loading below the fold. Always set dimensions with width and height to avoid layout shift and protect CLS, preload the hero image for LCP, and serve images from a CDN with long caching.

questions.q: Design a reusable autocomplete component for a large React application. What would you consider?
questions.ideal: I would design the API as a headless, controlled component so teams style it freely. Input changes use debounce, results get caching by query, and old requests are aborted to avoid race conditions. It follows the ARIA combobox pattern for accessibility with full keyboard navigation using arrow keys, Enter and Escape, and highlights matches. Large result sets use virtualization, and loading, empty and error states are handled.

questions.q: What is Angular, and what are components, modules, services and directives?
questions.ideal: Angular is a TypeScript framework. Components combine a template and class, services hold shared logic provided through dependency injection, directives like ngIf and ngFor change the DOM, and modules or standalone components organise the app, scaffolded by the Angular CLI.

questions.q: Explain data binding in Angular: interpolation, property, event and two way binding.
questions.ideal: Interpolation shows values, property binding [prop] sets DOM properties, event binding (event) handles events, and two way binding [(ngModel)] combines them. Pipes transform displayed values.

questions.q: What are Observables, Subjects and common RxJS operators, and how do you avoid memory leaks?
questions.ideal: Observables are lazy streams you subscribe to, Subjects multicast values, and operators like map, switchMap and debounceTime transform them. Avoid leaks with the async pipe, takeUntil or unsubscribing on destroy, and use switchMap to cancel stale HTTP requests.

questions.q: What are Angular lifecycle hooks, and what is change detection?
questions.ideal: ngOnInit runs after inputs are set, ngOnChanges on input changes and ngOnDestroy for cleanup. Change detection checks bindings after async events through zone.js, and OnPush with immutable inputs or signals reduces the work.

questions.q: How do routing, guards, resolvers and lazy loading work in Angular?
questions.ideal: The router maps URLs to components shown in a router outlet. Guards like canActivate protect routes, resolvers fetch data before activation, and lazy loading loads feature code on demand to cut bundle size. HTTP interceptors add auth headers.

questions.q: Compare template driven and reactive forms, and how you do validation in Angular.
questions.ideal: Template driven forms use ngModel and suit simple cases, reactive forms build a FormGroup in code and are more scalable and testable. Validation uses built in, custom and async validators and form state like touched, dirty and invalid.

questions.q: How do you improve Angular app performance?
questions.ideal: Use OnPush change detection, lazy loading, trackBy in ngFor, pure pipes instead of methods in templates, virtual scrolling, AOT and tree shaking, SSR with hydration, and analyse bundle size.

questions.q: How do Vue and Angular differ, and how do you structure large apps with state management and testing?
questions.ideal: Vue is progressive and lighter with a reactivity system, the Composition API and Pinia, while Angular is opinionated with built in routing, forms and dependency injection. Large apps use feature modules, state libraries like NgRx, signals or Pinia, monorepos, strict TypeScript and unit plus end to end tests.

questions.q: What is the Angular CLI and which commands do you use most often?
questions.ideal: The Angular CLI is a command line tool to create and manage projects. ng new creates a project, ng serve runs a dev server with live reload, ng generate scaffolds components, services and pipes, ng build makes an optimized production build, ng test runs unit tests, and ng update upgrades Angular and dependencies with automatic migrations.

questions.q: What are pipes in Angular? Give examples of built in and custom pipes.
questions.ideal: Pipes transform values for display in a template without changing the underlying data. Built in examples are date, currency, uppercase, decimal and the async pipe. You write a custom pipe with the Pipe decorator and a class implementing PipeTransform with a transform method, for example to truncate text, and use it with the pipe symbol in interpolation.

questions.q: What is the difference between structural and attribute directives? Give examples.
questions.ideal: Structural directives change the DOM layout by adding or removing elements, like ngIf and ngFor, written with an asterisk. Attribute directives change the appearance or behavior of an existing element, like ngClass and ngStyle, or a custom highlight directive. Newer Angular versions also offer built in control flow syntax, at if and at for, replacing the structural directives.

questions.q: How do parent and child components communicate in Angular?
questions.ideal: A parent passes data down with Input properties and the child sends events up with Output and an EventEmitter that emits values. Sibling or distant components use a shared service, often holding a Subject or signal. A parent can also call child methods through ViewChild or a template reference variable. Newer versions offer signal inputs through the input function.

questions.q: What is dependency injection in Angular and why is it useful?
questions.ideal: Dependency injection means Angular creates and supplies dependencies instead of classes creating them. A service is marked Injectable, often providedIn root so it is a singleton, and received through the constructor or the inject function. This gives loose coupling, lets components share one instance, and makes testing easy because you can provide a mock instead of the real service.

questions.q: Why does Angular use TypeScript, and what are interfaces, types and generics?
questions.ideal: TypeScript adds static typing to JavaScript, catching errors at compile time and enabling better tooling like IntelliSense and safe refactoring. Interfaces describe object shapes, type aliases can also express unions, and generics make reusable typed code, like a service returning Observable of User. Angular relies on decorators such as Component and Injectable, which TypeScript supports.

questions.q: What is Vue.js, and what do v-if, v-for, v-bind and v-model do?
questions.ideal: Vue is a progressive framework for building UIs, usually with single file components containing template, script and style. v-if conditionally renders an element, v-for loops over a list with a key, v-bind, shortened to a colon, binds an attribute to data, and v-model creates two way binding on form inputs.

questions.q: Explain the main files in a new Angular project.
questions.ideal: angular.json holds workspace and build configuration, package.json lists dependencies and scripts, and tsconfig sets TypeScript options. main.ts bootstraps the application with the root app component or module, and index.html contains the root selector. Environment files or configuration replacements hold settings such as API URLs for development and production builds.

questions.q: What is the difference between pure and impure pipes, and how does the async pipe work?
questions.ideal: A pure pipe runs only when its input reference or primitive value changes, so it is cheap. An impure pipe runs on every change detection cycle, which can hurt performance, and is needed only for mutated arrays or objects. The async pipe is impure: it subscribes to an Observable or Promise, returns the latest value, marks the view for check and unsubscribes automatically on destroy.

questions.q: What are HTTP interceptors in Angular and what do you use them for?
questions.ideal: An HTTP interceptor sits between HttpClient and the server and can modify every outgoing request and response. Since requests are immutable, you clone them, for example to add an Authorization header with a token. Interceptors also handle errors centrally with catchError, such as redirecting on 401, show a global loading spinner, add logging, retry or caching. Functional interceptors are registered with withInterceptors.

questions.q: What is content projection with ng-content, and how do ViewChild and ContentChild differ?
questions.ideal: Content projection with ng-content lets a parent insert markup into a child component, and the select attribute supports multi slot projection, useful for cards and dialogs. ViewChild queries elements in the component's own template and is ready in ngAfterViewInit. ContentChild queries projected content passed from the parent and is ready in ngAfterContentInit.

questions.q: What is the difference between providing a service in root, in a module and in a component?
questions.ideal: providedIn root registers a tree shakable singleton for the whole application. Providing in a lazy loaded module or route providers creates an instance scoped to that feature. Putting a service in a component's providers array creates a new instance per component and its children. Angular resolves through the hierarchical injector tree, walking up from the component to the root.

questions.q: What are standalone components in Angular and what benefits do they bring?
questions.ideal: Standalone components do not need an NgModule; they declare their dependencies in their own imports array. The app starts with bootstrapApplication, and routes can lazy load a single component using loadComponent. This removes boilerplate, makes dependencies explicit and easier to tree shake, and simplifies learning. Since Angular 17 standalone is the default for new projects.

questions.q: Explain switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap and exhaustMap with a use case for each.
questions.ideal: All map a value to an inner Observable. switchMap cancels the previous inner request, ideal for search typeahead. mergeMap runs inner requests in parallel, good for independent uploads. concatMap queues them and keeps order, useful for sequential saves. exhaustMap ignores new values while one is running, preventing duplicate submissions on a double click of a login button.

questions.q: What is the difference between computed properties and watchers in Vue?
questions.ideal: A computed property returns a derived value and is cached, recalculating only when its reactive dependencies change, so it is ideal for filtering or formatting in templates. A watch or watchEffect runs a side effect in response to changes, such as an async API call or saving to storage. Use computed for values, watchers for actions.

questions.q: Compare the Options API and the Composition API in Vue 3.
questions.ideal: The Options API organizes code by option type such as data, methods and computed, which is simple but scatters a feature across sections and relies on mixins for reuse. The Composition API uses setup or script setup with ref and reactive, grouping code by logical concern. Logic is shared through composables, and TypeScript inference is much better.

questions.q: How does OnPush change detection work and what must you do to use it correctly?
questions.ideal: With OnPush, Angular checks a component only when an Input reference changes, an event fires inside it, an async pipe or signal emits, or you call markForCheck on ChangeDetectorRef. The default strategy checks every component on each cycle. So you must use immutable data and create new references instead of mutating objects, otherwise the view will not update. It greatly improves performance in large trees.

questions.q: What are signals in Angular and how do they compare to RxJS observables?
questions.ideal: Signals are reactive values you read by calling them and update with set or update. computed creates derived signals and effect runs side effects. They are synchronous, always have a current value and enable fine grained change detection, paving the way to zoneless apps. RxJS observables remain better for async streams like HTTP and events, and toSignal and toObservable provide interop.

questions.q: Explain the NgRx store pattern and when it is worth using.
questions.ideal: NgRx implements Redux style global state as a single source of truth. Components dispatch actions, pure reducers produce new immutable state, memoized selectors read slices, and effects handle side effects like API calls. It helps large apps with shared complex state, time travel debugging and predictability. For small features it is overkill and boilerplate heavy, so component store, signal store or services suffice.

questions.q: How does server side rendering work in Angular and what are common pitfalls?
questions.ideal: Angular SSR, formerly Angular Universal, renders pages on the server for better SEO and faster first contentful paint, then non destructive hydration reuses the DOM. Pitfalls are using window, document or localStorage on the server, so you guard with isPlatformBrowser or afterNextRender. TransferState or HTTP cache transfer avoids calling APIs twice. Static routes can be prerendered at build time.

questions.q: How do you handle errors globally and in HTTP calls in an Angular app?
questions.ideal: I implement a custom global ErrorHandler to catch unhandled errors and send logging to a tool like Sentry. HTTP errors are handled in an interceptor using catchError, with retry and backoff for transient failures, and mapped to friendly user messages shown as a toast. Components can catch specific errors or rethrow with throwError, and forms show validation errors returned from the API.

questions.q: How do you unit test Angular components and services?
questions.ideal: Unit tests use TestBed to configure a testing module and create a ComponentFixture, calling detectChanges to render. Tests run with Jasmine and Karma or Jest. Dependencies are replaced with a mock or spy, and HTTP is tested with HttpTestingController. fakeAsync with tick controls timers and async code. Critical user flows are covered with e2e tests in Cypress or Playwright.

questions.q: How does Vue 3 reactivity work, and when do you use ref versus reactive?
questions.ideal: Vue 3 wraps state in an ES6 Proxy that tracks which effects read each property and triggers them on change, unlike Vue 2 which used Object.defineProperty. ref works for primitives and any value, accessed with dot value. reactive works only on objects and loses reactivity if you destructure it, unless you use toRefs. Many teams default to ref for consistency.

questions.q: How do you build a custom form control that works with reactive forms?
questions.ideal: Implement the ControlValueAccessor interface so the component plugs into reactive forms and works with formControlName. writeValue receives values from the model, registerOnChange and registerOnTouched store callbacks you call when the user changes or blurs the control, and setDisabledState handles disabling. You register it with the NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR provider using forwardRef.

questions.q: How would you migrate a large AngularJS application to modern Angular?
questions.ideal: A big bang rewrite is risky, so I migrate incrementally using a strangler approach. ngUpgrade runs a hybrid app where AngularJS and Angular coexist, using downgradeComponent and upgraded services. I migrate leaf components and services first, then routing feature by feature, and finally remove AngularJS. Regression tests guard each step. Alternatively, micro frontends can host old and new apps side by side.

questions.q: What is Zone.js, how does it trigger change detection, and why is Angular moving towards zoneless?
questions.ideal: Zone.js monkey patches async APIs like setTimeout, promises and events so NgZone knows when tasks finish and triggers change detection for the whole tree. For heavy work like scroll handlers you use runOutsideAngular. Zoneless Angular relies on signals and explicit notifications instead, giving better performance, smaller bundle size, cleaner stack traces and easier debugging.

questions.q: How would you organize a large enterprise Angular codebase shared by several teams?
questions.ideal: I would use an Nx monorepo with apps and libraries grouped by domain: feature, ui, data access and util libraries. Feature libraries hold smart container components while ui libraries hold dumb presentational ones. Module boundaries are enforced with lint rules and tags. Nx affected commands and build cache keep CI fast. If teams need independent releases, module federation micro frontends can be added.

questions.q: How does Angular protect against XSS, and what else do you do to secure an Angular app?
questions.ideal: Angular treats all values as untrusted and applies sanitization and escaping by default, including for innerHTML bindings. Using DomSanitizer bypassSecurityTrust methods disables this, so it must be reviewed carefully. HttpClient supports XSRF tokens for CSRF protection. I add a content security policy, keep JWT tokens in httpOnly cookies where possible, and never rely on route guards alone because the server must authorize.

questions.q: How do you plan and execute a major Angular version upgrade across a large application?
questions.ideal: I follow the Angular update guide and run ng update one major version at a time, letting schematics apply automatic migrations. Before that I check third party libraries for compatible versions and fix deprecations in the current version. Breaking changes are read from the changelog. Each step runs through CI with unit and e2e tests to catch regression before merging.

questions.q: Compare Pinia and Vuex, and when would you choose Nuxt for a Vue project?
questions.ideal: Pinia is the official Vue store now, replacing Vuex. It removes mutations, uses simple actions, offers modular stores, strong TypeScript type safety and devtools support. Vuex is legacy for older apps. Nuxt is a Vue meta framework adding SSR, static generation, file based routing and auto imports, so I choose it when SEO or fast first load matter.

questions.q: How would you build a real time dashboard in Angular that receives frequent WebSocket updates without freezing the UI?
questions.ideal: I wrap the WebSocket in an RxJS webSocketSubject and use throttleTime or bufferTime so hundreds of messages become a few UI updates. Components use OnPush or signals, lists use trackBy and virtual scroll, and high frequency handlers run with runOutsideAngular. The connection has reconnect logic with retry and backoff, and shared streams use shareReplay so multiple widgets reuse one socket.

questions.q: How do you implement internationalization in an Angular application?
questions.ideal: Angular's built in i18n uses the i18n attribute and angular localize, extracting text into XLIFF translation files and producing a separate build per locale, which is fast but needs a reload to switch language. Libraries like Transloco or ngx translate do runtime translation from JSON. Date, currency and number pipes follow locale formats, and layouts must support RTL right to left direction.

questions.q: What is the difference between the constructor and ngOnInit in an Angular component?
questions.ideal: The constructor is a TypeScript class feature used mainly for dependency injection, and it runs before Angular sets input properties. ngOnInit is a lifecycle hook Angular calls once after the first inputs are set, so it is the right place for initialization logic such as reading inputs or starting data loading. Keep constructors light.

questions.q: What is the new built-in control flow syntax in Angular, such as @if and @for?
questions.ideal: Angular 17 introduced built in control flow blocks. At if replaces ngIf with clean else branches, at for replaces ngFor and requires a track expression, with an at empty block when the list is empty, and at switch replaces ngSwitch. It needs no import of CommonModule, gives better type checking and better performance than the older structural directives.

questions.q: What is a template reference variable in Angular and how do you use it?
questions.ideal: A template reference variable is declared with a hash sign, like hash name input, on an element in the template. It gives you the DOM element or, on a component, the component instance, so you can read input values or call methods elsewhere in the template. To access it from the class, use ViewChild with the same name.

questions.q: How do you call a REST API in Angular using HttpClient?
questions.ideal: You enable HttpClient with provideHttpClient, or HttpClientModule in older apps, and inject it into a service. Methods like get and post return an Observable, so nothing happens until you subscribe or use the async pipe in the template. You type the response with a generic, and handle errors with catchError in the pipe.

questions.q: How do Vue components pass data down with props and send events up with emits?
questions.ideal: In Vue a parent passes data down to a child with props, declared with defineProps, and props are one way and read only, so the child should not mutate them. The child sends events up with defineEmits and calls emit, and the parent listens with an at or v on handler. v model on components uses a modelValue prop plus an update event.

questions.q: How do you apply CSS classes and styles dynamically in Angular templates?
questions.ideal: You can use class binding, such as square brackets class dot active equals a condition, or style binding like style dot width. For several classes, ngClass accepts an object, array or string expression where each key is applied when its boolean condition is true. ngStyle does the same for inline styles. Direct class and style bindings are now preferred.

questions.q: How do you manage environment specific configuration such as API URLs in Angular?
questions.ideal: Angular projects keep settings in environment files like environment ts and environment prod ts. In angular json, file replacements under build configurations swap the file when you run ng build with the production configuration. They hold values like the API base URL and feature flags. They are compiled into the bundle and public, so never store secrets there.

questions.q: What is a single file component in Vue and what are its sections?
questions.ideal: A single file component is a dot vue file containing a template section for markup, a script section, often script setup with the Composition API, for logic, and a style section for CSS. Adding scoped limits styles to that component. A build tool such as Vite with the Vue compiler turns it into JavaScript.

questions.q: How do you read route parameters and query parameters in Angular?
questions.ideal: Inject ActivatedRoute and read paramMap or queryParamMap, either from the snapshot for a one time value or as an observable when the same component is reused with new params. Newer Angular can bind route params directly to component inputs with withComponentInputBinding. You navigate with routerLink in templates or router navigate in code, passing params and query params.

questions.q: What are decorators in Angular, and which ones are most common?
questions.ideal: Decorators are TypeScript functions, written with an at sign, that attach metadata to classes and properties. At Component marks a component with its selector and template, at Injectable marks a service for dependency injection, at Input and at Output with EventEmitter define component communication, and at NgModule describes a module. Angular reads this metadata at compile time.

questions.q: Why do you need trackBy or the track expression when rendering lists in Angular?
questions.ideal: Without tracking, when a list array changes, especially a new array from an API, Angular cannot match items by identity and may recreate all DOM nodes, which hurts performance and loses state like input focus. trackBy, or the required track expression in at for, tells Angular to use a unique id, so only changed items re render.

questions.q: What are deferrable views with @defer in Angular?
questions.ideal: At defer blocks lazy load part of a template and its dependencies into a separate chunk, reducing the initial bundle size. Triggers such as on viewport, on interaction, on idle or a condition decide when to load. At placeholder shows content before loading starts, at loading shows during loading, and at error handles failures. It also supports prefetching.

questions.q: What are signal based inputs, outputs and model in modern Angular?
questions.ideal: Modern Angular offers functions instead of decorators. The input function creates a read only signal input, input required marks it mandatory, and you derive values with computed. The output function replaces at Output with EventEmitter. Model creates a writable signal for two way binding. They give better type safety and work naturally with signal based change detection.

questions.q: How do navigation guards work in Vue Router?
questions.ideal: Vue Router navigation guards run before a route changes. A global beforeEach guard is common for authentication: check route meta such as requiresAuth and redirect to login by returning a route, or return false to cancel. There are also per route beforeEnter guards and in component guards like onBeforeRouteLeave for unsaved changes warnings.

questions.q: What are slots in Vue, including named and scoped slots?
questions.ideal: Slots let a parent pass template content into a child component. The default slot takes unnamed content, named slots use v slot or the hash shorthand to fill regions like header and footer, and scoped slots let the child pass slot props back, such as each row in a table. They make reusable, flexible layout components.

questions.q: How do you build dynamic forms in Angular where users can add and remove fields?
questions.ideal: With reactive forms, use a FormArray inside a FormGroup, usually built with FormBuilder. To add a field, push a new control or group; to remove, call removeAt with the index. In the template you loop over the controls. Each item can have its own validators, and typed forms give type safety on the values dynamically added.

questions.q: What is the inject function in Angular, and how does it compare to constructor injection?
questions.ideal: The inject function retrieves a dependency without a constructor parameter. It must run in an injection context, like field initializers, constructors or factory functions. It enables functional guards, resolvers and interceptors, and simplifies inheritance because subclasses do not pass dependencies to a base class constructor. Code is more readable, and it is now the recommended style over constructor injection.

questions.q: What are provide and inject in Vue and when do you use them?
questions.ideal: Provide and inject let an ancestor component share a value with any descendant without prop drilling through every nested level. The ancestor calls provide with a key, often a Symbol injection key for typing, and descendants call inject. Provide a ref or reactive object to keep reactivity. For global app state, Pinia is usually better.

questions.q: How does view encapsulation work for component styles in Angular?
questions.ideal: Angular defaults to emulated view encapsulation, adding unique attributes so component styles only apply to that component. ShadowDom mode uses the browser's native shadow DOM, while None makes styles global. The colon host selector styles the component's own element. ng deep pierces encapsulation to style children, but it is deprecated, so prefer global styles or CSS variables.

questions.q: How do forkJoin, combineLatest and withLatestFrom differ in RxJS?
questions.ideal: forkJoin waits for all observables to complete and emits their last values once, ideal for parallel HTTP calls. combineLatest emits whenever any source emits, after each has emitted at least once, using the latest value of each, good for combining filters. withLatestFrom emits only when the main stream emits, adding the latest value from another stream.

questions.q: How would you build a custom structural directive in Angular?
questions.ideal: A custom structural directive injects TemplateRef for the content and ViewContainerRef for where to render it. Through an input setter, it calls createEmbeddedView to show the template or clear to remove it, for example a has permission directive. You can pass a context object so the template uses let syntax, and the asterisk microsyntax maps to the inputs.

questions.q: How do you create components dynamically at runtime in Angular?
questions.ideal: Use ViewContainerRef createComponent with the component class, which returns a ComponentRef; set values with setInput and subscribe to outputs. With standalone components you can lazy import the class first. In templates, ngComponentOutlet renders a component chosen at runtime. Remember to destroy the ComponentRef for cleanup when it is no longer needed, as in dialogs or dashboard widgets.

questions.q: How do computed, effect, linkedSignal and the resource API work together in Angular signals?
questions.ideal: Computed creates a read only derived signal with automatic dependency tracking and lazy memoized evaluation. Effect runs side effects such as logging or syncing storage when signals change, and should not be used to set state. linkedSignal is writable but resets when its source changes. The resource API, including httpResource, loads async data and exposes value, loading and error signals.

questions.q: How do you do end-to-end testing for an Angular application now that Protractor is deprecated?
questions.ideal: Protractor is deprecated, so teams use Cypress or Playwright for end to end tests, added through ng e2e schematics.
