Tests cover critical user journeys, use stable selectors like data test ids, and mock or seed the backend. They run headless in the CI pipeline, with retries, traces and screenshots to reduce and debug flaky tests.

questions.q: How do you add offline support to an Angular app using the Angular service worker?
questions.ideal: Run ng add for the PWA schematic, which registers the Angular service worker and adds ngsw config json and a manifest. Asset groups cache app files with prefetch or lazy mode, and data groups cache API responses with freshness or performance strategies. SwUpdate detects a new version so you can prompt users to reload. It requires HTTPS.

questions.q: What are composables in Vue 3, and why are they better than mixins?
questions.ideal: A composable is a function, named like useMouse, that uses the Composition API to package reusable stateful logic and returns refs. Unlike mixins, there are no naming conflicts, it is explicit where each value comes from, and parameters make them flexible and type safe. Libraries like VueUse provide many ready made composables.

questions.q: How do you optimize performance in a large Vue 3 application?
questions.ideal: Use defineAsyncComponent and route level lazy loading to shrink bundles. For big immutable data use shallowRef to avoid deep reactivity. v once and v memo skip re rendering static or unchanged parts, keep alive caches toggled components, and virtual scrolling handles long lists. Prefer computed over methods for caching, and find bottlenecks with Vue DevTools profiling.

questions.q: How do preloading strategies work in Angular routing, and when would you write a custom one?
questions.ideal: Lazy loading splits routes into chunks, and a preloading strategy decides whether to download them in the background after startup. NoPreloading is the default, while PreloadAllModules fetches everything. A custom strategy implements PreloadingStrategy and preloads only routes flagged in route data, or skips preloading on a slow connection, balancing speed against bandwidth.

questions.q: How do you write an async validator in Angular reactive forms, for example to check if a username is taken?
questions.ideal: An async validator is a function returning an Observable or promise that resolves to null when valid or an error object such as username taken. While it runs, the control status is pending, so the UI can show a spinner. To reduce calls, use debounce via timer and switchMap to cancel old requests, or set updateOn to blur.

questions.q: How would you implement micro frontends in Angular, and what are the risks?
questions.ideal: In a micro frontends setup, a shell host app loads remote apps at runtime with Module Federation or Native Federation, so teams get independent deployment. Shared dependencies like Angular and RxJS must be singletons with aligned versions, or bundles bloat and break. Angular Elements web components help mix frameworks. Risks include version drift, runtime failures, and UX consistency, so a shared design system is essential.

questions.q: How would you choose between plain services with signals, NgRx Store and NgRx SignalStore in a large Angular app?
questions.ideal: For simple feature state, services with signals are enough and have little boilerplate. NgRx SignalStore adds structure, computed state and methods with less code, fitting most feature stores. The classic NgRx Store with actions, reducers and effects suits large teams needing strict event flows, DevTools time travel debugging and complex side effects. I match complexity to scale.

questions.q: Your company is choosing between Angular and React for a new enterprise platform. How would you make the decision?
questions.ideal: Angular is opinionated and batteries included with routing, forms, DI and TypeScript built in, which enforces consistency across many teams. React offers flexibility and a huge ecosystem but needs more decisions on libraries. I weigh team skills and hiring, long term maintenance and release support, existing code, and performance needs, then validate with a short proof of concept.

questions.q: How would you build a reusable Angular component library for many product teams?
questions.ideal: I generate an Angular component library built with ng packagr, using standalone components and the Angular CDK for overlays, focus and accessibility primitives. Theming uses design tokens as CSS variables. Storybook provides documentation and visual tests. Releases follow semver with a changelog and migration schematics, and every component meets a11y standards with automated checks.

questions.q: How do you ensure accessibility in a large Angular application?
questions.ideal: I start with semantic HTML and native elements, adding ARIA only where needed. Keyboard navigation and focus management matter, especially focus trap in dialogs and restoring focus on route changes. The CDK a11y package provides FocusTrap and LiveAnnouncer for screen reader messages. Automated testing with axe and Lighthouse in CI, plus manual screen reader checks, keeps us aligned with WCAG.

questions.q: How would you migrate a large Vue 2 application to Vue 3?
questions.ideal: Vue 2 reached end of life, so migration is required. I first audit breaking changes and third party dependencies, then use the Vue compat migration build to run incrementally while fixing deprecation warnings. Upgrade to Vue Router 4, move Vuex to Pinia, and switch the build to Vite. Options API still works, so Composition API adoption can be step by step.

questions.q: Users report an Angular app becomes slow after hours of use. How would you investigate?
questions.ideal: Slowness after hours suggests a memory leak. I reproduce by repeating navigation steps and compare heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools, looking for growing detached DOM nodes and retained components. Common causes are subscriptions not unsubscribed, fixable with takeUntilDestroyed or the async pipe, plus event listeners and timers. Angular DevTools profiler reveals excessive change detection cycles.

questions.q: How would you support build once, deploy many across environments in Angular instead of separate builds per environment?
questions.ideal: Instead of compile time environment files, produce a single artifact and load runtime config from a config json file at startup using provideAppInitializer, the successor of APP_INITIALIZER, before the app boots. Values are exposed through an injection token. In Docker, the container entrypoint writes config json from environment variables, so the same image runs in staging and production.

questions.q: Karma is deprecated. How would you move a large Angular test suite to a newer test runner?
questions.ideal: Karma is deprecated, so I evaluate Jest, Vitest, which the Angular CLI now supports, and Web Test Runner for real browser runs. I run a pilot on one project, compare CI speed and compatibility with jsdom and zone based tests, then migrate incrementally, converting configs and fixing tests with codemods while both runners work in the pipeline.

questions.q: What is RouteReuseStrategy in Angular and when would you customize it?
questions.ideal: By default Angular destroys a component when you navigate away and recreates it on return, losing state. A custom RouteReuseStrategy can detach and store the component in a cache, then reattach it, so you preserve state such as filters and scroll position, useful for tabs or list detail back navigation. Watch memory usage and stale data, and invalidate cached routes when needed.

questions.q: How would you build an Angular data grid that shows hundreds of thousands of rows with live updates?
questions.ideal: I would load data with server side pagination, sorting and filtering, and render rows with CDK virtual scroll so only visible rows exist in the DOM. Components use OnPush or signals with track identity to update only changed rows. Live updates are batched with throttle or buffer, heavy calculations move to a web worker, and for complex needs a library like AG Grid is often worth it.

questions.q: What are primary, foreign and unique keys, and what is normalization?
questions.ideal: A primary key uniquely identifies a row, a foreign key enforces referential integrity with another table and a unique key prevents duplicates. Normalisation removes redundancy through normal forms, denormalisation trades it for read speed.

questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and between INNER and LEFT JOIN?
questions.ideal: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after aggregation. An inner join returns only matching rows, a left join keeps all rows from the left table with nulls where nothing matches.

questions.q: Explain window functions like ROW_NUMBER, RANK and LAG, and how to find the second highest salary.
questions.ideal: Window functions compute across related rows without collapsing them, using OVER with PARTITION BY and ORDER BY. ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK number rows, LAG and LEAD read neighbours. The second highest salary is DENSE_RANK = 2, or a subquery or LIMIT OFFSET.

questions.q: What are ACID properties and isolation levels, and what problems do they prevent?
questions.ideal: ACID means atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Isolation levels from read uncommitted to serializable trade performance against anomalies like dirty reads, non repeatable reads and phantom reads.

questions.q: How do indexes work, and when do they hurt? Explain clustered, non clustered and covering indexes.
questions.ideal: Most indexes are B-trees that speed lookups. A clustered index defines physical order, non clustered indexes store pointers, a covering index holds all columns a query needs. Indexes slow writes and use space, composite indexes depend on column order, and EXPLAIN shows whether they are used.

questions.q: A query on a million row table is slow. How do you optimise it?
questions.ideal: Read the execution plan, add or fix indexes, select only needed columns, write sargable conditions without functions on indexed columns, rewrite subqueries as joins, update statistics, consider partitioning or materialised views, and paginate large results.

questions.q: How would you design a schema for an e-commerce system, and when would you denormalize or partition?
questions.ideal: Model customers, products, orders and order items with foreign keys in third normal form, store price snapshots on order items, index common lookups, protect inventory with transactions, and partition or archive big order tables by date, denormalising only for read heavy reporting.

questions.q: How do you scale a relational database: replication, sharding, caching and read replicas, and what are the trade offs?
questions.ideal: Scale reads with replicas and caching and writes with sharding on a partition key, accepting replication lag, harder joins and operational complexity. Use connection pooling, scale vertically first, and understand the CAP trade offs.

questions.q: What are DDL, DML, DCL and TCL commands in SQL? Give examples of each.
questions.ideal: DDL defines structure, with CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE. DML changes rows, with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and SELECT is sometimes called DQL for querying. DCL controls permissions with GRANT and REVOKE. TCL manages transactions with COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT. Knowing the category tells you whether a statement changes the schema or the data.

questions.q: How does SQL treat NULL values in comparisons, aggregates and sorting?
questions.ideal: NULL means unknown, so any comparison with equals returns unknown under three valued logic and you must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Aggregates like SUM and AVG ignore nulls. COALESCE or IFNULL substitutes a default. NOT IN with a subquery that returns a null gives no rows, a classic trap. Sorting places nulls first or last depending on the database, controllable with NULLS FIRST.

questions.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column)?
questions.ideal: COUNT star counts all rows including those with nulls. COUNT of a column counts only non null values in that column. COUNT DISTINCT counts unique non null values. Combined with GROUP BY they give per group counts, and other aggregates like SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX also ignore nulls, so results can differ from what beginners expect.

questions.q: Explain LIKE, IN, BETWEEN and EXISTS operators with examples.
questions.ideal: LIKE matches a pattern, where percent means any characters and underscore means a single character, and case sensitivity depends on collation. IN checks against a list of values or a subquery. BETWEEN is an inclusive range, so both ends match. EXISTS returns true when a subquery returns any row. Each can be negated with NOT, keeping null behaviour in mind.

questions.q: What is a view, what are its advantages, and does it store data?
questions.ideal: A view is a saved query that behaves like a virtual table and does not store data itself; it runs the underlying query each time. Views simplify complex joins for reuse and add security by exposing only some columns or rows. Simple views can be updatable, with WITH CHECK OPTION enforcing their filter. A materialized view does store results and must be refreshed.

questions.q: How do you choose data types in SQL, for example CHAR versus VARCHAR, DECIMAL versus FLOAT and DATE versus DATETIME?
questions.ideal: CHAR is fixed length and suits codes like country codes, VARCHAR is variable length for names. DECIMAL or NUMERIC is exact and right for money, while FLOAT and DOUBLE are approximate and cause rounding errors. Use DATE for dates and DATETIME or TIMESTAMP for moments, considering time zone. Pick INT or BIGINT by range, because smaller types save storage and index size.

questions.q: How do you generate auto incrementing IDs in MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, and what are the pitfalls?
questions.ideal: MySQL uses AUTO_INCREMENT, PostgreSQL uses SERIAL or GENERATED AS IDENTITY backed by a sequence, and SQL Server uses IDENTITY. Values can have gaps after rollback or deletes, so never rely on them being continuous. Fetch the new id with LAST_INSERT_ID, RETURNING or SCOPE_IDENTITY. For distributed systems a UUID or GUID avoids central coordination but makes indexes larger.

questions.q: What do UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT or MINUS do in SQL, and what rules apply to them?
questions.ideal: UNION combines results of two queries and removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them and is faster. INTERSECT returns only rows common to both, and EXCEPT, called MINUS in Oracle, returns rows in the first query but not the second. Both queries need the same number of columns with compatible types, and a single ORDER BY goes at the end.

questions.q: What is a correlated subquery, and when should you use EXISTS instead of IN?
questions.ideal: A correlated subquery references the outer query and logically runs for each row, while a non correlated subquery runs once independently. EXISTS stops at the first match and behaves like a semi join, good for large inner tables. IN is fine for small lists. Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN because a null breaks NOT IN. Many subqueries can be rewritten as a join for performance.

questions.q: What is a common table expression, and how does a recursive CTE work?
questions.ideal: A common table expression is a named subquery defined with the WITH clause that improves readability and can be referenced several times. A recursive CTE has an anchor member as the base case, joined with UNION ALL to a recursive member that references the CTE itself, repeating until no rows return. It walks a hierarchy like an org chart, and a depth column or max recursion setting guards termination.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stored procedure and a function in SQL, and when do you use each?
questions.ideal: A stored procedure is called with CALL or EXEC, can have output parameters, run DML and control transactions. A function must return a value and can be used inside a SELECT statement, but usually cannot change data. Procedures reduce network round trips, are precompiled for performance and allow security by granting execute permissions instead of table access.

questions.q: What are triggers, what types exist, and why do many teams avoid business logic in triggers?
questions.ideal: A trigger fires automatically on an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE event, either before or after it, and at row level or statement level, accessing NEW and OLD values. Triggers are useful for audit logging into a history table. Teams avoid heavy business logic in them because it is hidden logic, hard for debugging, slows bulk performance and can cause cascade effects.

questions.q: How do you find and delete duplicate rows from a table while keeping one copy?
questions.ideal: Find duplicates with GROUP BY on the key columns HAVING COUNT greater than one. To delete, number rows with ROW_NUMBER over PARTITION BY those columns in a CTE and delete rows where the number is above one, or keep the MIN id using a self join. Afterwards add a unique constraint to prevent duplicates from coming back.

questions.q: How do you use CASE expressions for conditional logic and to pivot rows into columns?
questions.ideal: A CASE WHEN THEN ELSE END expression adds conditional logic inside SELECT, WHERE or ORDER BY. For a pivot report, use conditional aggregation such as SUM of CASE WHEN month equals Jan THEN amount END, grouped by product, turning rows to columns. Some databases offer a PIVOT operator or crosstab function, and UNPIVOT turns columns back into rows.

questions.q: How do you handle dates in SQL queries, for example monthly totals, date differences and filtering a day correctly?
questions.ideal: Use functions like DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT or DATE_FORMAT to group by month, and DATEDIFF or interval arithmetic for differences. To filter one day, use a range filter of greater than or equal to the day and less than the next day, instead of wrapping the column in a function, which keeps it sargable and lets the index work. Store timestamps in UTC and convert time zone for display.

questions.q: How do you write an upsert that inserts a row or updates it if it already exists?
questions.ideal: An upsert inserts a new row or updates an existing one atomically. MySQL uses INSERT ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, PostgreSQL uses INSERT ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and SQL Server and Oracle use MERGE. All rely on a unique constraint or primary key to detect the conflict. Doing a select then insert in application code causes a race condition under concurrency.

questions.q: Explain row locks, table locks and SELECT FOR UPDATE, and how you prevent deadlocks.
questions.ideal: Databases take shared locks for reads in some isolation levels and exclusive locks for writes, usually at row level, sometimes escalating to a table lock. SELECT FOR UPDATE locks rows you intend to change. A deadlock is a cycle where each transaction waits on the other, and the database kills a victim. Prevent it by accessing rows in a consistent order, keeping short transactions, indexing filters and retrying.

questions.q: What is table partitioning, and how does it differ from sharding? When does it help queries?
questions.ideal: Partitioning splits one table into range, list or hash partitions within a single database server, while sharding spreads data across multiple servers. It helps when queries filter on the partition key, so partition pruning scans fewer partitions, and makes maintenance easy, like dropping an old partition to archive. Indexes are local or global, and too many partitions add planning overhead.

questions.q: How would you find users who logged in on three or more consecutive days using SQL?
questions.ideal: This is a gaps and islands problem. First keep one row per user per day with DISTINCT. Then subtract ROW_NUMBER, ordered by date per user, from the login date, so consecutive days share the same group key. GROUP BY user and that key and keep groups HAVING COUNT of three or more. LAG to compare with the previous day is an alternative.

questions.q: Why is OFFSET pagination slow on large tables, and how does keyset pagination fix it?
questions.ideal: OFFSET with LIMIT still reads and discards all skipped rows, so deep pages get slow, and inserts shift rows between pages. Keyset pagination, the seek method, remembers the last seen value and asks WHERE id greater than it ORDER BY id LIMIT n, using the index directly with consistent results. The trade off is you cannot jump to an arbitrary page number, so APIs expose a cursor.

questions.q: How do relational databases store and query JSON data, and when is a JSON column a bad idea?
questions.ideal: PostgreSQL offers JSONB and MySQL a JSON type, queried with JSON functions or arrow operators, and indexed with GIN indexes or a generated column. JSON is good for a flexible schema of optional attributes. It is a bad idea for data you filter, join or report on heavily, because you lose constraints, integrity and type validation and get poorer query performance than normalized relational columns.

questions.q: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking, and how do you implement optimistic locking?
questions.ideal: Pessimistic locking locks rows up front with SELECT FOR UPDATE and suits high contention. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: add a version column, read it, then UPDATE WHERE id and version match while incrementing it. If rows affected is zero someone else changed it, so retry or show a conflict error. Both prevent the lost update problem, optimistic suits low contention web apps.

questions.q: How do you manage database schema changes across environments and deploy them without downtime?
questions.ideal: Keep versioned migration scripts in source control and apply them with tools like Flyway, Liquibase or Alembic in every environment through CI. For zero downtime use expand and contract: make backward compatible changes like adding a nullable column, backfill in batches, deploy code using it, then remove the old column later. Plan rollback steps and use online DDL for large tables.

questions.q: What is the N plus one query problem with ORMs, and how do you detect and fix it?
questions.ideal: The N plus one problem happens when an ORM such as Hibernate or Entity Framework loads a list with one query and then lazy loading fires one extra query for each row. Detect it in the SQL query log or a profiler. Fix it with eager loading using a join fetch or include, batch loading with an IN clause, or projection queries that select only needed columns.

questions.q: How would you design a data warehouse for sales reporting? Explain star schema and slowly changing dimensions.
questions.ideal: Start with the grain, such as one row per order line, in a fact table holding measures like quantity and amount. Surround it with dimension tables for customer, product, date and store in a star schema using surrogate keys. Track history with slowly changing dimension type 2, adding a new row with effective dates. A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions further, and ETL or ELT pipelines load it.

questions.q: How do you design tables to keep a full history of changes to records for audit and point in time queries?
questions.ideal: Store history in a separate history table or use system versioned temporal tables, which keep valid from and valid to columns automatically. Otherwise populate it from a trigger, application code or CDC, recording who changed it, the user and timestamp. An AS OF query then returns the point in time state. Partition history by date and define retention, as audit storage grows fast.

questions.q: How would you design a database for a multi tenant SaaS application?
questions.ideal: Options are a shared schema with a tenant_id column on every table, a schema per tenant, or a database per tenant for strong isolation. Shared schema is cheapest; enforce isolation with row level security and lead composite indexes with tenant id. Schema per tenant complicates migration and operations across many schemas. Move a large tenant causing a noisy neighbor problem to its own database.

questions.q: Design the database logic for a ticket or seat booking system so that no seat is ever double booked.
questions.ideal: Prevent double booking at the database level with a unique constraint on show and seat in the bookings table. Inside a transaction, lock the seat with SELECT FOR UPDATE or use an optimistic conditional update WHERE status is available. Create a temporary hold with an expiry timeout while payment completes, release expired holds by a job, and use an idempotency key so payment retries do not create duplicates.

questions.q: What are the options to store tree data like categories or org charts in a relational database?
questions.ideal: An adjacency list stores a parent id and is simple to update but needs a recursive CTE to fetch a subtree. A nested set stores left and right values for fast subtree reads but costly writes. A materialized path keeps a path string queried with LIKE. A closure table stores every ancestor descendant pair with depth for fast reads. Choose by read heavy versus write heavy trade off.

questions.q: How do you design incremental data loads from an OLTP database to a reporting system without slowing production?
questions.ideal: Avoid full extracts and load only deltas. A simple approach uses a watermark on a last updated timestamp column, but it misses hard deletes, so use soft delete flags. Better, change data capture with Debezium reads the binlog or WAL with little load. Extract from a read replica to offload production, and make loads idempotent with MERGE or upsert so reruns are safe.

questions.q: A counter row such as likes on a viral post gets thousands of updates per second. How do you design around this contention?
questions.ideal: Updating one counter row serialises on a row lock, causing contention and lock waits. Spread writes over a sharded counter with many rows and sum them when reading. Or buffer increments in Redis with INCR or a queue and periodically flush aggregated batches to the database, accepting eventual consistency. For likes, slightly approximate counts are usually acceptable to the business.

questions.q: A transactions table has grown to 2 billion rows. How do you archive or purge old data safely?
questions.ideal: Agree a retention policy with business and compliance first. If the table is partitioned by date, detach or drop old partitions instantly after copying them to an archive table, separate database or data lake. Otherwise delete in small batches by key ranges, pausing to limit locks, replication lag and log growth. Take a backup first, verify counts, then partition the table to make future archival simple.

questions.q: In what logical order does SQL process the clauses of a SELECT statement?
questions.ideal: Logically SQL processes FROM and JOIN first, then WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT computes the columns and aliases, ORDER BY sorts, and finally LIMIT or TOP restricts the rows. This explains why a column alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE but can usually be used in ORDER BY.

questions.q: How do you return only the first N rows of a result in MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server?
questions.ideal: MySQL and PostgreSQL use LIMIT, SQL Server uses TOP or OFFSET FETCH, and the standard is FETCH FIRST N ROWS ONLY, while old Oracle used ROWNUM. Always add ORDER BY, otherwise the rows returned are not deterministic. If there may be a tie on the sort column, add a unique tiebreaker or use WITH TIES.

questions.q: What does DISTINCT do, and how is it different from GROUP BY?
questions.ideal: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result across all selected columns. GROUP BY also collapses rows but is meant for aggregate functions such as COUNT or SUM per group. Both need a sort or hash, which affects performance. Adding DISTINCT to fix duplicates is often hiding a bad join, so first check the join conditions.

questions.q: What are CHECK and DEFAULT constraints, and when do you use NOT NULL?
questions.ideal: A CHECK constraint enforces a rule such as price greater than zero, rejecting rows that cause a violation. DEFAULT supplies a default value when an insert omits the column, like the current timestamp or a status. NOT NULL makes a column mandatory. Together they enforce data integrity in the database instead of trusting every application to validate.

questions.q: What is a CROSS JOIN, and how can a missing join condition cause a problem?
questions.ideal: A CROSS JOIN returns the cartesian product, every combination of rows from both tables, so 1000 by 1000 rows gives one million. It is useful intentionally, for example combining a calendar of dates with products. A missing join condition in old comma style joins creates an accidental row explosion, with inflated totals and slow queries.

questions.q: What is a self join, and give an example where you need one?
questions.ideal: A self join joins a table to itself using two different table aliases. The classic example is an employees table where each row has a manager id, so you join employee e to employee m to show each employee with the manager name. A left join keeps the top level person with no manager. It is also used to compare rows or find pairs.

questions.q: How do you copy rows from one table to another, and how do you create a table from a query?
questions.ideal: INSERT INTO target with a column list followed by a SELECT copies rows from a query, optionally with a WHERE filter. CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, or SELECT INTO in SQL Server, creates a new table from the result, often to take a quick backup before a risky update. Note that constraints, indexes and defaults are not copied, only columns and data.

questions.q: Which SQL string functions do you commonly use, and how do you search text case insensitively?
questions.ideal: Common string functions are CONCAT, SUBSTRING, TRIM, REPLACE, UPPER and LOWER, and LENGTH or LEN, where CHAR_LENGTH counts characters rather than bytes. For case insensitive searching you compare LOWER of both sides, use ILIKE in PostgreSQL, or rely on a case insensitive collation as in MySQL defaults. Functions on a column can prevent index use.

questions.q: What do ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL do on a foreign key?
questions.ideal: They are referential actions on a foreign key that decide what happens to child rows when the parent row is deleted. CASCADE deletes the children too, SET NULL clears the reference, and RESTRICT or NO ACTION blocks the delete. Cascade prevents orphan rows but can cause an accidental delete of large amounts of data, so use it carefully.

questions.q: What are temporary tables, and when would you use one instead of a CTE?
questions.ideal: A temporary table lives only for the session or connection and is dropped automatically, like #temp in SQL Server or CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE in MySQL and PostgreSQL. Unlike a CTE, which exists only within one statement, you can reuse it multiple times, add an index and get statistics, which helps break a complex report into steps.

questions.q: How do you calculate a running total and a seven day moving average in SQL?
questions.ideal: Use a window function: SUM of amount OVER with ORDER BY date gives a running total, and PARTITION BY restarts it per customer. For a moving average use AVG OVER ORDER BY date with a window frame ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Be careful that the default frame is RANGE, which treats ties together, so specify ROWS explicitly.

questions.q: What is a collation, and how can it cause problems in comparisons and joins?
questions.ideal: A collation defines how text is compared and sorted, including case sensitivity and accent sensitivity. Different collations change sorting and whether a and A are equal. Joining columns with a collation mismatch causes collation conflict errors in SQL Server or implicit conversion in MySQL, which can stop index use and hurt join performance. Keep collations consistent across the database.

questions.q: What is a materialized view, and how does it differ from a regular view?
questions.ideal: A regular view is virtual and runs its query each time, while a materialized view stores precomputed results on disk, like an indexed view in SQL Server. It makes heavy reporting aggregates fast but must be refreshed, fully or incrementally, so data can be stale between refreshes. PostgreSQL supports REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking readers.

questions.q: How do you find customers who have never placed an order?
questions.ideal: This is an anti join. The best way is NOT EXISTS with a subquery on orders by customer id, or a LEFT JOIN to orders and filtering where the order id IS NULL. Avoid NOT IN if the column can contain nulls, because one null makes the result empty. EXCEPT also works on keys. An index on the orders customer id makes it fast.

questions.q: What are computed or generated columns, and when are they useful?
questions.ideal: A generated or computed column holds a value derived from an expression on other columns, such as total equals price times quantity or lower case email. It can be virtual, computed on read, or stored and persisted on disk. You can often index it to speed searches on expressions, and it keeps consistency because no application logic needs to maintain it.

questions.q: How do you implement text search in a database instead of using LIKE with a leading wildcard?
questions.ideal: LIKE with a leading wildcard cannot use a normal index and scans the whole table. Full text search builds a full text index of words with stemming by language. PostgreSQL uses tsvector and tsquery with a GIN index, MySQL uses a FULLTEXT index with MATCH AGAINST, SQL Server has CONTAINS. They also provide ranking by relevance. For fuzzy search PostgreSQL offers trigram indexes.

questions.q: What is SQL injection, and how do developers prevent it?
questions.ideal: SQL injection happens when user input is put into a query through string concatenation, letting an attacker change the query, for example adding OR 1=1. Prevent it with parameterized queries or prepared statements, which send values separately from the SQL text, or a safe ORM or query builder. Add input validation with whitelists for dynamic column names and least privilege accounts.

questions.q: What is a LATERAL join or CROSS APPLY, and what problem does it solve?
questions.ideal: A LATERAL join, called CROSS APPLY in SQL Server, lets a subquery in the FROM clause be correlated and reference columns of earlier tables. It solves top N per row problems, such as the three latest orders per customer using ORDER BY and LIMIT inside, or calling a table function per row. OUTER APPLY or LEFT JOIN LATERAL keeps rows with no matches.

questions.q: How do you get the latest order for each customer efficiently?
questions.ideal: This is the greatest N per group problem. Use ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order date DESC and keep row 1, or DISTINCT ON in PostgreSQL, or join back to MAX date per customer. Handle ties with a tiebreaker such as order id. A composite index on customer and order date makes it efficient.

questions.q: Why do emojis or some characters fail to save in MySQL, and how do you fix character set problems?
questions.ideal: MySQL utf8 is actually utf8mb3, storing at most three bytes, so four byte characters such as emoji fail or are corrupted. The fix is the utf8mb4 character set with a matching collation on the database, tables and columns, and also the connection or client encoding. Mismatched encoding between application and database causes garbled text, so keep UTF-8 end to end.

questions.q: Should you use UUIDs or auto increment integers as primary keys? Explain the trade offs.
questions.ideal: Auto increment integers are small and sequential, so indexes stay compact, but they expose counts and need a central generator. UUIDs can be generated anywhere, which helps distributed systems and merging data, but they take 16 bytes and random values cause index fragmentation and page splits in clustered indexes. Time ordered UUID v7 or ULID gives most benefits without random insert cost.

questions.q: How do you decide the column order in a composite index?
questions.ideal: A composite index is usable by the leftmost prefix, so the leading column must appear in the query. Put equality conditions first and the range condition last, because columns after a range cannot be used for seeking. Consider selectivity, but query patterns matter more. Adding columns to support ORDER BY or a covering index with INCLUDE can avoid sorts and table lookups.

questions.q: What does it mean for a predicate to be sargable, and give examples of non sargable conditions?
questions.ideal: A sargable predicate can use an index seek. Wrapping a function on a column such as YEAR of order date, implicit conversion from comparing a varchar column to a number, arithmetic on the column, or a leading wildcard LIKE make it non sargable, forcing scans. Rewrite to a date range like order date greater or equal to January first and less than next year, or use expression indexes.

questions.q: What is parameter sniffing, and how do you deal with a stored procedure that is fast for some inputs and slow for others?
questions.ideal: The optimizer builds a cached plan using the first parameter values it sees. With skewed data, a plan good for a rare value is terrible for a common one. Fixes include OPTION RECOMPILE for that statement, OPTIMIZE FOR specific or unknown values, splitting code paths, or using Query Store to force a known good plan. PostgreSQL has similar generic versus custom plan behaviour.

questions.q: What are partial or filtered indexes, and when are they useful?
questions.ideal: A partial or filtered index includes only rows matching a WHERE predicate, such as status equals pending or deleted at is null, so it has a smaller size and cheaper maintenance. It is ideal when queries target a small active subset. It also allows conditional uniqueness, like a unique email only for active users. The query predicate must match the index condition for it to be used.

questions.q: You need to update 50 million rows in a live table. How do you do it safely?
questions.ideal: Running one huge update holds locks for a long time, risks lock escalation, bloats the transaction log or WAL and causes replication lag. Instead update in batches of a few thousand rows by primary key range, committing each chunk, with a throttle pause between them while monitoring lag. Make the job idempotent so it can resume after failure, and test on a copy first.

questions.q: What are the trade offs of soft delete with a deleted flag versus hard delete?
questions.ideal: Soft delete marks rows with a deleted flag or deleted_at, keeping history and allowing undo, while hard delete physically removes them. Soft delete means every query needs a filter, and a forgotten filter leaks deleted data. It breaks unique constraints unless you use a partial index, and the table keeps growing. Alternatives are moving rows to an archive table or audit history.

questions.q: What is the entity attribute value pattern, and why is it often considered an anti pattern?
questions.ideal: Entity attribute value stores each attribute as a row of entity, attribute name and value, giving flexible dynamic attributes. But you lose data types and type safety, cannot enforce constraints or foreign keys, and simple reads need complex queries with many joins or pivots that perform badly. Today a JSONB or JSON column with indexes is usually a better choice for flexible attributes.

questions.q: How do you load millions of rows quickly into a database?
questions.ideal: Use the native bulk load path such as COPY in PostgreSQL, LOAD DATA INFILE in MySQL or BULK INSERT and bcp in SQL Server, instead of row by row inserts; otherwise use multi row batch inserts. Load into a staging table, disable or drop indexes and triggers and re-create them after, defer constraints, and use minimal logging or unlogged tables where recovery allows.

questions.q: A query became slow overnight with no code change. How can statistics be the cause?
questions.ideal: The optimizer uses statistics to estimate cardinality. After large data growth or loads, stats become stale, especially for ascending keys where new dates fall outside the histogram, so estimates show one row while millions exist and the execution plan changes badly. Compare estimated and actual rows in the plan, then run ANALYZE or UPDATE STATISTICS and tune auto stats thresholds.

questions.q: How do you reliably update the database and publish an event to Kafka without losing or duplicating messages?
questions.ideal: Writing to the database and Kafka separately is a dual write and can fail halfway. The transactional outbox pattern inserts the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, so it is atomic. A relay or change data capture tool such as Debezium publishes the rows. Delivery is at least once, so consumers must be idempotent and handle duplicates.

questions.q: Design the database schema for a wallet or payment ledger that must never lose money.
questions.ideal: Use double entry bookkeeping: every transfer writes balanced debit and credit rows to an immutable, append only ledger table, with corrections as new reversing entries rather than updates. The balance is derived from the sum, optionally cached in an account row updated in the same atomic transaction with row locks or serializable isolation. An idempotency key with a unique constraint prevents duplicate payments.

questions.q: How do you design a database to support GDPR deletion requests while keeping reporting and audit data?
questions.ideal: First build a data map of where personal data lives, including copies and logs. Separate PII into dedicated tables so you can delete or anonymize it while keeping pseudonymized facts for reporting. Backups are a challenge, handled by retention limits or crypto shredding, where each user data is encrypted with a key that you delete. Audit legally required records with documented retention.

questions.q: How do you store and query dates and times for a global application with users in many time zones?
questions.ideal: Store instants in UTC using timestamp with time zone types, and convert to the user time zone only at display. For future events like meetings, store the local time plus the IANA zone name, because daylight saving rules can change. Reporting by day must define which time zone sets the day boundary, otherwise daily totals differ by region.

questions.q: When would you move product search from the relational database to Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, and how do you keep them in sync?
questions.ideal: Move search when you need relevance tuning, fuzzy matching, facets and high query volume that full text indexes cannot handle. The relational database stays the source of truth, and you sync changes through CDC or an outbox with an indexing service. The search engine is eventually consistent, so tolerate lag, and design the ability to reindex fully from the database when mappings change.

questions.q: For a new product, how do you decide between a relational database and a NoSQL database?
questions.ideal: Start from access patterns and consistency needs. A relational database gives ACID transactions, joins and flexible ad hoc queries, and Postgres scales far for most products. NoSQL document or key value stores suit known access patterns, schema flexibility and massive horizontal scaling through sharding, but make joins and multi record transactions harder. Also weigh team skills and operations cost.

questions.q: How do you split a shared monolith database when moving to microservices?
questions.ideal: Aim for database per service so each service owns its data, removing coupling of a shared database. Do it incrementally with the strangler approach: identify ownership, make other services use an API or events instead of direct access, then move tables. Cross service joins become API calls or a reporting read model, and lost foreign keys mean referential integrity is handled in application logic during carefully planned migration phases.

questions.q: Design a leaderboard that shows a user rank among millions of players and updates in real time.
questions.ideal: Computing rank with a window function or counting higher scores over millions of rows on every request is too slow. Keep the database as the durable store and use a Redis sorted set for real time rank and top N. In SQL, an index on score helps top lists, and for global rank you can show approximate buckets or percentiles, recomputed periodically and cached.

questions.q: Two systems disagree on order totals at month end. How do you design reconciliation to find and prevent such mismatches?
questions.ideal: Define the system of record, then build an automated daily reconciliation that compares control totals and counts, then records by key using a full outer join to find missing records, duplicates and amount differences. Checksums or hashes of rows speed comparison. Root causes are usually non idempotent retries, time zone cutoffs or failed loads, so fix those and add alerting.

questions.q: How do you keep data consistent across services that each have their own database without two phase commit?
questions.ideal: Two phase commit across services is slow and fragile. Instead use a saga, a sequence of local transactions where each step publishes an event and failures trigger compensating transactions, such as refunding a payment if inventory fails. Coordinate by orchestration with a central coordinator or choreography with events. Accept eventual consistency and make steps idempotent so retries are safe.

questions.q: What does a DBA do, and what is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
questions.ideal: A DBA keeps databases available, secure and fast: backups and recovery, tuning, user access, replication, monitoring and capacity planning. SQL databases are relational with schemas and ACID, NoSQL databases like MongoDB or Redis offer flexible models and horizontal scale.

questions.q: What types of backups exist, and what are RPO and RTO?
questions.ideal: Backups are full, incremental or differential, logical like mysqldump or pg_dump or physical, with point in time recovery from binlogs or WAL. RPO is acceptable data loss, RTO is acceptable downtime, and restores must be tested regularly.

questions.q: Explain replication and high availability in MySQL or PostgreSQL, including failover.
questions.ideal: A primary streams changes (binlog or WAL) to replicas, synchronously or asynchronously with some lag. On failure a replica is promoted using tools like Patroni or Orchestrator, with fencing to avoid split brain, and replicas can serve reads.

questions.q: How do you find slow queries and tune a database server?
questions.ideal: Enable the slow query log or pg_stat_statements, analyse with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, add indexes, tune memory such as the InnoDB buffer pool or shared_buffers, use connection pooling, keep statistics and vacuum healthy and check lock waits.

questions.q: Explain MVCC, VACUUM and WAL in PostgreSQL.
questions.ideal: MVCC keeps multiple row versions so readers do not block writers. VACUUM reclaims dead tuples and prevents bloat and transaction id wraparound, and WAL logs changes before they reach data files for durability, recovery and replication.

questions.q: How do you secure a production database?
questions.ideal: Use least privilege roles, encrypt in transit and at rest, restrict network access, audit access, patch regularly, rotate secrets, encrypt backups and enforce parameterised queries in applications.

questions.q: Compare MongoDB, Redis and Cassandra, and when would you pick each? Explain sharding and consistency.
questions.ideal: MongoDB suits flexible documents with replica sets and sharding on a shard key, Redis is an in memory store for caching, sessions and queues, and Cassandra suits very high write volume with tunable consistency and partition keys. Choose by access pattern and consistency needs under CAP.

questions.q: Production data was corrupted by a bad deployment at 2 pm. How do you recover?
questions.ideal: Stop further damage, communicate, restore the latest backup to a separate instance and replay logs to just before 2 pm (point in time recovery), verify and selectively copy back or switch over, then find the root cause and prevent it, for example with a delayed replica, approvals and migration testing.

questions.q: How do you create users, roles and grant privileges in MySQL or PostgreSQL?
questions.ideal: Create a login with CREATE USER or CREATE ROLE and a strong password. Group privileges into roles for role based access, then GRANT privileges like SELECT or INSERT on specific schemas or tables, and REVOKE them when no longer needed. Follow least privilege, giving applications only what they need, and review access with SHOW GRANTS in MySQL or the du command in psql.

questions.q: What is the difference between a database server, an instance, a database and a schema?
questions.ideal: An instance is the running server process with its memory and background processes listening on a port. A database is a set of data files holding objects. A schema is a namespace grouping tables and views inside a database. In PostgreSQL one cluster, a single data directory, holds many databases each with schemas, while in MySQL a schema equals a database.

questions.q: What is the difference between InnoDB and MyISAM in MySQL, and why is InnoDB the default?
questions.ideal: InnoDB is the default because it supports ACID transactions, row level locking for concurrency, foreign keys and automatic crash recovery using its redo log. MyISAM is a legacy engine with only table level locking, no transactions and no foreign keys, and it can corrupt after a crash. MyISAM was once used for full text search or read heavy tables, but InnoDB now covers those.

questions.q: A developer cannot connect to the PostgreSQL server. What do you check?
questions.ideal: First check the error message and server logs, and that the service is running. Confirm listen_addresses allows remote connections and the port, usually 5432, is open in the firewall or security group. Check pg_hba.conf has a host based authentication line for that user, database and IP with the right method like scram or md5, then reload. Finally confirm the role exists with a correct password.

questions.q: What daily health checks does a DBA perform on production databases?
questions.ideal: Each day I confirm backup status and that the last backup succeeded, check disk space and growth trends, verify replication status and lag, review the error log for failures, and look for long running queries or blocking. I also check CPU, memory and connection counts on the monitoring dashboard and make sure alerts are working and acknowledged.

questions.q: Which configuration files and key parameters would you look at first on a new MySQL or PostgreSQL server?
questions.ideal: In MySQL I check my.cnf, especially innodb_buffer_pool_size, max_connections and the slow query log. In PostgreSQL I check postgresql.conf, especially shared_buffers, work_mem, effective_cache_size, max_connections and log settings like log_min_duration_statement. Some parameters are dynamic and need only a reload, while others like the buffer pool size in older versions or shared_buffers require a restart.

questions.q: What routine maintenance tasks do you schedule on a database?
questions.ideal: I schedule statistics updates with ANALYZE so the optimizer has fresh information, index rebuild or REINDEX for fragmentation and bloat, VACUUM or OPTIMIZE TABLE, log rotation and purging old binlogs, and regular backup verification with a restore test. Patching with minor updates happens in an agreed maintenance window, and jobs run through cron or a scheduler with alerts on failure.

questions.q: What is a tablespace, and how do you handle a database running out of disk space?
questions.ideal: A tablespace maps database objects to a storage location such as a directory of data files. When disk space runs low, monitoring should alert early. You can extend the volume or add a disk, move large tables or indexes to another tablespace, purge old logs or archive old data, and then review the growth trend for proper capacity planning.

questions.q: How do you plan and apply a minor version patch to a production database with minimal risk?
questions.ideal: Read the release notes for bug fixes and known issues, apply the patch in a test environment or staging and run application tests. Take a backup before upgrade. In production do a rolling upgrade, patching the replica or standby first, then a planned switchover so the primary is patched last, inside a maintenance window. Verify health after and keep a rollback plan ready.

questions.q: Why do you need a connection pooler like PgBouncer or ProxySQL, and what pooling modes exist?
questions.ideal: Each PostgreSQL connection is a process using memory, so thousands of idle app connections exhaust max_connections and RAM. A pooler like PgBouncer, or ProxySQL for MySQL, shares a few server connections. Session pooling assigns one per client session, transaction pooling returns it after each transaction and scales best, and statement pooling after each statement. Transaction pooling has limitations with prepared statements and session features.

questions.q: How do you find unused, duplicate or bloated indexes, and why does it matter?
questions.ideal: Every index adds write overhead and storage, so unused and duplicate indexes should go. In PostgreSQL check idx_scan in pg_stat_user_indexes, and in MySQL use the sys schema view schema_unused_indexes and redundant index reports. Bloat and fragmentation make indexes larger and slower. Fix with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY or an online rebuild, and confirm with developers before dropping any index.

questions.q: How do you investigate deadlocks in MySQL InnoDB?
questions.ideal: Run SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS to see the latest detected deadlock with both transactions, their queries and the locks held and waited for. Enable innodb_print_all_deadlocks to log every deadlock in the error log. Common causes are inconsistent lock order and missing indexes that cause gap locks on ranges. Fix by indexing, keeping short transactions, consistent order and adding retry logic in the application.

questions.q: The database server disk is 98 percent full and growing. What do you do immediately and afterwards?
questions.ideal: Find what is growing with du. Often it is logs, WAL or binlogs not being removed, for example an inactive replication slot holding WAL, failed archiving, or temp files from a large query. Purge safely through the database, such as PURGE BINARY LOGS or dropping the stale slot, never deleting files by hand. Extend the volume if needed, then fix the root cause and lower the alert threshold.

questions.q: How does a MongoDB replica set work, including elections, write concern and read preference?
questions.ideal: A replica set has one primary taking writes and secondaries that replicate its oplog. If the primary fails, members hold an election and the node with a majority of votes becomes primary, giving automatic failover, so use an odd number of members or an arbiter. Write concern w majority confirms writes reached most nodes. Read preference decides whether reads go to secondaries.

questions.q: How does Redis persist data, and what is the difference between RDB and AOF?
questions.ideal: Redis is in memory but persists through RDB snapshots at intervals, which are compact and fast to load but can lose recent data. AOF, the append only file, logs every write with fsync set to always, everysec or no, giving better durability with larger files that BGREWRITEAOF compacts. Many setups use both, a hybrid, so restart recovery is fast and data loss small.

questions.q: How do you set up monitoring and alerting for databases? Which metrics matter most?
questions.ideal: I use Prometheus with database exporters and Grafana dashboards, or tools like PMM, Datadog or CloudWatch. Key metrics are connections and active sessions, query latency and throughput, replication lag, disk usage, IOPS, CPU, cache hit ratio and locks. Alerting uses sensible thresholds and routes critical issues to PagerDuty for the on call DBA, while warnings go to chat.

questions.q: Explain the InnoDB buffer pool, redo log, undo log and doublewrite buffer.
questions.ideal: The buffer pool caches data and index pages in memory. Changes are written first to the redo log for crash recovery, and dirty pages are flushed later at checkpoints. The undo log holds old versions for rollback and MVCC reads. The doublewrite buffer protects against torn pages from partial writes. innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit trades durability for speed, and the change buffer delays secondary index updates.

questions.q: How do shared_buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem and effective_cache_size affect PostgreSQL performance?
questions.ideal: shared_buffers is PostgreSQL's own cache, often around 25 percent of RAM. work_mem is used per sort or hash operation, so too low causes temp files that spill to disk, but too high multiplied by many connections risks out of memory. maintenance_work_mem speeds VACUUM and CREATE INDEX. effective_cache_size is only a planner estimate of OS cache that influences index choices.

questions.q: What is the difference between physical and logical replication, and when would you use logical replication or CDC?
questions.ideal: Physical replication streams WAL at byte level and copies the whole cluster to an identical version. Logical replication decodes row changes, so you can choose tables through publication and subscription and replicate across versions, useful for a major version upgrade or migration. CDC tools like Debezium read the same stream into Kafka. Replication slots retain WAL, and DDL is not replicated, which are its limitations.

questions.q: How do you add a column or index to a 500 GB MySQL table in production without locking it?
questions.ideal: First check if MySQL online DDL supports it with ALGORITHM INSTANT or INPLACE. Otherwise use pt-online-schema-change, which copies rows into a shadow table and keeps it in sync with triggers, or gh-ost, which is trigger free and reads the binlog. Both throttle on replication lag and finish with an atomic cutover rename, which needs a short metadata lock, so run it off peak.

questions.q: A read replica is lagging by 30 minutes. How do you troubleshoot it?
questions.ideal: Check the lag metric, then look for a large transaction like a bulk update being applied. In MySQL single threaded apply is common, so enable parallel replication workers, and tables without a primary key make row based replication very slow. Check replica resources like disk IO and CPU, the network bandwidth, and in PostgreSQL long queries on the replica causing conflicts with hot_standby_feedback settings.

questions.q: Explain Galera Cluster or MySQL Group Replication. What are their trade offs compared to async replication?
questions.ideal: Galera and MySQL Group Replication give virtually synchronous replication where each transaction passes certification on all nodes, allowing multi primary or single primary modes with no data loss on failover. Trade offs are write conflicts causing certification failure on hot rows, the need for quorum with at least three nodes to avoid split brain, higher latency over WAN, flow control slowdowns and limits on large transactions.

questions.q: What are the trade offs of using a managed database like Amazon RDS or Aurora instead of self managed databases on VMs?
questions.ideal: Managed services such as RDS, Aurora or Cloud SQL handle automated backups, patching, monitoring and multi AZ failover, reducing DBA toil. Trade offs include no superuser or OS access, limited extensions, configuration only through parameter groups, higher cost for storage and IOPS, and some vendor lock in, especially with Aurora specific features. Self managed VMs give full control but more operational work.

questions.q: Redis memory is full and clients get OOM errors. How do you handle it?
questions.ideal: Check maxmemory and the eviction policy; for a cache use allkeys lru so old keys are evicted instead of OOM errors. Ensure keys have a TTL so they expire. Find big keys with redis-cli bigkeys or MEMORY USAGE, check the memory fragmentation ratio, and remember RDB fork uses copy on write memory. Long term, scale out with Redis Cluster shards or a larger node.

questions.q: How would you upgrade a large PostgreSQL database from version 12 to 16 with minimal downtime?
questions.ideal: pg_upgrade in link mode with hard links finishes in minutes but needs downtime and makes rollback harder. For near zero downtime, set up the new version as a logical replication subscriber, sync data, then do a quick cutover, while dump and restore is too slow for large databases. Check extension compatibility, rehearse in staging, run ANALYZE after the upgrade to rebuild statistics, and plan rollback.

questions.q: Your company wants to migrate from Oracle to PostgreSQL to save licensing costs. How do you plan it?
questions.ideal: Start with an assessment of schemas, PL/SQL volume and features using ora2pg or AWS SCT to estimate complexity. Convert schema and data types such as NUMBER and VARCHAR2, and rewrite PL/SQL to PL/pgSQL, handling packages, sequences and empty string versus null differences. Migrate data with bulk load plus CDC through DMS, run functional and performance regression testing, then plan cutover with rollback or a parallel run.

questions.q: How do you do capacity planning for a database expected to grow ten times in two years?
questions.ideal: Collect historical metrics to build a growth trend and forecast storage, CPU, memory, IOPS and connections against business projections. Run a load test or benchmark with pgbench or sysbench at future volumes to find bottlenecks. Keep headroom of about 30 percent above peak. Plan when to scale up, add read replicas or sharding, and use archiving and retention policies to control cost.

questions.q: Design a database setup for an application serving users in India, Europe and the US with low latency and regional failure tolerance.
questions.ideal: A simple design keeps one primary region for writes with cross region read replicas for local reads, accepting write latency and failover with some RPO. True active active needs multi master with conflict resolution or distributed SQL like CockroachDB, Spanner or YugabyteDB using consensus. Consider data residency rules like GDPR by partitioning users per region, and test regional failover, DNS changes, RPO and RTO.

questions.q: Would you run production databases on Kubernetes? How do operators help, and what are the risks?
questions.ideal: It is viable with mature operators such as CloudNativePG, Zalando, Crunchy or the Percona operator, which manage StatefulSets, persistent volumes, automated failover and backups declaratively. Risks are storage performance on network storage, added complexity and the need for Kubernetes expertise. Use anti affinity across nodes and zones, pod disruption budgets, tested backups and local or high IOPS disks for critical databases.

questions.q: During a sale, database CPU suddenly hits 100 percent and the site slows down. Walk through your response.
questions.ideal: Declare an incident and keep communication going with stakeholders. Look at active sessions through pg_stat_activity or the processlist and top queries by CPU, checking for a new deployment, a plan change or a missing index. Kill or cancel runaway queries, limit a connection spike through the pooler, add an index concurrently, and offload reads to replicas or cache. Afterwards run a postmortem on root cause and add load tests.

questions.q: How do you design backups for a 20 TB database where a full backup takes too long?
questions.ideal: Use incremental or differential block level backups with tools like pgBackRest, Barman or XtraBackup, with parallel jobs and compression, plus continuous WAL archiving or binlog streaming for point in time recovery. Storage snapshots such as EBS snapshots give fast consistent copies. Take backups from a replica to offload the primary. Regularly do a restore test to prove the RTO is achievable and verify integrity.

questions.q: Developers want a copy of production data for testing. How do you provide it safely?
questions.ideal: Never hand over raw production PII. Build an automated pipeline that restores a backup into an isolated environment, applies data masking to anonymize names, emails, phones and card data while keeping referential integrity consistent, and optionally takes a subset to keep it smaller. This meets compliance like GDPR, India's DPDP Act and PCI. Synthetic data suits highly sensitive fields, and access control still applies to the copy.

questions.q: How do pg_dump and mysqldump work, and what are their limitations?
questions.ideal: pg_dump and mysqldump create a logical backup of SQL statements or an archive. pg_dump is consistent through a snapshot, and mysqldump with single transaction is consistent for InnoDB; pg_dumpall adds roles. They are portable across versions, but restore time is slow because indexes are rebuilt, so for large databases physical backups are preferred, and logical dumps cannot do point in time recovery.

questions.q: How do you see what queries are running right now and stop a runaway query?
questions.ideal: In PostgreSQL query pg_stat_activity to see each session, its state, query and how long running. In MySQL use SHOW PROCESSLIST or performance schema. To stop a query, use pg_cancel_backend to cancel only the statement, or pg_terminate_backend to kill the connection; in MySQL use KILL QUERY or KILL. Confirm with the owner first.

questions.q: How do you enable and use the slow query log?
questions.ideal: In MySQL set slow_query_log on with long_query_time as the threshold, optionally logging queries not using indexes. In PostgreSQL set log_min_duration_statement. Then analyze the log with pt-query-digest or pgBadger to rank queries by total time. Keep the threshold sensible because logging everything adds overhead and fills the disk.

questions.q: Where do you look first when a database will not start, and what do you look for?
questions.ideal: Check the error log first: the PostgreSQL log directory or journalctl for the service, and the MySQL error log or .err file. Typical causes are a config syntax error after a change, wrong permissions or ownership on the data directory, the port already in use, disk full, or memory settings larger than the server. Fix the cause and restart.

questions.q: How do you check the size of databases, tables and indexes, and find the biggest objects?
questions.ideal: In PostgreSQL use pg_database_size and pg_total_relation_size with pg_size_pretty, ordering by size to list the largest tables including indexes. In MySQL query information_schema tables, summing data_length and index_length. Record these values regularly to see the growth trend, which feeds capacity planning and spotting bloat or runaway log tables.

questions.q: Why should backups be regularly restored and tested, and how do you do it?
questions.ideal: A backup that has never been restored is untested and may be corrupt or incomplete. Automate scheduled restore tests into a separate server, then verify with checksums, row counts and application queries. Measure how long it takes to confirm the RTO can be met, and keep a documented runbook so anyone on call can perform the restore under pressure.

questions.q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP workloads, and how does it affect database configuration?
questions.ideal: OLTP workloads have many short transactions reading and writing few rows, needing normalized tables, good indexes and many connections. OLAP or analytical workloads run large scans and aggregations over history, favouring columnar storage, a data warehouse, more memory per query and parallelism. Mixing heavy reporting on the OLTP primary hurts users, so offload it to replicas or a warehouse.

questions.q: How do you safely restart a PostgreSQL or MySQL server, and what shutdown modes exist?
questions.ideal: PostgreSQL pg_ctl has smart mode, which waits for clients, fast mode, which rolls back transactions and disconnects cleanly with a checkpoint, and immediate mode, which aborts and needs crash recovery on start. MySQL uses systemctl or mysqladmin shutdown, with innodb_fast_shutdown controlling how much cleanup happens. Use fast for planned restarts and announce a maintenance window.

questions.q: What is a blocking session, and how do you find who is blocking whom?
questions.ideal: Blocking happens when one session holds a lock that another needs, so the second waits. In PostgreSQL use pg_blocking_pids with pg_stat_activity or pg_locks; in MySQL use the sys schema innodb_lock_waits view or innodb_trx and data_lock_waits. Often the blocker is idle in transaction, an open transaction an application forgot to commit. Fix the code; terminate it in an emergency.

questions.q: How should a DBA handle changes on production databases?
questions.ideal: Every production change should go through a change request with peer review and approval, tested first in staging. Plan a rollback or backout plan, take a backup or snapshot before, schedule a maintenance window if there is risk, and follow a written runbook. Afterwards verify and update documentation, so changes are traceable during incidents.

questions.q: How does point in time recovery work in PostgreSQL or MySQL?
questions.ideal: Point in time recovery restores a base backup and then replays logs up to a chosen moment. In PostgreSQL you need WAL archiving with archive_command or a tool such as pgBackRest, then set recovery_target_time. In MySQL you restore the backup and apply binary log events with mysqlbinlog until the position before the bad statement. It needs continuous, tested log archives.

questions.q: What are GTIDs in MySQL replication, and why are they better than file and position replication?
questions.ideal: A GTID is a global transaction identifier, unique for each committed transaction. With binlog file and position, repointing replicas after failover requires calculating coordinates. With GTID and auto position, a replica tells the new source which transactions it has and gets the rest automatically. Watch for errant transactions executed directly on replicas, which break failover.

questions.q: What is pg_stat_statements, and how do you use it to find the most expensive queries?
questions.ideal: pg_stat_statements is an extension loaded through shared_preload_libraries. It aggregates normalized queries, with constants replaced, and records calls, total_exec_time, mean time, rows and buffer usage. Sorting by total time finds the queries consuming most of the server, which often are fast but very frequent. Reset periodically with pg_stat_statements_reset to measure a fresh window.

questions.q: What is a checkpoint, and how does checkpoint tuning affect performance?
questions.ideal: A checkpoint flushes dirty pages from memory to data files, so crash recovery only replays WAL since the last checkpoint. Frequent checkpoints cause IO spikes and more full page writes, increasing WAL volume. In PostgreSQL raise max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout and spread writes with checkpoint_completion_target, accepting longer recovery time. Logs warning that checkpoints occur too frequently signal tuning is needed.

questions.q: Which timeout settings protect a database from runaway queries and stuck transactions?
questions.ideal: statement_timeout in PostgreSQL or max_execution_time in MySQL kill runaway queries. lock_timeout and innodb_lock_wait_timeout limit waiting on locks, which is important for DDL. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ends sessions holding open transactions, and wait_timeout closes idle connections. Set these per role or per user, for example strict for web users and looser for reporting.

questions.q: How do you enable database auditing to track who changed or read sensitive data?
questions.ideal: In PostgreSQL use the pgaudit extension to log DDL, DML or reads on selected objects and roles; in MySQL use an audit plugin like MySQL Enterprise Audit or Percona audit log. Capture logins and privileged actions. Ship logs to a central SIEM so DBAs cannot alter them, and scope auditing carefully because logging everything adds performance cost and huge volume.

questions.q: How do you enforce encrypted TLS connections to a database server?
questions.ideal: Configure the server with a certificate from a trusted CA and enable SSL. Enforce it with hostssl rules in pg_hba.conf or require_secure_transport in MySQL, or require SSL per user. Clients should use sslmode verify-full to check server identity, not just encrypt. Track certificate expiry and plan rotation, since expired certificates cause outages.

questions.q: How do you analyze and index slow queries in MongoDB?
questions.ideal: Run explain with executionStats to see whether the query uses a COLLSCAN collection scan or an IXSCAN, and compare docs examined to documents returned. Build a compound index following the ESR rule: equality fields first, then sort, then range. The database profiler or slow ops log finds problem queries, and Atlas Performance Advisor suggests indexes.

questions.q: What are physical backup tools like pgBackRest and Percona XtraBackup, and why use them over dumps?
questions.ideal: Physical backup tools copy data files, so backup and restore are much faster than logical dumps for large databases. pgBackRest and Barman for PostgreSQL and Percona XtraBackup for MySQL take a hot backup online, support incremental or differential backups, compression, parallel processing and integration with WAL or binlogs for point in time recovery.

questions.q: What are the MySQL binary log formats, and which would you choose?
questions.ideal: Statement based logging records SQL statements, which is compact but unsafe for non deterministic statements like those using UUID or LIMIT without ORDER BY, causing replica drift. Row based logging records changed rows, which is safe and needed for CDC but increases volume; binlog_row_image minimal reduces size. Mixed switches automatically. Row is the default and the usual choice.

questions.q: What is transaction ID wraparound in PostgreSQL, and how do you prevent it?
questions.ideal: PostgreSQL uses 32 bit transaction IDs, so old rows must be frozen by VACUUM FREEZE before the counter wraps around. Autovacuum does this, but long transactions, disabled autovacuum or huge tables can fall behind. Monitor age of datfrozenxid and relfrozenxid. If it gets too close, PostgreSQL stops writes to protect data, causing an outage, so tune autovacuum and freeze proactively.

questions.q: How do tools like Patroni or Orchestrator provide automatic failover, and how do they avoid split brain?
questions.ideal: Patroni uses a distributed consensus store such as etcd as a leader lock; only the node holding the lease is primary, and if it loses the lock it demotes itself, which prevents split brain. Orchestrator detects MySQL failures and promotes the best replica. Fencing ensures an old primary cannot accept writes, and HAProxy, a virtual IP or DNS handles routing clients to the new primary.

questions.q: How do you detect and remove table bloat in PostgreSQL without long locks?
questions.ideal: Bloat comes from dead tuples that autovacuum cannot reclaim fast enough, often due to long transactions holding the xmin horizon. Measure with pgstattuple or bloat estimate queries. VACUUM FULL takes an exclusive lock, so instead use pg_repack or pg_squeeze, which rebuild the table online. Then prevent recurrence with autovacuum tuning, lower scale factors per table and killing long transactions.

questions.q: How do you choose a shard key for MongoDB or another sharded database?
questions.ideal: A good shard key has high cardinality and even write distribution, and appears in most queries so they are targeted rather than scatter gather. A monotonic key like a timestamp sends all inserts to one hot shard, so use hashed sharding or a compound key. Range sharding helps range queries. Choose carefully because resharding is expensive, though newer MongoDB supports it online.

questions.q: An ALTER TABLE on PostgreSQL hung and suddenly all queries on that table blocked. What happened, and how do you avoid it?
questions.ideal: ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. A long running query or transaction held a conflicting lock, so the ALTER waited, and every new query queued behind the ALTER in the lock queue, causing an outage. Always set a short lock_timeout before DDL and retry in a loop, and check for long transactions first.

questions.q: How do you automate partition maintenance for a large time series table?
questions.ideal: Use range partitioning by time and automate it with pg_partman or a scheduled job through pg_cron. The job premakes future partitions so inserts never fail, and enforces retention by detaching and dropping old partitions, which is instant compared with deleting rows. Monitor the default partition, which catches rows outside ranges and can slow down attaching new partitions.

questions.q: What are tombstones in Cassandra, and why can they cause slow reads or failures?
questions.ideal: In Cassandra a delete or TTL expiry writes a tombstone marker instead of removing data. Reads must scan tombstones until compaction removes them after gc_grace_seconds. Using a table as a queue with frequent deletes creates many tombstones, causing slow reads and errors once tombstone_failure_threshold is hit. Fix the data model, use time windowed compaction and avoid that anti pattern.

questions.q: What is the difference between Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster?
questions.ideal: Redis Sentinel monitors a single primary with replicas and performs automatic failover, telling clients the new primary, but does not shard. Redis Cluster provides sharding across nodes using 16384 hash slots plus built in failover. Cluster needs a cluster aware client and restricts multi key operations to the same slot, avoiding cross slot errors by using hash tags.

questions.q: What operating system settings matter for database servers?
questions.ideal: Disable transparent huge pages, which cause latency spikes, but configure explicit huge pages for large shared buffers. Set low swappiness to avoid swapping, raise ulimit file descriptors, use XFS or ext4 with noatime and a suitable IO scheduler, handle NUMA interleaving, and configure memory overcommit so the OOM killer does not kill the database.

questions.q: What is semi synchronous replication in MySQL, and what trade offs does it bring?
questions.ideal: With semi synchronous replication a commit waits until at least one replica acknowledges receiving the events into its relay log, reducing data loss risk on failover compared with asynchronous. The trade off is added commit latency, especially across regions. If no replica answers within the timeout it falls back to async, which must be monitored. After sync, lossless mode prevents phantom reads.

questions.q: How do you protect database backups against ransomware or a malicious insider?
